en: Preface to the *Jiaokan yichao*, composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Yuanzhao of Yuhang Prefecture.
This commentary has been transmitted through the world for a long time; some have provided annotated explanations, while others have transmitted it orally, yet [the text] has been lost...
The Sage’s legacy is remote and humanity is of meager virtue; the milk within the city has gradually strayed from its truth, while the verses in the forest have been handed down in error.
Consequently, the Great Compassionate One’s preserved instructions have long had their spirit obscured, leaving later descendants at a loss for where to seek the path.

Therefore, having spent many years in deep study and traveling everywhere to search for them, I desire to broaden my own knowledge and见闻 (jiànwén—what is seen and heard) and shall, accordingly, provide a critical exposition and clarification. Now...
In this preface, I have roughly set forth three sections so that the wise who examine them may understand more than half of what needs to be considered.
First, the intent behind composing this work; second, the refutation of ancient dissenting opinions; and third, the correction of discrepancies among various editions. Regarding the first:

the Vinaya is the teaching of the Buddha, its title signifying the "explanation of practice. Practice depends upon ritual procedures (*dharmas*), and regarding these ritual forms, the virtuous masters of antiquity—

Failing to exhaustively fathom this essential principle, [other commentators] vied with one another to compose commentaries (*yishu*), extensively citing verbose and redundant terminology. Only our own Founding Master transcended these various views;

he edited, excised, and supplemented [the texts] to manifest the practice of worldly affairs, arranging them in systematic detail under the two categories of "Observance" (*chi*) and "Conduct" (*xing*).

Thus, the *Gaoseng Faxian Zhuchi Shigao* (The Record of the Conduct of the High Monk Faxian) stands foremost among his works. Furthermore, since "Observance" requires brevity and concision, while "Conduct" must rely upon exemplary models, [he did not compose a separate work for the latter].
The Chapter on the Broad Meaning merely extends the orthodox model directly. Thus, the holy teachings are vast and far-reaching, while their ultimate principles are profound and subtle.

Whether they be deep texts that remain hidden or the causes for their decline or flourishing, all are nothing other than the correct teaching; how could one worry about the multiplicity of paths? Study must be gentle and patient, yet its meaning requires refinement.
For this reason, I have compiled these essential meanings and recorded them as a separate chapter; such is the emergence of this work.

This is, however, the next best [option]. Thus we know that the *Shishi yaoyong chao* (Essentials for Practice) and the *Yiyi chao* (Explication of Meaning) are like the obverse and reverse of a single surface, mutually supporting one another.

Without the *Shishi yaoyong chao*, practice would have nothing to rely upon, thereby losing the foundation of the teaching; without the *Yiyi chao*, understanding would have no means to dispel ignorance regarding future expositions.

Examining their titles, they are divided into two parts, yet in reality they represent the simultaneous elevation of both practice and understanding; the intent behind the composition of these two treatises lies precisely here. Some say:
Regarding the compilation of the未尽之義 (unexhausted meanings) from the two commentaries on the *Śīla* and *Karma*, I have previously compared them;

since their textual meanings largely coincide, where they do not exhaust the subject matter, one may simply pick up what was omitted. How could there be a need for mutual redundancy? Thus, we know this is not the case.
As for the claim that it serves as a "basis" (*zhāngběn*) for the two commentaries: the three categories (*sānbù*) pointed out by the *Shìchāo* are already manifest; how could this be so?
This work is a rough and preliminary draft; those who study our school must examine it with great care. Should any doubts arise, one may attempt to cite authentic evidence.
The *Xingyi* (Explanatory Notes) states: "In every instance of citation, I have first subjected them to repeated verification.

Regarding individual points, there are many discarded positions and the various masters' subjective views are extensive and manifold; I have now deleted these all at once, retaining only the textual evidence."

(Regarding this, the *Xiaxu Yijiao* [Commentary on the Meaning of the Preface to the *Shishi Yaolan*] states: "Furthermore, as for the teachings that extend to other treatises, their principles and characteristics are difficult to comprehend; were it not for one of universal understanding, how could they be fully investigated?
This is as extensively revealed in the *Jiyi Chao* [Commentary on the Collected Meanings]," which cites these textual proofs.

Moreover, regarding the subsequent clarification of the meaning of ignorance regarding the observance and violation of precepts when one has not studied, the two commentaries (*Chao*) remain largely identical; however, upon reaching the two sub-commentaries (*Su*), there begin to be many points of modification and supplementation, or even instances of abolition."
That there were previously not just one such work is proven by this meaning.

Furthermore, the *Shìshāo* (Matters Commentary) was compiled at the end of the Wǔdé era (the ninth year), while this present commentary was composed at the beginning of the Zhēnguān era (the first year). The span of years between them is sufficient to demonstrate that they were contemporaneous;

moreover, it was during the Zhēnguān period that the two commentaries (*Jièshū* in the eighth year and *Yèshū* in the ninth year) were first established, which shows that what was said previously regarding the "incompleteness" of the *Shìshū* [was not so].
Is this not free from error? This is a verification based on the timing [of the texts]. Furthermore, Master Fabao (Xuanchang) annotated it, saying:

"This commentary was composed by the Patriarch Nanshan at the beginning of the dynasty to assist in the explanation of the *Xingshichao*. According to what is clarified herein, one attains its true essence.
Since it is called 'assisting in the explanation,' the meaning of mutual support is as clear as a double halo; moreover, it points to the beginning of the dynasty and shares the same origin."

The phrasing of this text is as if it were a perfect seal meeting its impression; this serves as a citation of ancient authority to provide proof. Regarding the resolution of doubts and the reconciliation of differences, the details are contained in a separate treatise.

Second, concerning the refutation of ancient dissenting views, the *Tonghui Senglü* (Zanning) evaluates this *Chao* [the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*] as having three characteristics that establish it was certainly composed prior to the *Shishi yaolan*:
first, its literary style is coarse and simple, with many instances of "initial explanations" (*shoujie*); second, the composition is incomplete, leaving certain sections buried or missing.

The title lacks a preface to introduce what precedes it and an afterword to conclude what follows; thirdly, it merely provides a summary to prevent forgetfulness and briefly indicates the chapters of the meaning, simply stating "I shall now lecture," etc.
Although ancient records sought to rectify this, how could they succeed when the principles are meager while the phrasing is rambling?

Furthermore, not knowing the origin of one's doubts is truly for a reason. Having repeatedly reflected on these words three times, I privately find them unsatisfactory; thus, I have [addressed] them in detail.
I have examined this work to ensure there is no further confusion. To trace its origins, this *Chao* (Excerpts) was compiled by gathering the commentaries (*zhangshu*) of various masters;
the compositions of the ancient worthies directly express their intended meanings without striving for ornate embellishment.

I have now followed those original texts to prune and record the essentials, adding refinement only at the commencement of the two commentaries. Compared to the great canonical works, the language and principles herein are elegant and well-balanced.
In collating and verifying this work, how could one possibly harbor doubts? Furthermore, among the compositions of successive generations, there are only about twenty schools;

the interpretations of other masters merely provide a general overview of past exegeses. As for the commentaries, only the Great Commentary (*Mahāṭīkā*) of the Primary Master possesses a profound and far-reaching principle that serves as our current standard.

Therefore, his name alone is prominently displayed to distinguish it from other doctrines. This is truly based on a fundamental source of reliance and does not obscure the lineage of its transmission.
Moreover, as for the words at the beginning of the commentary, they were intended to be concise and essential; what substance could there possibly be [in them]?

That he should immediately point out and criticize them is the first thing that cannot be accepted. Furthermore, when examining ancient versions, it is true—as you have said—that the beginning and end are incomplete, the chapters are out of order, and the names and eras are not apparent.
Nevertheless, one still cannot condemn the author; therefore, I shall now briefly provide several points of consideration.
I sought it and found it recorded that as soon as the draft was completed, it was stolen by another; I had no leisure to revise and compile it, which is one reason for my previous communication.
Furthermore, during the decline of the Tang dynasty and the chaos of the Five Dynasties, the world was in turmoil and the monastic community dispersed;

consequently, the scriptures and teachings of the various schools were damaged and incomplete—this is the second reason. Moreover, the dissemination of the Patriarchal Teachings is fundamentally based upon...
Third, from the regions of Guanzhong and Jiangzhe to this distant place, spanning several thousand *li*, as the texts were transmitted here, errors and omissions are beyond our knowledge.

Furthermore, since the composition [of these works] until the present day, a vast span of time has elapsed; whether through scribal omissions during transcription or the physical disintegration of paper and silk, for example, the text of the *Guījìng yí* lacks its introductory preface.
Compared to the lost portions of the Confucian classics such as the *Shū* and the *Lǐ*, this is even more lamentable.
Furthermore, how much more so in this case, where the practices seen [in the text] are still incomplete; could the lower fascicle not serve as a verification? These are the four points of intent.

Yet, since he has not yet examined them thoroughly, it is improper for him to disparage them so lightly; these two points are unacceptable. Moreover, the authors of such compositions do not follow a single method.

Here, I have merely gathered related categories of meaning without establishing formal headings, summarizing them according to their essential principles. Furthermore, there are no appended commentaries; I have simply set forth the headings.
I have expounded the essential sections as major topical divisions, distinguishing between what is acceptable and what is not by examining the differences and agreements among various schools;

I have set forth successive difficult questions to dispel deep-seated doubts, ensuring that the terminology and meaning remain perfectly intact. This is not merely for the purpose of providing a personal memorandum;

rather, based on these aforementioned intentions, I have refuted those three types [of interpretations] to demonstrate that former masters never previously discussed them, and that those who merely transmit and recite [the texts] have never actually practiced them.
Regarding the third section on the discrepancies among the various editions, there are three distinct differences. First, concerning the analysis of the various editions:

the edition collated and annotated by the Tiantai Vinaya Master (Yunkan) consists of three fascicles and is currently in circulation. Later, an ancient edition was obtained, which contains only the first two fascicles (the upper and middle).
When compared with the three-fascicle version, the beginning and end are identical; thus, I have long harbored doubts but had no place to seek a resolution until recently.
In Yongjia, I obtained one copy in four fascicles from the late Vinaya Master Changning (Wentu). He had personally divided each of the first two [fascicles] into two parts.
On the manuscript itself, he had inscribed: "According to the *Fǎbǎo Mùlù*, there were three fascicles; now only two have been recovered.

Examining this statement closely and further consulting his later notes, I finally learned that when the text was sent back from the Eastern Barbarians (Japan), there were originally three fascicles, including the lower fascicle.
That [the text] alone was lost and did not transmit to the region south of the Yangtze River does not mean it was originally non-existent.

Later generations, failing to understand its classification within the *Zhong* (Middle) category as being "inferior," merely included it in the count of the catalog; how could they know that the loss lay in its failure to reach its original purpose rather than in its subsequent transmission?

Furthermore, having carefully examined the various sections, the omissions and abridgments are pointed out in the *Yìchāo* (Explanatory Notes), yet many passages do not appear therein precisely for this reason. When the masters of the various commentaries (*zhāngjì*) speak thus at random:

The criticism that the text lacks citations from other sources stems from a failure to understand how to properly edit it; consequently, much of the commentary was written with superficial haste. Now, following the ancient manuscript, we retain only the first two fascicles (the Middle and Upper).
Fearing that these alone would be too voluminous, we have divided them into four parts, leaving the final fascicle incomplete for future supplementation.

Regarding the formal title, many editions seen here throughout the past and present all state: *The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, in One Hundred Fascicles, Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.* ... [as stated] in various ancient and modern versions.

Regarding the *Shi-bin-yi-chao* (Notes on the Meaning of the Vinaya) for the *Sifen-lü*, while the edition from Yongjia alone refers to it as the *Shi-bin-yi-yao* (Essentials of the Vinaya Notes), although their underlying principles are consistent, they differ in being either complete or incomplete.
Furthermore, there are many variations in the titles indicated by the *Shi-sa-chao* (Notes on the Rituals):

some refer to it as the *Ji-yi-chao* (Notes on Collected Meanings), some simply as the *Yi-chao* (Meaning Notes), all of which are abbreviated forms; others refer to it as the *Bie-chao* (Separate Notes), indicating it is not the same [as the aforementioned].
Regarding the section: for now, we follow the majority as it appears in the title of the text. Furthermore, according to Tonghui, the name was buried and the era passed away;

one can verify that there was originally no author’s colophon at the beginning of the scroll, which was added by later generations, though it remains here today. As for the sequence of the "Three Certainties" (San ding pin):
from the beginning of the upper fascicle to the end of the middle fascicle, there are a total of sixteen sections, each marked with a heading at its start.

Although there is no sequential outline for the lecture, various ancient manuscripts list the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and the two *aniyata* rules immediately after the general introduction to the "Breaking of the Saṃgha" (*bhikṣu-saṃghabheda*), followed by the distinctions between appropriate and inappropriate times;
only then do they list the four *pārājika* offenses, which are then directly followed by the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
When compared with the formal arrangement of the *piṭaka* (the *varga* sections), this is clearly a disorderly inversion. One cannot ascertain the reason for this.

Formerly, when the Tiantai Vinaya Master [Zhiyi] rearranged the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *Aniyata* rules to follow the sequence of the four *Pārājika* offenses— placing those concerning improper times (*akāla*) and those concerning schism (*saṃghabheda*) at the beginning—

although it was said that he had altered the order, the sequence of the texts remained perfectly coherent and did not detract from the underlying principle. Now, following his intention, I have listed them all at the beginning of this volume.
The Great Outline of the Vinaya: The distinctions in the arising of the precepts; the thirteen *ānantarya* offenses; ignorance regarding the rules of training;
the transformation of karma and the shifting of faculties; the general meaning of schism in the Saṃgha; the proper and improper times;
and the four *pārājika* and thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
The two indeterminate rules, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, the ninety *pāyattika* rules, the four *pratideśanīya* rules,
the *saikṣa* rules of training, the seven methods for settling disputes, and the four types of disputes.
*The Commentary on the Meaning of the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle One, Part One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
Before expounding the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, I shall briefly present six topical gates.

Regarding the first point—that although the Tathāgata established five categories of names while in the world, they were not divided—this is because from his beginning at the Deer Park until his final passing at the Śāla Grove, the Tathāgata established precepts according to the capacities of beings, resulting in ten thousand variations.

This is truly because the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings differ and their inclinations for what they wish to hear vary; thus, the Sage’s regulations differ in lightness and gravity, and in their degree of laxity or urgency.

Although the categories of light and heavy are immeasurable and differ from one another, each accords with the faculties and natures [of practitioners], and thus all possess the benefit of being practiced.

For this reason, the Sage established the original five names; were it otherwise, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fu fazang zhuan) states that while the Buddha was in the world, dividing [the teachings] into five schools would have rendered them meaningless.
Furthermore, the *Vaipulya-sūtra* states regarding the fivefold monastic community: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific passage from the cited sūtra.*
Furthermore, in the *Vinaya* and the *Vaipulya* sūtras, it is stated that the property of the five divisions of the Saṃgha may be used interchangeably; such scriptures must also be cited.

If one relies on texts such as the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā*, when the Buddha was still in the world, there were no differences whatsoever in the meaning or intent regarding the five divisions.
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefiting others, attained enlightenment and realized the wondrous bliss of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and was about to expound it.
It is said that because the practices of sentient beings differ and cannot be reduced to a single stream, expedient means were employed to speak of the distinctions of the Three Vehicles;

this is an illustration of that principle. Now, regarding the Vinaya-piṭaka, since the Tathāgata himself did not explicitly designate it as such during his own lifetime when the noble ones were present, and even if those five intentions [for such a designation] had existed, they would have been applied by giving it a name just as the Three Vehicles were distinguished; it could not have remained unnamed.
Question: If there were no five intentions (*pañca-abhiprāya*) nor any common purpose (*samāna-artha*), yet there were still light and heavy regulations established, why does the Sūtra say:
"After my parinirvāṇa, divide my Vinaya into five sections"? Answer: As stated in the *Daśasvapna-sūtra* of King Ajātaśatru:
"Even if after I have passed away the teachings are divided into five canons, this does not mean that while I am still in the world there were already five intentions. This refers to that.
Regarding the term "divisions," one may understand them by analogy with that [previous case]. Furthermore, the reason they are not divided is due to two meanings:

first, the Master is one; with whom could he contend so as to warrant a division? Although there are five names for the Buddha’s disciples, they all represent lineages transmitted through different eras to transform sentient beings;
thus, they are said to be "one. Second, the sentient beings who are the objects of his teaching do not... [text truncated]

As for this matter of right and wrong, sentient beings possess various faculties, each thinking to themselves, "This is precisely because our own capacities differ that the Sage’s regulations vary in their severity.
What is there to dispute? Each should personally grasp the intent of the transformation [of the Buddha] and practice according to one's own lot.
For this reason, the regulations established by the Noble One do not manifest five specific intentions; rather, they consist only of prophetic declarations made after the Buddha had passed away.
Only after the passing of the World-Honored One did the various schools begin to proliferate.

Second, regarding the distinction between the extensive and the abbreviated versions: according to the *Ekottarika-āgama*, during the time when the six Buddhas all remained for a long duration, both the extensive and abbreviated versions were fully taught.

During the first [Buddha’s] era, when the lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, the extensive precepts were established one hundred years later; during the second [Buddha’s] era, when the lifespan was seventy thousand years, [the same occurred]. Eight.

Ten years later, he established the *Vistara-vinaya* (Extensive Prohibitions); the third [period] lasted for seventy thousand years. Seventy years later, he established the *Vistara-śāsana* (Extensive Teachings);
the fourth [period] lasted for sixty thousand years. Sixty years later, he established the *Vistara-śāsana*; the fifth [period] lasted for forty thousand years.

Forty years later, he established the *Vistara-śīla* (Extensive Precepts); the sixth [period] lasted for twenty thousand years. Twenty years later, he established the *Vistara-śīla-prcchā* (Inquiries on Extensive Precepts).

If that is so, since it is stated in both the detailed and abbreviated versions that the duration of the abiding [of the Dharma] should be equal, why does the *Caturvargika* state: "The Buddha told Śāriputra:
'The Brahma-faring of the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Krakucchanda, and Kāśyapa shall abide for a long time,' and so on at length, until:
'the Brahma-faring of the Buddhas Śākyamuni and Kanakamuni shall not abide for long'"? Thus, [there is a contradiction].

Regarding the four [Buddhas] being long-lived and the two short-lived: how can this discrepancy be reconciled? First, as for the two Buddhas who are said to have entered parinirvāṇa, this is stated in reference to a partial or abbreviated perspective;

when compared to a comprehensive perspective, it is said that they abide for a long time. Thus, those two Buddhas concealed their extensive teachings and manifested only their abbreviated ones, saying they did not abide for long.
The four Buddhas, however, concealed the abbreviated and revealed the extensive to guide beings toward long-term abiding; therefore, this serves as the introduction to Śāriputra’s request.
If one relies on the statement regarding the five categories [of offenses], it is said that the first three do not endure for long while the latter three endure for a long time.

Furthermore, if one asks: "If that is so, since there is an extensive teaching (*vaipulya-śāsana*), why does it perish so quickly? The explanation is as follows: the various precepts of the five categories constitute the extensive teaching;

the performance of ritual acts and the reception of the precepts exist in both extensive and abbreviated forms, and are not restricted to only one. The principles regarding the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) are also the same. It is on this basis that it is said.

Although the Dharma may perish, there is still the activity of receiving the precepts, which differs from the other four types of reception; it is received only by those on the stage of the Inner Ordinary (āryapudgala) and does not apply to the final age.
Question: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha remained in the world for seven days. Why, then, is it said here that it remains for a long time? Answer:
This refers to those of sharp faculties who practice based on the provisional teaching for seven days. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Seven days, seven days. If...
Because those who have transcended [the stages] attain natural maturity without relying on instruction or cultivation, it is further said that they "extinguish their dull faculties";

because those at the beginning and end must rely on instruction and cultivation, it is now said that they "abide for a long time. These are merely differences of extensive and concise formulations within the *vinaya* (prescriptive teachings);

while the *dharmaparyāya* (transformative teachings) are not without the principle of being extensive or concise, the distinction in the fixed sequence—being concise first and extensive later—is easily understood.
Third, regarding the timing for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*): while the Tathāgata was in the world, he taught only the abbreviated instructions (*saṃkṣipta-śikṣā*).
Regarding these abbreviated teachings, it is said that "abbreviated" encompasses both light and heavy offenses, as both provide benefit to practitioners.

Furthermore, there are two interpretations: first, that the Buddha is not the Saṃgha and therefore cannot preside over the ceremony; second, that the extensive version is a distinct teaching intended for the benefit of those who practice in groups of five.
Furthermore, because their benefits are not universal and their gravity differs, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"All Buddhas teach only the *prātimokṣa* of instruction (*śikṣā-prātimokṣa*), not the *prātimokṣa* of majestic power (*anubhāva-prātimokṣa*). The commentary explains:

the abbreviated teaching merely points to the three karmas and offers direct admonition, hence it is called "instruction"; the extensive teaching follows specific events and involves the presence of fear, hence it is called "majestic power. Furthermore, there are four [types].
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "You yourselves have declared that this is the Tathāgata’s final teaching on the precepts; this is the proof.

When asked for the reason why a disciple may be granted absolution for an offense, it says: The Buddha stated in the *Pañcavargika* and other texts that one should not suspend another for an offense by means of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), but rather by means of the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*).
Furthermore, one must not cause the head of the offender to split into seven pieces.

The Tathāgata reverses the previous [method], and thus it cannot be said [that he always taught extensively]; however, regarding the duration—whether long or short—of the time when the Buddha preached the precepts, the sūtras and śāstras are not uniform.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that for twenty years prior to his attainment of enlightenment, the Tathāgata constantly preached the abbreviated teaching (*saṃkṣipta-śikṣā*), and later entrusted it to his disciples.

The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states that the one who preached this abbreviated teaching within twelve years of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment did so for the sake of the "monks without affairs" (*niḥsāṃghika-bhikṣu*).
The four divisions are likewise so, for they differ according to what is perceived by their respective faculties.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* also states that the Buddhas of the past did not establish precepts for their śrāvaka disciples because there were no transgressions;
nor did they establish the *Vinaya-śīla-prātimokṣa*, nor did they recite the precepts every half-month, but rather recited them only once every six years. All bhikṣus...

When they gathered at the Buddha’s location for the *poṣadha* ceremony, six full years had passed; those monks who possessed supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) came, while those without such powers were brought by the devas.
Having received their robes and bowls through the power of the devas, they arrived at the place of the *poṣadha*.
There, he preached that "patience is the supreme path," and so forth, as detailed extensively in the Great Commentary (*Mahā-ṭīkā*).
Regarding the fourth and fifth masters, their tenure was held as an undivided whole;

based on the *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary), they were harmonized and averaged over twenty years per master, totaling one hundred years for the succession and entrustment of the Dharma-treasury (*dharmagañja*). As there was no deficiency among these five masters, the specific number of years is not recorded.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the [teaching] first divided. The first master was named the Bhikṣu Kāśyapa. Regarding the Buddha...

After his parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the preservation of both the principles and practices of the two-fold teaching, remaining fully present and accessible to guide sentient beings according to their capacities until the end of time.
As the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states, having finished entrusting the Dharma-treasury to Ānanda, he manifested the vow of great compassion at Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
Sustained by the power of that vow, he did not enter final nirvāṇa, but transformed himself eighteen times to serve as a disciple of Maitreya Buddha, making solemn vows.

Having finished [his teaching], he immediately entered parinirvāṇa. In this manner, the second [succession], the Bhikṣu Ānanda, received this entrustment and caused it to circulate fully, as stated in the sūtras:
"Ānanda was traveling by boat on the waters of the Ganges when two kings both invited him;
not knowing whom to accept, he entered parinirvāṇa in midstream in order to settle their dispute. Furthermore—
It is said that he entrusted two disciples: the first was Śāṇakavāsin, the "Womb-Cloth Bhikṣu.
Because he felt shame while in the womb and wore a garment there, being born already clothed and growing up with it, he was thus named "Womb-Cloth. The second was Madhyāntika.
While Śāṇakavāsin taught and transformed beings in the kingdom of Mathurā, Madhyāntika did so in Kaśmīra; the two worked together side by side to teach and transform others.

Regarding this, it is said that the third master Madhyāntika and the fourth master Śāṇakavāsin upheld the Buddha-dharma in its entirety without deficiency, maintaining the eighty recitations of the Vinaya while teaching in the kingdom of Mathurā;
people there called them the "Vinaya Masters of Mathurā. When they were about to enter parinirvāṇa, they entrusted this Dharma to the fifth master, Upagupta.
Kūtadanta was highly skilled at preaching the Dharma, yet because he lacked the thirty-two marks, people called him the Buddha Without Marks and Excellences;

however, in terms of upholding the teachings, he surpassed his own teacher. Although he selectively practiced only the essential points of the Vinaya, these five masters all harbored inner clarity, profoundly penetrating the profound and subtle mysteries.
They realized the Way through diverse methods and were also adept at perceiving transformations.
It is fitting that the holy teachings be properly transmitted to benefit the times and the world; even a hundred years ago, they were still not divided and remained as a single Great Vinaya Piṭaka.
As for the fifth division into five parts, it was because the fifth master had five disciples whose spiritual understandings differed.

Not all [of them] had exhausted the depths of principle, but merely adhered to a single view as their standard; they were unable to achieve a harmonious integration, and thus divided the One Piṭaka into the names of various schools.

During the time of Kūṭadanta, and later in the final age, when King Śātavāhana convened a great assembly of masters to discuss the Buddha-dharma, each held different personal views and was biased toward certain attachments; it was Kūṭadanta who received and upheld [the teachings].

Since the Buddha-dharma was scarce, they were unable to distinguish what was correct; consequently, they divided the One Canon into five scriptures, each transmitted through its own lineage during the final age.
This was truly because the teachers were not one, and as the five masters lived in the same era, their worldly views conflicted and their explanations differed.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, due to these differences, factions supported one another and engaged in mutual disputes based upon them.

There are none among those who practice who do not awaken to the Way. Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples will misunderstand the meaning and misrepresent the teachings;

therefore, they shall conceal the Dharma-treasury. This refers to the Dharmaguptaka school. The commentary explains that this name signifies "those who misunderstand the meaning," while the name of the Dharma is the *Caturvarga-vinaya*.
Regarding the sequence of the transformative ritual, it is said to be "reversed" because it first explains the fruit and subsequently the cause. Thus, it is called "reversed."

Because he explains erroneously, he conceals and obscures from others the principle that cause precedes effect. Furthermore, it is said that he understands the three time periods and the internal and external aspects of the Dharma;
he is skilled in debating doctrines and refuting non-Buddhists; he asserts that all natures can receive the precepts;
and he is adept at answering all challenges and inquiries. For these reasons, he is named Sarvāstivāda. The commentary explains: this name has three meanings.
The world also calls it the *Huài wàidào fǎ* (Destruction of Non-Buddhist Teachings), which is named the *Shísòng* (Ten Recitations).

It is also said that because it teaches there is no self (*ātman*) nor a recipient (*vedaka*), and because it turns away all afflictions (*kleśa*) like a corpse, it is named *Jiāshèpí*. The explanation says this name signifies the realization of the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*);

it is also called the Dharma of the "Repeated Contemplation of Emptiness" (*punar-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, it is named *Tuōjiè* (Liberation), and it is also said that one does not construct the marks (*nimitta*) of earth, up to and including the marks of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Therefore, it is named Mīśāsaka; this name signifies "Extensive Explanation" (*vaipulya-vyākhyāna*). It is also named "Non-attachment to Existence and Non-existence," and "Five Parts" (*Pañcavastuka*).

Furthermore, it is said that [this school] asserts the existence of a self (*ātman*) and does not speak of the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), being like a child; for this reason, it is named Bāhuśrutīya. The commentary explains:

this name refers to those who practice the adherence to existence (*bhāvābhiniveśa-caryā*). Within this [tradition], there is no original text, and it is unknown what the term for "Dharma" (*dharma-nāman*) is. It is further said:

Because he has extensively and universally studied the five divisions of the scriptures, he is named Mahāsāṃghika; the commentary explains that this name means "Great Assembly" (Mahāsāṃgha) and also "Great Number" (Mahāsāṃghika), as they do not know even a fraction of the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that although these five divisions differ from one another, they do not hinder the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.
If one follows the *Śāsanāntima-dharma* and the chapter on the vestments and colors of the five masters, [the text] offers praise.

The one who praises the Sarvāstivāda is a person whose name signifies one who is widely learned, sagacious, and insightful, guiding others through the transformation of the Dharma; he wears a crimson *kāṣāya*.
The one who praises the Mahīśāsaka is a person whose name signifies one who upholds pure prohibitions and strictly adheres to the laws and regulations; he wears a black *kāṣāya*.

The one who praises the Mūlasarvāstivāda (Mi-sha-se) is a person whose name signifies one who contemplates in meditation, penetrating deeply and thoroughly elucidating the profound essence; he wears a blue *kāṣāya*.
The one called Kāśyapīya is a person who is diligent, courageous, and decisive in rescuing and protecting sentient beings; he wears a madder-colored *kāṣāya*.
The one called Mahāsāṃghika is a person who diligently studies the various sūtras and expounds their meanings and principles; he wears a yellow *kāṣāya*.
Among these, the Tripitaka was first explained orally for two hundred years, after which it was divided into twelve sections (*nikāya*).

From the Bhadrayānīya school, the Bhadrāyanīya branch was separated; from within the Bhadrāyanīya, three further branches were separated: first, Dharmottarīya; second, Bhadrayānīya; and third, Saṇṇāgārika.
Thus, combining the root and the branches, there are five schools. From the Kāśyapīya school, two branches were separated:
first, Saṃmatīya; and second, Sāmmitīya. Combining the root and the branches, there are three; adding these to the previous five, there are eight.
Thus, the eight schools of the Mahīśāsaka branch out into one school called the Madhyamika; these two combined with the original eight constitute ten schools.
Only the Dharmaguptaka and Mahāsaṃghika schools do not further divide, so including the previous ones, there are twelve.

After four hundred years, they further divide into eighteen; specifically, within the Mahāsaṃghika alone, six more schools are further divided: first, the Haimavata; (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. A complete translation would continue with the remaining names of the six schools.)
The six branches of the *Vaitulya* are: first, the *Mitra*; second, the *Miśra*; third, the *Pratiṣṭhāna*; fourth, the *Veda*; fifth, the *Śīla*; and sixth, the *Ucchīla*.
These six branches, when combined with the preceding twelve, total eighteen schools. Because there will be twenty schools after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"In the future, my disciples shall consist of twenty schools, all of which I shall [establish]."

Those who maintain that there are twenty schools all equally attain the four fruits; the Tripitaka is uniform, without inferior, middling, or superior distinctions, as explained at length in the *Great Commentary* (*Da shu*).
Regarding the sixth point, "general and specific": the first five are specific because they are biased attachments to their own views; thus, the Sūtra says, "although each is distinct..."

Because they are distinct, one knows that these are the specific *saṃghas* and this is the general [classification]. Since the practice and realization of these various assemblies are empty and pervasive, one knows that they do not give rise to biased attachments;
thus, one knows that those specific views each accord with their respective capacities without discrepancy.

Furthermore, because it is said that they "universally survey the scriptures of the five divisions," one knows that this refers to the general [classification]. Question: If this is so, why does the Tathāgata, in his exhortation, speak only of "these five"?

Regarding the fact that the [Mahīśāsaka] school does not mention "six," the commentary explains: The Tathāgata, seeing that people might not accept it if he were to point out their individual views separately, specifically cited the individual views as "five" in order to exhort them;

this does not preclude the *Saṃghāṭi* (Mahāsāṃghika) school from treating it as a general category. Because they practice these five views, there is no fear that people will fail to practice them, and thus no need for such exhortation.
Furthermore, even if one practices all five, there is no hindrance; therefore, this discussion focuses exclusively on the general and specific aspects of the *Dharmaguptaka* school.
The differences are as detailed in other commentaries; such is a brief explanation of the general outline of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Now, in preparing to lecture on the distinctions regarding the arising of the precepts, there are ten sections.

Regarding the first, the "Brief Explanation of the Title of the Introduction," the "Brief Account of the Arising of the Precepts" consists of five points. What are these five? First, the "Come Hither" (Svāgata) [ordination]—[the following section] proceeds...

Having planted good causes, his roots of the Path were profound; following the teaching, he gave rise to understanding and severed delusions. With the Wheel of the Path completed, he attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Deeply weary of birth and death, he longed for renunciation. When the Buddha called out "Welcome," he immediately received the full precepts as if they had been conferred a hundred years prior.

The bhikṣu said: "Among the two supreme dharmas within the *Saṃgha*, there is the desireless [state]. Kāśyapa cultivated the Path and advanced in virtue until his delusions were exhausted and he attained liberation."

The three sets of three words for receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*) while the assembly is filled with the nature of emptiness and the supreme Dharma are as follows: first, to honor virtue that is not distant and to move the Great Sage;
second, to rely upon those lesser sages who, weary of existence, seek liberation by shaving their hair and donning the dyed robes;

and third, to take refuge in the Triple Gem and thereby receive the full precepts. Regarding the four *gurudharmas*: when the woman Āṣāḍhā, the most intelligent among women, heard that the Buddha would not permit women to go forth...
The lady of the house conceived a profound sense of weary detachment and subsequently shaved her own head and donned the dyed robes.

Standing leaning against the gate of Jetavana, Ānanda made three requests to the Tathāgata, who from afar proclaimed the Eight Rules of Respect. He entrusted them to Ānanda, who received them upon his head as a venerable instruction.
Upon hearing this, Mahāprajāpatī intended to follow these eight rules and practice them accordingly; she then immediately gave rise to the five acts that constitute full ordination.
Those whose faculties and nature are most dull cannot give rise to the thought of receiving the precepts unless supported by superior conditions; this can be understood through reflection.
Among these, there are those who do not establish that one obtains the precepts through the "Unsurpassed Dharma" (anuttara-dharma). Why? First, because there is no person of the Unsurpassed Dharma;

second, because there is no teaching of the Unsurpassed Dharma. Yet the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "When one completes the path of cultivation and becomes an Arhat, this is called 'leaving home' and 'receiving full ordination'. This refers to such a case.
Prior to performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*), one should ordain them using the *karmavācanā* procedure, merely adding the Arhat to those who are less than twenty years of age.

Furthermore, all doubts regarding the fetal months and intercalary months are based on the former [calculation]; the case of the Arhat is likewise. Moreover, it is explained that the Arhat is ordained later.
As stated in the Vinaya: "If one counts the fetal months and intercalary months, when the fourteen-day *poṣadha* is completed, [he becomes] two..."
Tenth, this is called "attaining the precepts. Even if one has not yet fulfilled the path of cultivation to become an Arhat, one still attains the complete precepts (*saṃvara*).

Thus, we know there are superior dharmas. Regarding the five factors for the ordination of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), Kāśyapa should also be cited. Among the procedures for receiving the precepts, there is a difference between monks and nuns.
Within the monastic community, there are two types: first, the assembly of ten; second, the assembly of five. [The latter applies] in China and in border regions.
The sequence may be understood as follows: for a *bhikṣuṇī*, there are four types of ordination. First, ordination by a group of twenty; second, ordination by a group of twenty.

Regarding these two types of ordination by twenty, the details of the center and the borderlands are as previously stated. Third, ordination by messenger; fourth, ordination by verbal declaration. Because the full precepts (*upasampadā*) are generated immediately following the words of the messenger’s declaration, [these are distinct]. Regarding the twelve types of ordination:

because those who have previously been married [are included], why does it not mention "one who upholds the Vinaya" for the ten persons in the central lands, yet mention "one who upholds the Vinaya" for the five persons in the borderlands?
Answer: To explain the ten persons in general, four are required who are well-versed in the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures), while six suffice for the quorum;
thus, it is not said that all ten must be holders of the Vinaya. Regarding the rule for border regions (*pratyantaka*), five persons are required, all of whom must be holders of the Vinaya.

As the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "As the Buddha taught, in a border region, five persons who hold the Vinaya may confer full ordination (*upasampadā*); if there are ten persons who hold the Vinaya, [the same applies]."
Regarding the opening [of the rules] for receiving the precepts, the Buddha stated that one obtains full ordination (*upasampadā*), yet the one who grants it incurs an offense.

From this, three further matters are questioned: first, the opening for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) through ten persons; second, the opening for the reception [of precepts] through a formal motion and proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*);

third, the question of whether those who receive the precepts are few while those who perform repentance are many. As for the initial question, there are four meanings: first, to prevent the opening of "evil reception" (*duṣṭa-upasampadā*).

Since it is difficult to encounter [a qualified preceptor], one should naturally revere and serve him with care (2). To ensure the integrity of the whole community is not compromised (3), if one travels to other regions to perform repentance, provided no difficulties arise, the transgressions will likewise be extinguished (4).
This is because it opens the way for the five types of persons; as for the "borderland monks," this point is easily understood.

Furthermore, according to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, there is a brief *karmavācanā* procedure. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "As the roots of goodness grow increasingly thin, it is necessary to establish the position of the *upādhyāya* and the *ācārya*."

Pili first asked about the prohibitions (*dharmas of restraint*) and subsequently requested ordination from the great assembly; by reciting only the *ekajñapti* (single motion), he obtained full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Four people may perform this in the same manner as the extensive *karmavācanā*, for their roots of goodness are not superior [to those who undergo the full procedure]. Thus, it is explained that while all [monks] must undergo the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motion followed by three proclamations), nuns do not have this [exception].

Regarding the explanation of the third question: when one who has committed few offenses receives [the confession], and one who has committed many offenses receives it, the latter—having newly entered the order with a fervent mind—should be treated accordingly.

To generate wholesome states, one immediately enters *kauśalya* (skillfulness), yet wholesome minds are difficult to produce thereafter; subsequently, for the sake of extinguishing evil and eliminating karma by expelling it, twenty messengers are required to bring about the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*).
This is explained in the same way. Question: Regarding the reception of the precepts through messengers, must one wait for the return of the report before the precepts are actually obtained?

Is this not the case for [the precepts against] killing and stealing? Answer: The reception of the precepts is essential because it depends on the fulfillment of one’s intentional vow (*cetanā-praṇidhāna*).
It is sufficient to establish that "killing" and "theft" take the destruction of an object as their defining characteristic (*artha*), and thus they do not coexist [as distinct categories].

Nevertheless, these six types of feeling (*vedanā*) are subsumed under the preceding four types to constitute ten feelings. However, since none of these six fail to pertain universally to the performance of action (*karmasamutthāna*), while the specific distinctions are concealed and the universal aspect is emphasized, only five types of feeling are retained.
The details regarding the precepts (*śīla*) are extensive, as found in the Great Commentary (*Mahāvṛtti*).

Second, regarding the common and specific distinctions between monks and nuns, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Among the seven types of ordination, six are restricted [to monks] and one is common;
five apply only to bhikṣus and one only to bhikṣuṇīs. Regarding the commonality of their activities, the five that pertain to bhikṣus are:

being ordained by the name "Welcome" (*svāgata*), self-vowed ordination, the three refuges, the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*), and the third awakening. To prevent slander, the Tathāgata did not ordain anyone by the name "Welcome."
Regarding other women, the *Mātṛkā* explains that the "Welcome" (*svāgata*) is the supreme dharma; the performance of the ritual is as follows:
the three types of ordination are fully prepared for both assemblies, as in the account of the five hundred women who were ordained by the "Welcome" formula.

The *Saṃyukta-śataka-vastu* states that when the Buddha personally proclaimed "Welcome" to ordain nuns, they all attained arhatship—not merely one or two. The *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) refers to this as the "Lotus."
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states that the Buddha’s proclamation of "Welcome" (Ehi-bhikṣuṇī) for ordination applies to those who have attained clear realization;

this is also applicable to nuns who have transcended the fetters (*āsrava*) through the fourfold *pārājika* rules. Regarding the three-refuge (*tri-śaraṇa*) ordination not being applicable to nuns: according to the examination of the sūtras and śāstras, nuns do not obtain the precepts through the three refuges alone.
The *P'o-lun* (Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra? states that prior to the eighty years after his attainment of the Way, the three-refuge [ordination] was used for ordaining nuns.
At that time, the nun had no intention of ordaining people; it was only after eight years had passed that she began to grant the three refuges and perform the *karmavācanā* for ordination.
This is why [the rules] do not permit her to inquire [about the candidate’s qualifications]. If she does not reach the stage of granting the three refuges, she may not ordain via the three refuges;

if she reaches the stage of the "Come hither" (*ehi*) instruction, she should ordain via the "Come hither" formula. The answer is: the present citation of "not reaching" is intended to demonstrate that she does not ordain precisely because she had no prior intention.

Regarding the statement that "this [rule] does not apply" because of renunciation: this refers to the principles of the full precepts, the three refuges, and the five, eight, or ten precepts, which indeed apply to nuns.
The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Fourteen years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he ordained women by means of the Eight Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*);

As for the distinctions: the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu), the three statements, and the eight respects—these three are restricted to the period when the Buddha was in the world.

Although it is said within the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (or *Dharmakośa*) that Ānanda, while crossing the Ganges, converted five hundred rishis by simply saying "Come hither," whereby they immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship, one cannot rely on this as a method for obtaining the precepts through the aforementioned dharmas.
Furthermore, [the method of ordination] also applies to two periods: during the five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is understood [that these methods remain valid].
Once they have attained liberation, it may be that not a single person enters the fruit of Arhatship; the *karmavācanā* for their release [from the prohibitions] may then be performed.

As for the location, the "Come Hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) ordination and the Eightfold Respectful Observances (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*) are restricted to Jambudvīpa, because it was there that the Buddha attained enlightenment.

Furthermore, these two types of ordination were personally administered by the Buddha himself. Question: If this is so, why does he not travel through the other three continents to teach and transform beings? Answer: It is because [the Buddha's presence] is in Jambudvīpa.

There are four kinds of specific conditions for persons: namely, seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, leaving the household life, and attaining the Path. Therefore, in the two continents of Purvavideha and Aparagodānīya, there is no condition for seeing the Buddha.

It should be understood that *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) applies to all three [continents]. Regarding the applicability of the "Higher Dharma" (*uttaradharma*), it may be that among the three continents during the course of a Tathāgata’s lifetime, not a single person enters the fruit of Arhatship.

Regarding the third point, the two views on obtaining precepts: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one obtains precepts within the fruit of Tathāgata-hood; thus that Vinaya states:

"When the Buddha was beneath the Bodhi tree, in his final moment of mind, he attained great and clear enlightenment; having realized it for himself and personally verified it, this is called being fully endowed [with the precepts].
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*, one also obtains precepts through the fruit, because he himself declared, "I shall not rise from this seat," and thereby attained them.
When the outflows are exhausted, both the fruit and the precepts are attained simultaneously; because the precepts are obtained through the fivefold cause, that Vinaya states:
"At midnight on the eighth day of the second month, he leaped over the city walls and went beneath a *śumana* tree, where he shaved his hair and donned the *kāṣāya*, saying:

This was a *śuddhāvāsa* deva who manifested as a hunter to induce [the king] to feel weary of the world and renounce it.
