Since these are wholesome dharmas, there is therefore precept (*śīla*). Question: Does a Pratyekabuddha possess precepts? Answer: He does indeed possess them.
Although he appears in a world devoid of a Buddha, he attains liberation by relying on specific conditions; thus, he also possesses the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* (liberation-precept). Question:

If that is so, since the *prātimokṣa* exists when a Buddha has appeared in the world, how can it exist when a Buddha has not appeared? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, this is not the case.

The *Saṃghabhedavastu* (or *Sengshe*) answers that there are two types of *prātimokṣa*: first, for householders, such as the three refuges and the five or eight precepts; second, for those who have left the home life, the *prātimokṣa* of two hundred and fifty rules.
Because the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (the *Duolun*) speaks based on the former [category], it says that there are no precepts [for householders].
Now, let us further explain how one obtains the complete *prātimokṣa*. Why is this? When the five precepts pass away along with the physical form, they do not persist into the present.

The *Śarīra-śāstra* (*Shen lun*) argues that because a Buddha has not yet appeared in the world, there is no self-reception of the Dharma; it explains this based on the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (*Shan jian*).

According to it, the five precepts and the ten wholesome precepts exist at all times, even in the absence of a Buddha’s appearance in the world, because Pratyekabuddhas and Wheel-turning Kings (*cakravartin*) also teach and receive them.

If this were not the case, then the Tathāgata, as a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), would possess natural precepts (*svabhāva-śīla*), and the Buddha himself would also be present [in such a state].
The *Jiaye Zhendi Mingliao Shu* (Commentary Clarifying the True Meaning of the Householder) states:

"Having cultivated the practice of the precepts throughout many past kalpas, in his final birth, his very body was already perfected in the nature of the five precepts as a householder. Upon reaching the stage of *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*, he left the household life;

his hair and beard fell away naturally, and robes and bowl appeared upon his person. At that time, he fully attained the *prātimokṣa* and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts born of meditative concentration."

He also asked why the Tathāgata is named "Self-Existent" (Svayambhū) while his disciples have attained the Supreme Dharma. He replied: "Because during the causal stage [of practice], he did not rely on the teachings of another teacher;
thus, having realized the principle of self-existence, he attained the Knowledge of Exhaustion (kṣayajñāna). His disciples are not like this. He asked:

"Do both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas not rely on the teaching of another body, but rather rely on the teaching of their own bodies? The *Pō-lùn* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) states: "They rely on the teaching of their own bodies."
Upon attaining Buddhahood, he sat beneath a tree; this was the fulfillment of his physical instruction (*kāya-śikṣā*). He then spoke these words himself:

"I shall not rise from this seat until I have attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). This was the fulfillment of his verbal instruction (*vāk-śikṣā*). Subsequently, he attained the exhaustion of outflows, and the precepts were likewise fully acquired. This is explained in detail in the *Great Commentary* (*Da shu*).

Fourth, regarding the difference between self-attainment and receiving from a teacher: the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that these five types of "receiving" (upasampadā), when considered from a broad perspective, are all received from the Buddha, because it is due to the appearance of the Buddha in the world that this Dharma exists.
If one examines this through its meaning, the first [type], the attainment of the higher dharmas by oneself, is self-attained, while the remaining four are received from others. Why is this?
Because one attains realization of the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) through the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma; thus, in terms of its meaning, it is called "received from the Buddha."
Because one attains the precepts through self-realization when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests, they are not received from another.

Among those received from another, there is the attainment of the precepts from the Buddha via the "Come Hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) formula or the Eightfold Respectful Observances (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*), as well as for disciples through the *tri-śaraṇa* (three-refuge) *karmavācanā*.

Regarding the seven classes of followers (*sapta-saṃgha*), as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: "In broad terms, all receive them from the Buddha; in terms of specific matters, [the precepts are received by] bhikṣus, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
The three groups of Vaiśī women received the precepts from the Buddha; two śrāmaṇeras received the precepts from the Buddha: first, Nanda, and second, Yaśas.
Regarding these three groups, the Buddha did not accept them [into full ordination] in order to stop slander.

To repay their kindness, it is said that when the śrāmaṇera Cunda was addressed by the Buddha with "Come, well-come," he obtained the śrāmaṇera precepts but not the full precepts; later, through further preaching of the Dharma, he attained realization of the Noble Path.
Daowen asked: "For what reason does the Tathāgata receive the *svāgata* (welcome) greeting from the bhikṣu, while others do not? He replied: "It is because two conditions are fulfilled:

first, both coarse habits and [defilements] have been extinguished, and his majestic power is so great that he can transform conditions and enter the Path; second, he possesses excellent knowledge of the faculties and capacities [of beings], enabling him to administer the medicine according to their needs.
The bhikṣu is not like this. Daowen further asked: "Why did the Buddha proclaim the Eight Respectful Precepts from afar rather than transforming [the nuns] face-to-face?"
Answer: To indicate that those who have realized the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*) rely upon the Great Saṅgha to receive instruction in the Dharma, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"The World-Honored One himself took a vow; for them, there is the sense of having a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and a teacher (*ācārya*). However, although the Buddha does not act as a teacher for others, one obtains the precepts through the Three Refuges and may be called a Bhikṣu;
yet while one may act as an *ācārya*, one cannot act as an *upādhyāya*. [This applies to] obtaining the Eight Respectful Observances (*gurudharma*)."
Question: Why is it that one may be designated as an *ācārya* by receiving the precepts from Ānanda, yet one cannot be designated as an *upādhyāya*?
Answer: It is for the sake of accomplishing impartial transformation; for the sake of accomplishing the three refuges; for the sake of accomplishing the four kinds of faith;
and for the sake of accomplishing the six recollections. Question: For what reason is there no discussion of the meaning [of the precepts] among the nuns, yet they still obtain the precepts?
Question: Why is it that among the bhikṣus there is no one sent as a messenger?
Answer: Because women’s resolve is weak, they require a messenger; since men are firm and decisive, what need is there for a messenger? Question:
If that were so, would not the bhikṣus be unable to maintain the holy life (brahmacarya)? Answer: There is no difficulty regarding the holy life.

It is difficult to find a precedent for sending a messenger; furthermore, it is understood that a *bhikṣuṇī* may not invite monks to her own quarters to receive the precepts, which is why there is the practice of sending a messenger-bhikṣu.
Otherwise, how could these two cases be compared? According to the *Sifen lü mopi*, one who attains the fruit of Arhatship is called "one of the superior dharma" and receives the precepts.
In the *Wufen lü*, Dharmatrāta left home at fourteen and became an Arhat at sixteen, having reached full age at twenty-two.
Regarding the ordination through the ten *karmavācanās*, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (Xianyu jing) states: "Śāriputra ordained the śrāmaṇera Cūḍapanthaka;
after seven years of renunciation and fourteen years [since his initial entry], he attained arhatship. To repay his teacher's kindness, he did not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Furthermore, the *Aśoka-avadāna* (Yuwang zhuan) records that Kuvula (Kubjita) ordained two śrāmaṇeras who became arhats, yet even as they gathered flowers and plucked fruit, they were still called śrāmaṇeras. Such are the teachings.

What is the intended meaning? The answer is: According to the *Caturvargika-mātikā*, when one previously possesses the preparatory means (*upāya*) and the intention to receive the precepts, and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests, both the fruit and the precepts are obtained simultaneously.
The *Pañcavargika* and other texts state that when one previously lacks the preparatory means and the intention to receive the precepts, one obtains the fruit but not the precepts.

Furthermore, it is explained that for a layperson, a śrāmaṇera, or one who has attained the path and become an arhat, both the fruit and the precepts are obtained simultaneously. Question: If this is so, does one first obtain the precepts [before the fruit]?

Why does the Vinaya state that one must again chant the *karmavācanā* for "Come, Well-Come" (*ehi bhikṣu*)? The answer is: it is to eliminate worldly appearances and to resolve doubts regarding entry into the Saṃgha;

therefore, it must be chanted again. Furthermore, another explanation is that Kāśyapa attained the precepts through his own vow, yet this is called the "Supreme Dharma" (*uttama-dharma*), because in the world, that which flourishes as the Dharma is termed the "Supreme Dharma.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* (付法藏傳) states: "The self-vow is [classified as] 'lower'..."

The discipline of body and speech is fully and rigorously complete, differing from previous interpretations. Regarding the vow "I shall not [transgress] below," it does not mean that the category of precepts is not generated;
therefore, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One obtains the precepts through self-vow—only Kāśyapa did so. However, this does not mean they are obtained within the mind of an Arhat;
rather, the name is manifested based on superior conditions. If this is so, why does the Vinaya state that a śrāmaṇera becomes an Arhat?

The Han [master] immediately named this the "Complete Answer. This is also established prior to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual); here, it is designated by its most prominent feature. The *Sūtra on Questions* states:
"A layperson cultivates the path but does not realize the fourth fruit. Why, then, does the *Vinaya* state that a layperson can attain the fruit of an Arhat?

The answer is: although these meanings appear contradictory, there is no logical impediment. A lay devotee (*upāsaka*) possesses the three refuges, the five precepts, and the eight precepts, as previously explained.

Therefore, among those who take the three refuges and observe the five precepts, some hear the Buddha’s teaching and attain the two lower fruits (srotāpanna and sakṛdāgāmin), while others do not realize the third or fourth fruits;
likewise, those who receive the eight precepts may also realize the third or fourth fruits. One can understand this by reflecting upon the respective accounts in the Sūtras and Vinaya. Question:

For what reason does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* state that laymen (*upāsaka*) who have left home and distanced themselves from the five desires attain the fruit of anāgāmin, whereas bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs [attain other fruits]?

Regarding the four fruits of the path: the commentary explains that because the distinction between the laity and the ordained is to be clarified, it does not merely state that one attains the four fruits.

As for the fifth category, which enumerates ordinary beings and noble ones, according to the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, the "Come Hither" (*svāgata*) type applies exclusively to those at the level of the noble ones (*ārya*).
The understanding of both types of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) is not perfectly clear, and because their minds of renunciation are not ultimate, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"The reception of the precepts through the 'Come hither' (*ehi-bhikṣu*) formula is entirely in accordance with the Dharma, for it is the sovereign meaning of all Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma. One may personally confer the precepts;

there is no case where one dies while still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) and fails to become an Arhat. Under the words 'Come hither,' the full ordination is simultaneously produced, yet the fruit is not realized. The *Zhi shu* (Commentary on the Sutra) says:
Under the words "Welcome" (*svāgata*), one simultaneously attains both the precepts and the fruit; this refers to the first fruit (*srota-āpanna*).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that receiving the precepts through "Welcome" applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), as was the case for Sūdena’s reception of the precepts through "Welcome. The Three Refuges and the Eightfold Respect (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*) do not apply to external ordinary beings.

As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "These two types of persons are neither weak, nor do they abandon [the path], nor do they change their faculties, nor do they sever their roots of goodness; from beginning to end, they are firm."

Since there are indeed no such calamities or afflictions, we know that those who have reached the stage of the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala) attain indestructible faith (*akopya-śraddhā*) and achieve non-retrogression.
Why, then, does the Vinaya state that one may lose their original intention upon approaching the Buddha’s presence? The answer is that there are two kinds of faith:

first, the faith of renunciation regarding phenomena (*vastu-niḥsaraṇa-śraddhā*); second, the indestructible faith regarding principle (*tattva-akopya-śraddhā*). What the text refers to as "losing" means losing the faith regarding phenomena.

This is not reasonable. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that the Eightfold Respectful Precepts apply universally to ordinary persons (bālapṛthagjana), the female disciple Āmrapālī, those who have attained the first fruit (srotāpanna), and the five hundred women—how could it be that they are not ordinary persons?
The three-word formula does not apply to ordinary persons; rather, it is through the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of receiving the precepts that they first become ordinary persons.
Once this has been initiated, the three [precepts] apply universally. The explanation of these doctrinal principles is extensive, as found in the Great Commentary (*Dàsù*).

Sixth, regarding the timing of the formal undertaking of the precepts: for those who receive the "Come hither" (*ehi*) ordination, as soon as the proclamation "Come hither" is finished, they immediately give rise to the full precepts;
the supreme Dharma is received, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests, and they attain the threefold verbal ordination.

The *Mātṛkā* states that the first three refuges constitute the renunciation of the household life, and once the three knots are severed, the full precepts are immediately produced. Question: If this is so, then by the method of repentance, past transgressions are extinguished and...
Only after the body and mind are purified should one beg for and receive the precepts. Why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* state that one should repent after having completed the three refuges?
The answer is that, according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, there are five kinds of threefold refuge. First is the "refuge of turning away from heterodoxy":

this refers to those who have long believed in heterodox paths and only now enter the Buddha-dharma; they cannot receive the precepts immediately. First, they are taught to take refuge in the Triple Gem to turn away from heterodoxy and enter the correct path, and only thereafter [may they receive them].

Regarding the chapter on the non-arising of precepts through repentance, as explained in the *Śāriputra-bhrātṛ-sūtra*: one may obtain the Three Refuges within all five realms of existence, with the sole exception of those in the Avīci hell.

Regarding the Five Precepts and the Three Refuges—this refers to those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), those who live as thieves within the Sangha, those who have defiled nuns, those with both sexual organs, and those who have previously violated the Five Precepts;
all such individuals are ineligible to receive them. Question: When does one who receives the Five Precepts actually generate the precepts? Answer: It is required... [text ends]
Having received the Three Refuges and obtained the Five Precepts, one must further recite [the names] so that the person before them may recognize them.
Furthermore, at the time when the single precept of non-killing is explained, one obtains the Five Precepts because one is able to uphold the one precept and can fully uphold all five.
Moreover, because the force of the Five Precepts is mutually interconnected, after having completed the original intention and vow to receive the Five Precepts, [one then recites them].
Only then does one first understand among all the various expositions. Having received the Three Refuges, one who has obtained the Five Precepts—this is the definitive meaning.
The Eight Precepts and the Ten Precepts are also all like this. Thus, the Five Precepts, once received, are immeasurable and vast, as explained extensively in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*.

Regarding the Three Refuges for the Eight Precepts, one should also inquire about the obstacles and the time of obtaining the precepts, following the explanation of the Five Precepts; this applies to the Forty Precepts as well.

Regarding the three refuges: as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, after ordaining a śrāmaṇera, one first receives the three refuges and five precepts of an upāsaka, and subsequently receives the three refuges and ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera;
thus, the five precepts and so forth are complete with the three refuges. Regarding the three refuges for the full ordination (*upasampadā*): as stated in the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*: Question:
Since those who receive the five, eight, or ten precepts all receive the three refuges, why are they not called "fully ordained" (*upasampadā*)? Answer: The five, eight, and ten... [text continues]
It is appropriate to say that the Three Refuges alone are insufficient and require further addition, such as the Five Precepts and so forth;

however, since the Three Refuges are already complete, they should be administered first. Furthermore, at that time, the [categories of] five, eight, or ten precepts did not yet exist and thus could not have been enumerated. Therefore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Having taken refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one now goes forth under the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that when one realizes, "I am the World-Honored One," this is called going forth and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Furthermore, it says that one who possesses the three refuges, having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, recites three times, "I follow the Buddha and go forth"; thus, one immediately receives the precepts. Regarding the reception of the Eight Respectful Precepts (*gurudharma*), the eighth is concluded;
then, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for the attainment of full ordination is performed. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "I grant you full ordination."

If one has completed the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) and attained full ordination (*upasampadā*), and furthermore understands the ritual, then upon the completion of the three proclamations (*trivācanā*), one immediately attains the lifelong precepts (*yāvajjīva-śīla*).

Question: If I have performed the three proclamations for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), should I not also obtain the merit of a single summer? Answer: It is sufficient merely to have the intention to perform the retreat;

even without the three proclamations, the retreat is successfully established. Question: Likewise, it should be sufficient merely to have the intention to receive the precepts; would it not be so even without the three proclamations? Answer: It is so.

Since the precepts one should obtain are not the same as those [of the other], why raise this objection? Furthermore, the essential commitment for receiving the precepts is for "one lifetime," and they are only abandoned when that lifetime ends;

thus, there is nothing to which [the precepts] could belong [in the interim]. As for the *kaṭhina* ceremony, the mental resolve is for a short period of three months, and since they exist until that time is fulfilled, they can be said to belong [to that period];
therefore, it is only upon fulfillment that they are obtained. Consequently, these two principles do not coincide. Moreover, [the text continues:]...

The explanation is as follows: regarding the knowledge of receiving the precepts, entering the *dharma-anvaya* (formal) *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), and the timing thereof—if one enters according to the *dharma*, within a single period there may be many *dharmas*;
however, if one enters according to the time, within a single period one cannot have multiple times. Time is the general category while the *dharmas* are the particulars;
thus, the principle requires that the former must cease and the latter arise, for their meanings do not coexist.

Regarding the seventh point, the gradual and instantaneous nature of the five types of ordination, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Among the five types of ordination, the one by formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is both gradual and instantaneous;
the others are instantaneous and not gradual. This appears to be a loss of meaning. Why?

In the cases of the "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) and the "Three-fold recitation" (*tri-vācikā*), why is it that one cannot have previously received the eight precepts or the five precepts before receiving full ordination, yet still be said to be "gradual"? The same applies to the "Superior Dharma" (*uttara-dharma*).

As the Vinaya states that a *śrāmaṇera* and an *arhat* represent a gradual progression, the Eightfold Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) are likewise so. Why, then, do you say that the other four [precepts] are not gradual?

Although the *Pō-lùn* (Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra) states that among the seven types of ordination, the one by *jñapti-caturtha-karma* is obtained through three successive stages, while the remaining precepts are obtained all at once without the sequence of three stages—yet based on the aforementioned evidence, this cannot be definitively established.

My current interpretation is as follows: [The text continues with the argument that the distinction between gradual and instantaneous attainment depends on the specific nature of the ritual and the capacity of the recipient, rather than a rigid categorization.]

Regarding the five types [of precepts], whether they are obtained gradually or simultaneously, it is said that if one "opens" [the path] through this opening, there is no offense. As for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), only one type is gradual and not simultaneous;

the remaining four are both. Although the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts state that one first receives the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts and subsequently receives the Ten Precepts, they do not say that they may be received concurrently.
According to the *Zhen-di-ming-liao-shu* (The Commentary on the Clarification of Ultimate Truth), it is not [permissible] beforehand... [text fragment].
"One who has received the ten precepts does not yet possess the full precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*). These precepts are the means for fulfillment;

they are capable of encompassing the future full precepts and are thus called 'vow-vinaya' (*praṇidhāna-vinaya*). This must be what was taught by another school that no longer exists. [The opponent] asks:

"If one can obtain all three types of precepts at once, why is it necessary to receive them in succession? The *P'o-lun* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) answers: "To become habituated to the Buddha-dharma, one must necessarily..."
The sequence is thus: one attains the flavor of the Buddha-dharma in this gradual order, and one’s joyful devotion becomes firm and difficult to overturn;

it is not as if one receives [the fruits] all at once. Furthermore, it is said that sentient beings should receive the five precepts and thereby attain the fruit of the Way, and the same applies to the ten precepts.
For this reason, the Tathāgata taught this sequence. Moreover, although the text speaks of attaining the three [vehicles] simultaneously, there is no...
There is a distinct "non-action" (avijñapti) that is essentially one, yet is explained as three precepts according to their respective stages.

According to the *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātu-sūtra), it is said that if one does not receive the five precepts but directly receives the ten precepts, one cannot obtain the ten precepts; this is because the head-shaving has not been performed. I have not yet seen the original text of this sūtra. Regarding the reception of precepts for the duration of one's life:

even if one intends not to transgress them later, once a transgression occurs, the precepts are not lost. As for my own vow, I shall not stay overnight outside [the monastery] for a period of three months.
If one departs for a night, the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is not lost; this is because the precepts were received before departing, and thus they remain with oneself, so the *varṣā* is not lost.

This is because it was originally not yet obtained that it is now broken. If it has not yet been obtained, how can one say it is "broken"? There are two ways in which it is called "broken": first, having already obtained [the status] is called "broken";
second, that which ought to be obtained but is not obtained is called "broken. If the limit of the period has been fulfilled, there is no "breaking" to be broken.

Eighth, regarding the differences in the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*): the "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) ordination is obtained in one recitation; the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*) are obtained in three recitations; the *tri-vācika* (three-utterance) ordination is obtained in three recitations;

and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (fourth motion and three proclamations) ordination is obtained in four recitations. The "Come hither" ordination is superior as it is conferred directly by the Buddha, and thus one recitation is appropriate. Why is it that the Eight Respectful Rules, which are upheld by those still in training (*śaikṣa*), are also obtained in only one recitation?

If we consider the case of Ānanda, it should have required more recitations, as he was ordained in conjunction with the Buddha. If the World-Honored One were present [at such an ordination], [the procedure would differ].
According to the teaching, it is known that because the Buddha’s affection for the Path and his thirst for the Dharma were so earnest, he attained [the fruit] in a single recitation;

however, as for those who calculate that an Arhat should attain it in one recitation, it is because such a person’s thirst for the Dharma is hindered by pride, and thus they must attain it only after three recitations.

Why are there three recitations when addressing one beyond training (aśaikṣa)? Although there are differences among people, these are all distinctions regarding the breadth of their observance of the precepts.

The mind conditioned by [the Dharma] is the primary cause; because his affection for the Way was earnest, he first shaved his own hair to become a sage, thereby restraining the descendants of the noble Houyuan from seeking transformation through external means.

Only after he had left home did he lose his resolve midway; thus one knows that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is light, for although it involves a multitude, it applies universally to both ordinary persons and sages.
Consequently, four recitations suffice, and three verbal motions are required; although those addressed are *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training), they are distinguished [from others].

Because individuals possess slightly superior conditions, there are three grades [of ordination]: first, the *svāgata* (welcoming); second, the *tri-vākya* (three statements); and third, the *karma* (formal ritual).

The sequence of the eight *gurudharma* (venerable rules) and the higher laws (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) is established as follows. To cite the texts and point to the specific matters, it is explained at length in the *Great Commentary* (*Daisho*).
Regarding the sequence of these three—the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*), and the *karma*—how should they be understood? It is said: "Five..."
The initial establishment of the precepts was like that at the Deer Park upon attaining enlightenment; Yaśoda’s father alone received the five precepts first.

Eight years later, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) came into being. From that time onward, the method for the ten precepts was taught. Since the text of the ten precepts states, "The preceptor is [Name]," we know that the *karmavācanā* was established last.
Prior to five years [after the *karmavācanā*], the three-fold utterance (*tri-vācika*) flourished, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

It is said that committing the precept against sexual misconduct for five years constitutes a *pārājika* offense according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; however, the *Samantapāsādikā* states that committing it after eight years accords with the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.

Based on this, one may say it is after eight years; yet, one cannot definitively state that it is after eight years, as it is unknown whether the "eight precepts" (referring to the *pārājikas*) were incurred earlier or later.

The ninth [point], the similarity and difference regarding the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) associated with undertaking [the precepts], has four points of similarity: First, similarity of name: both are equally named "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).

Second, similarity of meaning: both equally prevent the seven branches of body and speech. Third, similarity of substance: both equally take that which is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*) as their substance;

alternatively, they are called "form-nature" (*rūpa-svabhāva*). Fourth, similarity of opposition: within the unmanifest associated with undertaking, the substance exists precisely as the prevention of specific actions (*vastu-pratiṣedha*).

Regarding the non-identical [nature] of the non-manifest (avijñapti) within the category of "conformity" (*anuvartana*), there are likewise four types. First, regarding the non-manifest within "reception" (*samādāna*):

it is established in general that once the mind has ceased all evil, one simultaneously and universally attains the non-manifest of both sentient and non-sentient objects, regardless of the distinction between them. Regarding the non-manifest within "conformity": this refers to the specific practice;

it is not attained instantaneously, but is accomplished gradually through successive stages. For one who practices, they give rise to the non-manifest; for one who does not practice, they do not give rise to the non-manifest.

Second, they differ in length and brevity: among the non-manifest actions (*avijñapti*) within the formal undertaking, those that arise from a solemn vow intended for the duration of one's entire life remain as long as the body exists;

these are called "long. Among the non-manifest actions within the subsequent observance, those that arise from practice and cease simultaneously with the physical and mental factors of the preparatory effort are called "brief.
Third, they differ in breadth and narrowness: once the non-manifest action within the formal undertaking has been received...
Subsequently, when the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) arise spontaneously, that which is constantly present without being lost is termed "broad" (*viśāla*).

Within the category of non-informative virtue (*avijñapti-kuśala*), there is evil and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), which are termed "narrow" (*saṃkucita*). Regarding the four roots and the two branches:
within the informative [action], non-informative action is its root; non-informative action arising in dependence upon the informative is explained as the branches. As for the discussion...
Second, regarding the identity of the agent, there are also four types: first, identity of name; second, identity of meaning; third, identity of substance; and fourth, identity of brevity.
Furthermore, there are many varieties of difference: receiving the primary act while severing the secondary act;

receiving the root act while severing the branch act; receiving the preventive act for the future while severing the preventive act for the present; and receiving the single category while severing the multiple categories. These details are as explained at length in the Great Commentary (*Da shu*).
The tenth question and answer concerns the ritual procedure for receiving the *śrāmaṇera* precepts.

According to the *Pañcavargika*, one should first receive the three refuges and five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), and subsequently receive the three refuges and ten precepts of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra* also states that the five come first and the ten follow.
The *Sukhavihāra-sūtra* says: "Having paid homage to the Saṃgha, one proceeds to the place of the *ācārya*. Having prostrated at his feet and knelt with palms joined, the *ācārya* instructs [him]."
It says: "You should follow my words; I shall instruct you to receive the Three Refuges. He answers, "Yes.

[The commentary] explains that one should also inquire regarding the thirteen *antarāyika* (obstructive) factors and the prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) so as to give rise to wholesome qualities. Question:

Why does the *śrāmaṇera* not simply explain the first four *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherently evil acts) and then conclude, rather than explaining the subsequent six prohibitions? Answer: These ten are prone to being transgressed with pleasure; therefore, they are explained first.

Regarding the other precept masters who subsequently taught separately, when asked why the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) were explained for the *bhikṣuṇīs* but not prescribed for the *śrāmaṇeras*, the explanation was:
"Because the *śrāmaṇeras* have weak resolve and timid dispositions, they are unable to inquire [about such matters]; furthermore, they do not request the *bhikṣus* to serve as their teachers.
When asked why the *śrāmaṇerīs* are not treated in the same way, the explanation was: "Because young nuns establish their practice without depending on men, they are not so commanded."
When a *bhikṣu* acts as a preceptor for the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*), the *bhikṣuṇī* does the reverse; the *bhikṣu* serves as the teacher. Question:

If that is so, should the *bhikṣu* also serve as the *upādhyāya*? Answer: It is explained that because they do not have the relationship of kinship (*na saṃbandha-lakṣaṇa*), he cannot serve as the *upādhyāya*.

Question: Why is it that there are rules of training (*śikṣā-dharma*) for young women (*kumārikā*), but none for men? Answer: The primary explanation is that there are two reasons. First, regarding women...
Because there is the fault of being pregnant, it is necessary to grant two years of training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*) to purify one's person through the Dharma;
since men do not have this [fault], why should they perform it? Second, because women’s afflictions and defilements are heavy, it is difficult for them to enter the Path immediately;

unless they apply themselves to the training in the Dharma, there is no means by which they can advance on the Path. Since men’s wholesome causes are already superior and they are capable of establishing their practice, [the training] is not required for them further.
One must undergo further training in the *śikṣādattaka* (the one granted training). What is this training? It consists of the initial instruction and the six rules.

If, before two years have passed, one commits another minor offense, the training is forfeited; one must again be granted two years. Regarding the six external offenses, only the *caryā* (conduct) is forfeited, but the *śikṣā* (training) is not.

However, if one commits any of the four *mūla* (root) offenses, one must be expelled (*pārājika*). Therefore, there is the "one undergoing training regarding the root" (*śikṣamāṇa-mūla*) and the "one undergoing training regarding the training" (*śikṣā-śikṣā*).

If one who has been practicing the *śikṣādattaka* (probationary) rules for two full years commits an offense, their status as one under training (*śikṣā*) is also forfeited; they must undergo probation for another two years. Question:

If that is so, then one who commits an offense after completing the period of concealment (*praticchādana*) should also lose their status. Explanation: The concealment is governed by the number of days; it is a disciplinary measure for the transgression of the mind, not something that lasts for the duration of one's life.
Therefore, once the days are completed, the status of being under training is not lost. The "duration of life" is not restricted to only two years; this is stated in contrast [to the previous case].
The brief limit of two years for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) does not mean that many years are required; it is simply a restriction on not permitting study [during that time].

The reason this is not treated as an exception to the eighteen rules of the *Mahāsāṃghika* is explained at length in the *Great Commentary* (*Daishu*). Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-garbha-śāstra*, if a layperson acts as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and confers full ordination upon another layperson, does the recipient obtain the precepts?
The answer is: they do obtain the precepts, but the monastic community commits a *duṣkṛta* offense, as one who is not a renunciant cannot serve as a preceptor.

Furthermore, when one receives the full precepts (*upasampadā*) from others, does one obtain the precepts? The answer is that one obtains the precepts. Although there is a textual passage regarding the primary explanation, it is also not to be relied upon;

if the *Saṃgha* commits an offense, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), which does not apply to laypeople. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a person does not request a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or ask for the precepts, one must not confer them;
[if one does so], it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Karmavastu-śāstra* states: "At the time of receiving the full precepts, one does not request a preceptor."

Regarding the attainment of the precepts when a monk commits a *duṣkṛta* offense, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one receives the precepts from a person who has no *upādhyāya*, the recipient attains the precepts, but the assembly of monks incurs an offense.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If one first requests an *upādhyāya* and receives the ten precepts while the *upādhyāya* is not present, one still attains the ten precepts.
However, if the *upādhyāya* dies while the ten precepts are being received, or if one learns of his death during the reception of the precepts, the ordination is invalid."

One who does not hear or know [the precepts] cannot receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). If the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) is not present, one does not obtain the precepts because the assembly (*saṃgha*) is incomplete.

Even if the number [of monks] is complete, if there is no *upādhyāya*, one still obtains the precepts. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one confers full ordination without an *upādhyāya*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
This person does obtain the precepts. If a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) acts as the *upādhyāya* and confers ordination upon another, the recipient obtains the precepts.

When the assembly of monks commits an offense, they inquire of the *karmavācanā* master (the *karmadāna*). Why is it that the instructor (*śikṣācārya*) alone is not appointed, while others are? The explanation is as follows:
When the instructor goes forth from the assembly to pose difficult questions, if he were not appointed by the Sangha, he would have no authority to ask them arbitrarily;

therefore, he must be appointed by the Sangha to carry out the mission and inquire. However, since the *karmadāna* remains within the assembly when inquiring, why does he require appointment by the Sangha? If that were the case, then regarding the compilation of the Dharma...
Question: The *piṭaka* is also compiled through communal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*). Why is it necessary to formally appoint [the reciters]? Answer:

The compilation is for the sake of the Saṃgha as a whole, not for the sake of any individual. If no one were appointed, it would be unknown who should ask and who should answer; therefore, it is necessary to appoint those who will engage in the questioning and answering. Only when the persons for the questioning and answering are fixed can the compilation proceed.

As for the *karmadāna* (the master of ceremonies), when conferring the full ordination upon an individual, the preceptors must first be formally requested and fixed; alternatively, they may already be present within the assembly.
Therefore, there is no formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha for the instructor who goes to question the *karmakāraka*.
The reason there is no formal motion to harmonize the Saṃgha is that the *karma* itself involves questioning within the assembly, and furthermore, the instructor is not appointed by the Saṃgha.

Since the instructor has been appointed by the Saṃgha and dispatched on its behalf to ask the questions, why would it be necessary to further harmonize the assembly? When asking about the fundamental rules, the *bhikṣuṇī* is permitted to hear the *karma*.

Regarding the *Mofa* (Method of Grinding), it states that although one has not yet received the precepts, because one has previously heard the *karmavācanā*, one should sit below the *mahābhikṣuṇīs* to listen;
thus, when others receive the precepts, one does not commit the offense of obstructing the *karmavācanā*, as this is no different from the Dharma originally heard.

Question: If that is so, why does the instructor (*śāstṛ*) who performs the single formal motion (*jñapti*) not commit the offense of obstruction? Answer: It is explained that he has previously heard the *karmavācanā*.

The teacher performs a single formal announcement (*jñapti*), and the person appointed by him likewise performs a single formal announcement; although the matters differ, they are not distinct in being a single formal announcement, and thus it is permitted without offense.
One must not generalize by saying that this also occurs when reaching the stage of the Great Saṃgha; for although the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is the same, the assemblies differ.

Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that after receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*), one first recites the eight heavy rules (*gurudharma*), next recites the four similes, and afterwards recites [the other rules].
The eight [precepts] do not transgress the Dharma; furthermore, when a nun recites the four *niśrayas*, she does not include sitting under a tree.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that after the *karmavācanā* has been recited, one first recites the four *niśrayas*, followed by the four grave offenses and the eight grave offenses, as detailed in that Vinaya.
Regarding the brief exposition of the thirteen difficulties, there are seven sections in total.

First, the brief explanation according to the difficulties: although the difficulties follow a thousand paths, they are explained here by prioritizing the most significant ones; thus, the thirteen are briefly presented. Among these, the first is the "offense of extreme transgression" (*antāpatti*).
Question: Why is this considered an offense of extreme transgression? Answer: It is not because of killing or stealing that it is defined as an extreme transgression. If...
If ordinary people who act in the same way should also be called "limit" (*anta*), then one who fails to receive the precepts should also be called a "limit.
If being outside the assembly is what defines a "limit," then those subject to banishment should not be considered "limits," as they have not yet been banished.
If being [guilty of] a *pārājika* offense is what defines a "limit," then a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) guilty of a *duṣkṛta* offense should not be a "limit. This is now discussed correctly.

The essence of a "liminal offense" (*pārājika*) consists of transgressing the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts; because one does not perform what should be done or performs what is forbidden, it is called a "liminal sin.
Question: Why is such a person not called a "one who has been expelled" (*pārivāsika*)? Answer: In truth, that term should indeed be used.

However, because this person has already undergone the formal renunciation of the precepts (*śīla-tyāga*), the previous designation is not applied. Furthermore, these two types of persons are designated by the name [of their status] based on the qualities they acquired while in the position of a *bhikṣu*.

Regarding "expulsion" (*pārājika*), it cannot be called a "limiting principle" (*antya-naya*) because it applies to only one person; however, since two distinct individuals are involved, the designation of the "limit" is retained for the sake of following the original terminology.

Second, regarding the "corruption of a nun's pure conduct": as the *Cīvara-vinaya* states, if two noble nuns—whether Arhats or Anāgāmins—engage in such conduct at the beginning, middle, or end, they are all termed "corruptors of pure conduct," regardless of whether they are abiding in those two fruits or are ordinary persons.

Now, regarding the observance of precepts: if one initially experiences pleasure [in breaking them], this destroys the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) of a *śrāmaṇerī*, and subsequently she is no longer called a *bhikṣuṇī*.

If it is asked: "If one does not destroy the sacred realm (*āryaviṣaya*), how can it constitute an obstacle? The explanation says: provided that the karmic action is completed, it constitutes an obstruction to the precepts regardless of whether there was prior destruction.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī* violates [the rules], it does not obstruct her from leaving the household life; however, for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it does."

If a *bhikṣuṇī* engages in sexual intercourse at any of the three places, it is all termed "corrupting a *bhikṣuṇī*. Even if a *bhikṣuṇī* herself takes pleasure in engaging in sexual intercourse with a layperson (*avadātavasana*), it does not obstruct her from leaving the household life.
Some say that as long as one possesses the full precepts, regardless of whether they are pure or impure, any act of arrogance or violation is grave;
however, because the object encountered by one who has not yet completed the [full] period is light, it does not obstruct the precepts. Therefore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says: "You have not..."

Regarding the offense of defiling a bhikṣuṇī, it is not necessary to distinguish between the two lower assemblies [of śrāmaṇerīs and śikṣamāṇās]; one need only ensure that she is fully ordained (upasampadā), regardless of whether her conduct is pure or impure.
When compared with laypeople, all bhikṣuṇīs are objects of veneration. This is consistent across both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Although the introductory sections of the three schools do not explicitly mention "purity or impurity," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is the most excellent on this point. Furthermore, the *Samantapāsādikā* states that killing an ordinary bhikṣuṇī—even one who has attained up to the third fruit of the path—constitutes a pārājika offense.
None of these obstruct the *vaipulya-daśacakra-śīla*. Why is it that killing a *pratyekabuddha* is not a *ānantarya* (heinous) offense, yet it defiles a *bhikṣuṇī* and obstructs the precepts?

The explanation says: because killing damages a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), the commission of the offense is established as a *ānantarya*. Those mentioned below are not ultimate fields of merit; therefore, killing them does not constitute a *ānantarya*. Question:
If one who has attained the two fruits (*phala*) experiences pleasure at that moment, yet incurs a grave offense, should they not fall into hell?

Question: Is it a retribution? Answer: It is explained that it is not received. If this is so, why is it that ordinary nuns receive retribution? Answer: Because they possess both "with-opposition" (*sapratigha*) and "without-opposition" (*apratigha*), they do not constitute a valid precedent.
Question: This may apply to laymen; however, for laywomen, there is no destruction of the *saṃgha* that surpasses this one-sided [offense].

If this is so, a monk has two ways of breaking the *saṃgha*, and thus there can be the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for violating a formal admonition; yet a nun lacks the breaking of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Since she lacks one [of these two conditions], she should not incur the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The commentary explains: Although a *bhikṣuṇī* lacks the power to break the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), the method of admonition applies to her; however, for a laywoman to corrupt a *bhikṣuṇī* is entirely impermissible.
Furthermore, it is explained that corrupting a *bhikṣu* also constitutes an obstacle (*vighna*). Because the case of a man corrupting a *bhikṣu* is rare, it is not explicitly mentioned;

yet, since the principle of obstructing the precepts (*śīla*) is established as an obstacle, Śraddhākaravarman states: "O you who receive the five precepts, do you not commit [the offense of] violating a *bhikṣu*?"
Regarding the bhikṣuṇī: as for the third type, one who receives the precepts with a thieving mind, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that there are three kinds of theft:

first, stealing the form, which means going forth on one's own without a teacher, not declaring one’s seniority as a bhikṣu, not receiving prostrations from others in accordance with their ordination age, not participating in the legal affairs of the Saṃgha, and not receiving offerings;
second, stealing the harmony, which means having a teacher and going forth to receive the ten precepts, yet [failing to complete the full ordination].

If one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) goes to another region, or if one who claims to have ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*) pays homage according to the sequence, enters the *saṃgha* for the *poṣadha*, or accepts the faithful offerings (*śraddhā-deya*) of others—whether two or three of these acts are committed as theft—it should be understood by analogy with what precedes. If one steals the form [of ordination], they do not participate in the Dharma-affairs;

yet, if they wish to leave the household life again and receive the precepts, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a *śrāmaṇera* thinks thus: 'When the *poṣadha* is being recited, what is being discussed?'"

[The candidate] immediately enters beneath the bed to eavesdrop. If they are clever enough to remember the words from the beginning, middle, and end [of the recitation], they shall not be granted the precepts;

otherwise, they may receive them. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one listens to two or three *poṣadha* ceremonies, one should not receive the precepts; even if already received, one should be expelled.
If one listens to only one *poṣadha*, whether one listens or does not listen, one should receive them. The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: "A śrāmaṇera falsely claims to be a bhikṣu..."
When a practitioner of the Way (a *dàorén*) receives a single prostration from a *mahābhikṣu*, this is called the "obstacle of dwelling like a thief" (*zézhù nán*).

Regarding this, one interpretation of the Vinaya states that it occurs when one goes before one, two, or three *bhikṣus*; thus, we know that this obstacle applies to both face-to-face (*duìshǒu*) and communal (*zhòngfǎ*) rituals.

Although the primary interpretation holds that even if one, two, or three members of the Saṃgha are present, the act of assuming the form [of a monk] in their presence does not constitute this obstacle—since these are cases of face-to-face interaction with individuals—it remains an obstacle nonetheless.

Dharma. Regarding the fourth point, the objection that the two paths are undermined: this primarily addresses the refutation of internal [paths] while also encompassing the refutation of external ones.

As for the question of why the objection that a śrāmaṇera’s offense does not constitute a "difficulty" (ānantarya) is raised—why are theft and killing equally obstacles to the precepts? The answer is: although the Great and Small Vehicles differ, they are identical in that these constitute root offenses.
If that is so, why do the latter four grave offenses committed by nuns and the two lower assemblies not obstruct the precepts? The answer is: the former four...
If there is a violation regarding the limited categories (*parimāṇa*), it constitutes an obstruction to the precepts; the latter four branches provide deep protection against dissimilar cases.

Regarding the fifth difficulty concerning eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are five types: first, those incapable from birth; second, those with a half-monthly [capacity];

third, those with uncertain capacity; fourth, those capable through envy of others' acts; and fifth, those capable due to others' sexual acts or those who are diseased and decayed. Among these, the first four constitute the formal obstacles.

Regarding the fifth [case]: if one remains unmoving while listening, even though they are unmoving; or if one who has returned to lay life and renounced the precepts comes again to receive them, they should not be granted them, and the recipient may be expelled. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are also six [cases]: first, those incapable of birth; second, those born from the jealousy of a husband and wife; third, those whose [genitals] were crushed at birth; fourth, those whose [genitals] were cut off by a king’s minister to serve as a gatekeeper; fifth, those [from] before...; sixth, those who have committed the five heinous crimes. As for the first, "incapable of birth," this refers to those who, having been castrated, have their male organ removed. The second, "born from the jealousy of a husband and wife," refers to those born from the union of a man and woman who harbor mutual jealousy. The third, "crushed at birth," refers to those whose organs were damaged during birth. The fourth, "cut off by a king’s minister," refers to those whose organs were severed by a royal official to serve as a gatekeeper. The fifth, "those from before," refers to those who have previously committed the five heinous crimes. A śrāmaṇera should not [possess it], yet if one who was formerly a great bhikṣu has discarded the precepts and now wishes to receive them, it may exist in terms of the relationship between principal and attendant;
therefore, this too must be asked. Regarding the tenth difficulty, the shedding of the Buddha’s blood:
among the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), why is only the shedding of the Buddha’s blood designated as being associated with an evil mind, while the other four heinous crimes are not?

Regarding the term "evil intent" (*duṣṭacitta*): the commentary explains that if one draws blood by means of medical acupuncture for the purpose of treating a disease, or strikes the Buddha [in such a context], this is not considered evil intent.
What is here called "evil intent" refers to Devadatta’s original intention to sever the Buddha’s life-force and draw blood; therefore, it is so named.
When the *Pañcavargika* monks drew blood with evil intent and caused a schism in the Saṃgha, they did not know how to conduct themselves. The Buddha said: [They should wait upon and serve him.]

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* asks: "In reality, no blood was shed and life could not have been severed;

Regarding the two categories of "definitive" (*niyata*) and "indeterminate" (*aniyata*), although both possess all the requisite conditions, they do not give rise to the precepts. Among these, those who possess the thirteen obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*) are designated as "obstacles" because they possess both [categories];

others, lacking these, are designated merely as "prohibitions" (*pratibandha*). Question: Why is it that among the thirteen, only the first obstacle alone receives the designation "extreme" (*anta*), while the others do not?
Answer: The term "extreme" possesses four meanings: (1) having previously attained the internal Dharma, one is now adrift among the external multitudes; thus, it may be called "extreme."
All others have not yet entered [the order], with the exception of those who have violated a bhikṣuṇī’s pure conduct; these two cases are common to both the great saṃgha and śrāmaṇeras.
Those who are ineligible for ordination are termed "borderline" (prāntakoṭika). The two types of schism—breaking the path and breaking the saṃgha—do not apply to śrāmaṇeras.

The "thieving mind" (caura-citta) is restricted to śrāmaṇeras and does not apply to the great saṃgha. Although these three obtain the internal dharma, they do not interpenetrate one another; therefore, they are designated as "others."

Regarding the three types of persons who do not constitute "ordinary people" (prākṛta-pudgala): eunuchs, those who have killed their parents, Arhats, non-humans, animals, and hermaphrodites—these seven are ordinary people for whom the designation of "extremes" (anta) is not established.

As for the four offenses that constitute ultimate transgressions (antya-avadya), they are established as extremes, with the exception of shedding the blood of a Buddha, because that is a preparatory act (prayoga) and because it concerns an ordinary person.
Question: If a nun commits one of the latter four grave offenses (pārājika) and then renounces her vows, does she fall into an extreme offense?

An objector says: "If that is so, then the latter four [offenses] do not apply to śrāmaṇerikās; yet those who receive the name 'one who has committed a pārājika offense' include those who have broken the harmony of the Saṃgha and so forth, which would also apply to śrāmaṇeras.
This creates a difficulty. The solution explains: "To avoid this difficulty, when a bhikṣuṇī commits any of the eight grave offenses (gurudharma), none are designated by the name 'pārājika.
Why? Because even if a bhikṣuṇī formally renounces the precepts according to the Dharma, she is not permitted to re-enter the order."
Why must one establish "offenses involving defeat" (*pārājika*)? This objection is without hindrance.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that the first [offense] is a violation of the Buddha’s teachings and thus incurs a grave offense, whereas for the remaining [offenses], there is no teaching to be violated in accordance with each specific matter. Moreover, this term "defeat" (*pārājika*) refers specifically to the thirteen [offenses];

if one were to see the first as "defeat" and thereby wish to name all the others "defeats," then one would also have to say that everything up to the "two-sexed" category [the thirteenth] is likewise a defeat.
Are all twelve [categories] characterized by both genders? "Difficulties" (*dūṣaṇa*) is a term for specific instances, while "objections" (*codya*) is a general designation.
Regarding the fourth point, which exhaustively encompasses objections, there are two ways of explaining it: first, as verbal objections, which are in fact infinite in number.

Furthermore, the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that those who find it difficult to receive the precepts number thirteen times thirteen. It also says that those who have severed their roots of goodness cannot obtain the precepts.

The *Saddharma-smṛty-upasthāna-sūtra* states that six types of persons do not obstruct the path of gods, but they do obstruct the noble path: eunuchs, animals, those with two sexual organs, those who live as thieves within the monastic community, those who have violated a nun, and those who have destroyed the path.
If one has committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), both the paths of gods and humans and the noble path are obstructed. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, furthermore...
Regarding the case of a śrāmaṇera with evil wrong views, the *Karmavastu-śīra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Head of the Karmavastu) states that he does not obtain the precepts.

The *Vinayottaragrantha-vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Clarification of Obtaining the Precepts) says: "The Vinaya states that twenty kinds of persons do not obtain the precepts," as detailed in that treatise. Furthermore, regarding the listing of thirteen [types of persons]:

if one asks, "Does one obtain the precepts immediately? the answer is that one does not obtain them. For the others, if there is [a defect], one does not obtain them; if there is none, one obtains the precepts even without asking.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one receives the precepts without robes and bowl, [is it still valid]? Question: "If that is so, why are robes and bowl strictly required? Answer:
"First, for the sake of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*); second, to inspire faith and reverence in others; third, to manifest a distinct appearance.

Since the internal virtues are different, the external appearances must also be different. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If one confers the precepts without robes and bowl, the preceptor and the assembly incur an offense."
Regarding the statement that "obtaining the precepts" does not exhaustively cover all difficulties because they are not uniform:

herein, we must take into account those who have left the household life with a sincere mind and seek the precepts through the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) performed by the Saṃgha; such cases are not classified as "difficulties. All others fall into the category of immeasurable difficulties and are not included here as primary concerns.
For example, it is a difficulty if an animal takes on the form of a person and seeks the precepts; other animals, however, do not come [to seek them].

Question: If all requests for ordination are not subsumed under this [category], then those who have not reached twenty years of age and yet possess the intention to receive the precepts but do not obtain them—should these not be included among the "difficult cases"?

Answer: They are definitely not included; they belong to the category of those under thirteen years of age. Once they reach the required age, they may obtain them; therefore, the principle does not apply to them. Question:
If that is so, then a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) who has been in office for nine years should also not be able to confer the precepts? Answer: No, because he has not yet completed [the full term].

Although these are all equally positions of exclusion (*pratiṣedha*), because they differ in being remote conditions (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*) versus direct causes (*hetu-pratyaya*), there is a distinction between attaining and not attaining [the precepts].

There should likewise be a difficulty regarding those whose *śikṣā* is incomplete; this should be resolved according to the specific circumstances. Question: Why are the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv antarāyāḥ*) not mentioned here? Answer: These obstruct the precepts, whereas those [eight] obstruct hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*);
therefore, they are omitted here. Furthermore, the interpretation is no different from what was stated previously. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The four disparagements destroy the eight."
The *Nanchengshi* (Establishment of Difficulties) states that there are four conditions for success: first, dwelling in a virtuous place; second, relying on virtuous persons;

third, giving rise to right mindfulness; and fourth, planting roots of goodness. The first cycle [of practice] overcomes five difficulties: long lifespans in the three miserable realms (*durgati*), birth in Uttarakuru, being born before or after a Buddha, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence, and being deaf, blind, or mute.
These have been detailed and distinguished previously; since those [beings] do not come with a mind [to seek the Dharma], they are excluded.
The request is therefore not an instance of this category.

Regarding the inclusion of the thirteen obstacles (*ānantarya*) within the fifth [category], the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*): the single obstacle of the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*) is comprised within the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) due to an abundance of desire;

furthermore, as one who lacks virility, it also falls on the side of the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). The remaining nine—the grave offenses (*pārājika*), the violation of a nun, the malicious intent to cause schism, and the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*)—are included therein.

The karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*) subsume those that obstruct the arising of the precepts; the former four [obstructions] are karmic, while those that obstruct realization consist only of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*).
The former four are not obstructions; the two regarding humans and animals with dual sexual organs are retributive obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

Question: Among the thirteen difficulties (*trayodaśa-duskaras*), how many are broad and how many are narrow? How many are light and how many are heavy? Answer: If distinguished according to the thirteen, the karmic [obstructions] are broad, while among the retributive, the afflictions are heavy.

The affliction-obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is the most narrow; if explained broadly, the three obstructions encompass all five destinies. The retribution-obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*) is the most extensive.

Among the afflictions, the karma-obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*) is the most narrow, as it arises only in a small portion of human beings. Regarding the correlation with the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*), the first seven are retribution, while the last one is affliction.
There is no karma-obstruction among the eight difficult conditions. As for their relative gravity: the affliction-obstruction is the root of all obstructions, because of this...
Regarding heavy karma, medium retribution, and light karma: as for whether they can be transformed or not, those karmic obstacles whose retribution cannot be transformed are considered heavy;
the other two, being transformable and thus able to be extinguished, are described as light.

Regarding the sixth point, "Penetration and Obstruction": Question: Why are non-humans, animals, and furthermore eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) not separately categorized?

Answer: Because the path is received among humans, it is explained in terms of obstructions starting from eunuchs and those with dual sexual organs. Animals lack the very capacity to receive the path; thus, they constitute a difficulty [of a different order].
Although there are eunuchs and those with dual sexual organs, these do not obstruct the precepts; therefore, they are not described as difficulties. Question: Why is this so?

Regarding the statement that gods constitute an obstacle, the response is that because gods are attached to pleasure, they do not seek to leave the household life; however, if one can cultivate revulsion toward it and seeks to receive the precepts, one obtains them.
This is why the *Caturvarga-vinaya* states that even a son of heaven (*devaputra*) is included among those who are obstacles. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Bā-śā-lùn*) states:
"Maudgalyāyana’s disciple was ill and sought Jīvaka, but upon encountering him in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he found Jīvaka so deeply immersed in pleasure that he could not show him respect."

The Master explains this extensively according to the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*. Regarding the locations: in the northern continent (Uttarakuru), there are obstacles regarding retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) and non-manifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*), but the meaning of obstructing the precepts is not taught;

although these obstacles may exist in the other three continents, they differ in degree. In the eastern and western continents, there are eleven [obstacles], excluding shedding the blood of a Buddha and causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
in the southern continent (Jambudvīpa), all thirteen are present. Regarding the timing: while the Buddha was alive, there were thirteen; after his passing, there are only ten.
First, regarding those facing others: among men there are thirteen, while for women there are only twelve. If categorized according to bhikṣus, there are eleven;

excluding one who has committed a grave offense against a nun (*niḥśīla*), one who is a thief-like resident (*steyāsaṃvāsika*), and a śrāmaṇera, there are ten. There are no two [cases] involving one who has destroyed a nun. Among the laity, there are also ten, with no two cases involving one who has committed a pārājika offense.

Seventh, regarding the determination of the arising of obstacles based on the sequence of precepts: if one has fundamentally never reached the point of receiving the precepts, one incurs only the ten obstacles as mentioned above.

If one has received the śrāmaṇera precepts, one incurs the ten obstacles as mentioned above. If one has previously received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and subsequently renounced it, there may be eleven obstacles, adding the offense of a grave transgression (*pārājika*).

If one has received the full ordination and not renounced it, the obstacle of "living like a thief" (*cora-vāsa*) does not arise; even if it were to arise, it would not [constitute a formal obstacle].
Conversely, regarding the name "offenses of extreme gravity" (*ānantarya*), there are eleven types; among these eleven, some are termed "obstacles" (*dūṣaṇa*) while others are not.

Those such as the destruction of the two sexual organs or the emergence of hermaphroditism are definitely a loss of the precepts; because they obstruct the precepts, they are termed "obstacles. As for the two classes of beings, such as animals, that are termed "obstacles":

if they are determined to be transformations where the retribution has changed such that they lose the precepts, they are termed "obstacles"; however, those resulting from supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) are merely temporary.
Regarding the five types of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs), if they were already so before receiving the precepts, none may obtain them due to the gravity of their prior offense.

However, if they become so after having received the precepts, these are not grave karmic offenses and they do not lose the precepts. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between those who are expelled and those who are not.

Specifically, one who self-amputates among the *paṇḍakas* must be expelled because of their loathing for their own body; this applies whether they were rendered so by another or as a result of karmic retribution.

Those such as those born [in the intermediate state] and so forth do not need to be expelled, for it is not because they are loathsome bodies that they are excluded; however, one cannot lose the precepts simply by being expelled.

Those who may be expelled lose the precepts, whereas others—even if they are born [in such states]—merely cease their own transgressions of the precepts. Now, expulsion certainly does not cause one to lose the precepts.

These thirteen cases, along with the sixteen cases of obstruction (*pārājika*), are not explained here because they are redundant. This also applies to the "extreme offenses" (*antimā āpatti*), the "thief-mind," and the "breaking of the two paths."
The general explanation of the reasons for the fourfold negation is as analyzed in the four sections.
*Sifenlü shi pin yi chao*, Scroll One, Part One;
*Sifenlü shi pin yi chao*, Scroll One, Part Two.
Regarding the discourse on "ignorance through non-learning," the gradual and sudden approaches are briefly preserved in four sections.
First, explaining the gradual and sudden by means of contrasting "non-learning" and "ignorance":

first, interpreting "non-learning" and "ignorance," this refers to ceasing transgressions across all phenomena; to cease the mind from learning is itself the attainment of the offense of non-learning.

Furthermore, regarding the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*), while one may simultaneously commit two offenses, there is no principle of "sudden" transgression whereby one could violate all precepts at once.

This resolves the great difficulty. At the time when one is not studying, it is precisely the offense of non-study; because of this non-study, one fails to comprehend the Dharma, and only then is the offense of ignorance incurred.

Since these preceding and succeeding mental states arise sequentially, they cannot be committed as a double offense simultaneously. How, then, can it be said that one incurs two names of offenses concurrently?
Regarding this "sudden" [attainment], it is further explained that the arising of the minds of "not learning" and "ignorance" occurs sequentially rather than simultaneously;

thus, this too is gradual and cannot be called sudden. As for textual evidence regarding "not learning" and "ignorance," the Vinaya states: "If one does not learn the *karmavācanā* or recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* for five years, one incurs an offense.
This is because if one does not recite and uphold the ritual procedures (*dharmas*), their performance will be difficult to accomplish.
Because [the precepts] were established and because they were sent forth for the purpose of study, it is said now that one incurs an offense if one does not recite them;

this too presents a difficulty. That [statement] is merely a general discussion of the methods for transforming others. If there were an offense therein, why did he later say, "You shall attain the four fruits"? If one does not attain them, one should likewise incur an offense;
why then was there no mention of repenting for the offense of failing to attain the four fruits? Furthermore, it says: "The 'establishment' (or 'prohibition') refers to..."
That which can be regulated includes the training rules (*śikṣā*) and the four fruits of the path (*catur-phala*); that which cannot be regulated includes independent afflictions (*svatantra-kleśa*).

That which can be regulated includes the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony). Regarding the teachings to be learned, they do not exceed two types of instruction. What are these two? First, prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), and second, permission (*anujñā*).
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "For those who commit offenses, there is prohibition; for those who do not commit offenses, there is permission. Prohibition is of two kinds.
1. To perform what is enjoined is without fault; to fail to comply is sinful. 2. To refrain from what is prohibited is without transgression;
to act contrary to it is a violation. For those who listen to the teachings, there is no offense whether they perform or do not perform [the prescribed acts].

Within this context, "observance through performance" (*kṛta-śīla*) and "violation through non-performance" (*akṛta-śīla*) are explained specifically in relation to matters within the two types of teachings. However, "observance through refraining" (*virati-śīla*) and "violation through performance" (*pravṛtti-śīla*) apply generally to both matters and the dharmas within the two types of teachings.
Within the category of various prohibitions (*pratiṣedha-dvāra*), there are two types of matters: first, matters that are not to be practiced, such as perceiving a human being as a non-human;

second, matters that are to be practiced, such as the substance, size, and dimensions of robes and alms bowls. Regarding matters within the category of permissions (*anujñā-dvāra*), these are exclusively those that are to be practiced, such as the dimensions of a dwelling in cubits, the length and breadth of extra robes, and so forth.
"Dharma" refers to the construction of a dwelling and the formal request for authorization (*jñapti*).
This is the second section, providing a detailed explanation of gradual and sudden transgressions. Regarding the offense of failing to train, there can be both gradual and sudden forms;
however, regarding the offense of ignorance, it is only gradual and not sudden. The reason for knowing this is as follows:

if one intends in one's mind to refrain from training in all dharmas that ought to be learned, one incurs the offense of failing to train suddenly with respect to each and every dharma; the opposite is true [in the case of ignorance].

Regarding the offenses for which one is culpable: at the very moment one originally received the precepts, one generated that many wholesome factors of restraint to prevent the fault of failing to train.
If one now generally adopts a mind of non-training, would this not constitute an immediate transgression of numerous offenses? How then can it be called "gradual"?

If one intends that although one does not train in the sūtras, one will train in everything else, then from the perspective of not training in the sūtras, one incurs only a single offense; this is what is designated as "gradual."
Regarding "gradual" (anupūrva): why is it that there is ignorance only gradually and not instantaneously? It is because the fault of ignorance must necessarily depend upon conditions;

only when one fails to understand due to these conditions is the offense established. Within a single moment of mind, it is impossible to encounter all phenomena simultaneously and thereby understand them all at once;
rather, it is through encountering them individually that one commits the offense. Therefore, it is prescribed as "gradual" and not called "instantaneous."
The third demarcation has three distinctions: namely, with respect to the teaching, in relation to practice, and in terms of the faculties.

Regarding "with respect to the teaching," this refers to the study itself; from beginning to end, one must study everything. If one does not study, one incurs the offense of non-study, which is the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

After five summer retreats (*varṣa*), one is then subject to different [rules] than those mentioned previously. "Relating to practice" means that there are degrees of depth [in realization]. Thus, there are distinctions.

Those with limited understanding truly hope that what is above them is not deficient and what is below them is sufficient; yet if they do not exercise restraint, it is because they rely on their slight understanding and equate themselves with those of high realization.
