Regarding the interpretation that one need not request the position again: although it is not identical [to the previous case], since the monks have already completed the formal act (*jñapti*) and the person is no different, there is no need for another request.

Furthermore, according to another interpretation, although the person is not different, because there is a distinction between being fully equipped and not fully equipped with the requisites, one must request it again. Question: Is the offense incurred when either one of the two conditions is violated, or is it incurred only when both are violated?

Answer: The *Śāriputrābhidharma* (or *Samantapāsādikā*, as indicated by "Sànjiàn") states: "If the length is reduced by one span (*vitasti*) or more, or if the width exceeds one span, [the robe is invalid]."

If the width is reduced by one *vitasti* (span) and the length exceeds one *vitasti*, both constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; since the offense applies even when only one dimension exceeds the limit, how much more so when both length and width exceed it?
Regarding the case of groundlessly slandering another with the expectation that the Saṃgha will understand the claim to be false: this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for lying.

However, the *Samantapāsādikā* states that there is no offense, because the slander is entirely based on a false pretext; this ruling concerns cases where the slander is uttered solely for the purpose of defaming the other.

If one speaks [falsely] while also intending to deceive the Saṃgha, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense with respect to the person [defamed], and a *pāyattika* offense with respect to the Saṃgha. What is the distinction between the offenses for monks and nuns?

Why is it that slandering is treated the same as for the great monks (*bhikṣu*), yet striking is treated the same as for a *śrāmaṇera*? Answer: Striking is categorized according to the status of the recipient, whereas slandering is categorized according to the formal qualifications (*upasaṃpadā*) of the recipient.
If one follows other Vinayas, striking and slandering are similar. Question: If one says that a *bhikṣu* must necessarily have a pure basis (*viśuddha-pratyaya*) [for his actions to be valid]?
Question: Since they have arisen with purity, why do they enter the *karmavācanā* (formal procedure) unanimously? Why does the Vinaya state that "those persons are not pure"? Answer:

Because they have committed offenses belonging to the lower four categories (*catur-apatti-skandha*), they are said to be impure. Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Impure" refers to those who have slandered the Dharma of the assembly;

both parties must be pure regarding what has been seen or heard in order to perform the ritual act (*karmavastu*). Now, these individuals intentionally violate this requirement for visible purity, falsely claiming that they have committed an offense, thereby distressing themselves and others.

Whether one questions [the object] as pure or impure, all constitute the offense of slander (*pāradūṣaṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that a monk who has broken the precepts commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for slander, this is discussed in terms of the general status of the person, because one takes [the matter] as a basis for slander and undergoes disciplinary punishment; thus, it distinguishes between the pure and the turbid. Question:

If what was previously slandered was actually impure, yet the mind of the slanderer considered it pure while telling others it was impure, and one obtains the ultimate *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) offense—[is this so] because my previous object was [actually pure]?
If one kills a non-human while perceiving them as a human, one should also incur the ultimate offense of *pārājika*.

If the one killed is actually a non-human, yet I have slandered [the victim] as being truly impure, and while perceiving them as pure in my mind, I perceive them as a human—if I speak of them as impure while having the perception of purity, I would immediately incur the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Likewise, if one kills a non-human while perceiving them as a human, one should similarly incur *pārājika*.

Regarding the statement that slandering others is a transgression committed through the mental formation of an evil intention (*āśaya*), one might argue: "If even the mere mental formation of an evil intention constitutes a sin, then the resolve to kill—which is the most heinous act—is certainly more than just a mental formation of an intention;
it must likewise constitute a sin through the mental formation [of the act]. One should simply form the intention to slander without desiring to end a life;

this evil mind is light, yet one still incurs a sin through the mental formation. Why, then, does one not incur a sin through the mental formation when one gives rise to a great evil mind and actually ends a human life? Furthermore, later...
If one perceives what is actually pure as impure and says to another, "This is impure," there is no offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Furthermore, if one perceives a living person as a wooden stump and kills them, there is likewise no *pārājika* offense. In both cases, the act of killing involves a discrepancy between the mind and the object; this slander also involves a discrepancy between the mind and the object.
How can one be established as complete while the other is not? The answer is: slander is defined by the falsity of the intention, whereas killing is defined by the [actual] death.

If both the object and the subject were equally real, one would then incur an offense. As it says in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: "Tapassa himself declared he was pure, while Maitrāyaṇī herself declared she had been slandered.
When asked by the Buddha—He who is the All-Knowing One and well-acquainted with purity and impurity—why did He not speak to testify that Tapassa was pure and Maitrāyaṇī was guilty?
The answer is given in the *Śāstra*, which states there are two meanings: first, if the Buddha were to testify...
First, because one is right and the other is wrong, people give rise to slander, claiming that the Buddha has likes and dislikes.

Second, if it were proven that Trapusa committed an offense, he would not be exempt from the offense in the present; therefore, if one does not speak of the transgression, the karmic fruit will follow.

For this reason, one must speak for oneself regarding the disciplinary punishment. What is called the "root"? Seeing and hearing are the roots, for they can give rise to the speech that brings forth the accusation. Question: If that is so...

If seeing and hearing cannot give rise to slanderous speech, why are they not called "roots"? If slander occurs only when spoken from a mind of hatred, then my proposal [that seeing and hearing are roots] is also stated with respect to the mind.
The explanation says: in reality, these should also apply proximately, as both are dependent on the mind; however, there is a distinction regarding their remote roots.
Since that [slanderous mind] arises only after seeing and hearing have occurred, seeing and hearing function as the roots. This is the absence [of such a root].

Question: When one is subjected to an unjust matter, it is necessary that a mind of anger first arises, after which slander is initiated; thus, this [anger] is the root of the existence [of slander]. Question:
If that were so, then for me as well, since the root does not exist, the subsequent arising of a mind of slander would also have to be preceded by the existence of that root.

Answer: This is not necessarily so. It is not because of the absence of a root that the mind of slander arises; rather, it arises precisely because of the perception [of an object], which gives rise to the mind of accusation. If that were so...
Since one who possesses groundless [knowledge] does not give rise to slander, that which lacks ground cannot serve as the basis for slander.

Just as one may possess a view yet fail to bring charges, so too there may be a view that is not the basis for bringing charges. The explanation is as follows: the Buddha prescribed that one must bring charges based on grounds, but did not prescribe that one may slander without grounds;
therefore, these two do not constitute a parallel case. Question: Among the three bases, why is it that only "seeing" and "hearing" are explicitly mentioned, while "touching" is not included?

Regarding the knowledge of contact (*sparśa*): it is simply the act of meeting [the object], for one cannot taste it otherwise; thus, "knowing" refers to knowing subsequent to seeing or hearing, and is therefore included within the category of seeing and hearing.

As for knowing subsequent to contact, there is no standard for its apprehension; if one were to say directly, "I know by intention," this would not constitute valid proof because it does not arise from seeing or hearing.
Question: If that is so, then after seeing or hearing, there is a mind that conforms to what was seen or heard.
If one follows that [position], how does one know what is "knowingly"? The answer is that this is not known by itself; it must be known through seeing or hearing.
Thus, the prior transgression is an external object that must be known through seeing or hearing; if there were no seeing or hearing, one would not know the transgression. Question:
If that is so, how can there be "knowledge" in the case of minor falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*)? Answer: In the case of minor falsehood, it is not necessarily required to apprehend an external object.

Therefore, it must be established that "knowing" (jñāna) is [the specific function]; thus, the denial of the object is not a separate category of the dharma-āyatana, and for this reason it is not termed "knowing.

According to the commentary on the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, doubt (*vicikitsā*) pervades the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); among these five objects, that which is not clearly distinguished is called the "root of doubt" (*vicikitsā-mūla*).

This can be understood by reflecting upon it. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that from hearing there arise doubts, each consisting of four matters; however, this pertains specifically to the generation of doubt regarding what is seen (*dṛṣṭa*).

Only the two matters of sexual misconduct and killing are explicitly mentioned because they serve as illustrations; thus, there is no doubt that theft and the root of views consist of only three [offenses], as one cannot speak of "seeing" regarding false speech.
Question: If that is so, why is "seeing" included among the nine minor forms of slander (*kṣudra-abhyākhyāna*) and the harsh speech (*pāruṣya*)?

Answer: This is also because it was seen with one's own eyes or heard being spoken at that time. Question: Is it only the case that doubt arises subsequent to seeing or hearing? [The text continues: No...
After seeing, doubt subsequently arises from hearing; furthermore, after hearing, doubt does not subsequently arise from seeing. The answer is the same:
although doubt may arise after both seeing and hearing, it may also not arise. If the faculties of seeing and hearing are intact, doubt will not arise;
if they are not clearly understood, a doubting mind can arise. However, hearing fundamentally relates to sound, whereas seeing and doubt are not related to sound, because seeing relates [to form].
Regarding doubt concerning form (*rūpa*), it is solely a matter of the mind and is not something heard by the ear; therefore, doubt cannot arise from hearing subsequent to seeing.

Furthermore, since seeing relates to form while hearing relates to doubt that is not form, and since doubt regarding sound relates solely to the internal mind and is not something perceived by the eyes, doubt cannot arise from seeing subsequent to hearing. Question: If it cannot arise [from one after the other]...
Regarding the question of why it is said in the Vinaya that "if one hears from another, this is called the faculty of seeing":

this answer is that while this seeing arises from hearing, it is designated as the "faculty of seeing. This is because the speaker originally possessed [the faculty] and subsequently gave rise to the expression;
furthermore, since hearing encompasses the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), one can speak of the five based on what is heard. Moreover, one cannot speak of hearing after having already seen.
This view is narrow and lacks universal applicability; furthermore, the principle that the five sensory objects do not arise simultaneously with hearing is as previously explained. Question:

Why is it that the offenses for slandering the first two [categories] differ, while the concealment of the first two is said to be the same, resulting in one *pārājika*? Answer: Generally speaking, when discussing slander, there are degrees of severity in the punishment.
Because the first category involves the wrongful suppression [of the Dharma], while the second is minor, the resulting offenses differ. However, regarding the concealment of both, they are the same.

Regarding *pāyattika* (offenses requiring expiation): because a heavy offense with sparse application requires light regulation, while a light offense with frequent application requires heavy regulation, they are categorized under the same heading.

Furthermore, although the first two differ, their purpose of protecting the mind is one and the same; since the impairment of the community is no different, they are categorized as the same *pāyattika*.

As for explaining the two as being the same *pāyattika*: it is because the heavy and sparse, as well as the light and frequent, are identical in their impairment of external protection, and laypeople are not trained to distinguish between light and heavy offenses.

Question: Why are the censure of a fellow monk (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), the same offense as a formal interrogation (*prcchā*), the slander (*abhyākhyāna*), and the concealment of a fault (*paticchādana*)—the latter three being offenses involving confession (*pratideśanīya*)—all concluded with a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) penalty?

Answer: Although there are gradations in the severity of these offenses, the punishment is slight; therefore, they are all classified as *duṣkṛta*. Question: Why is it that slander incurs three [offenses], while concealment incurs two, yet both censure and the formal admonition (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*) are equally concluded with one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?

Explanation: Regarding slander, the focus is on the disciplinary penalty (*daṇḍakarma*). As for concealment, there is a difference in the degree of harm caused to the Saṃgha; because the damage is more severe in one case than the other, there are two distinct categories.

Regarding the three cases of dissension, disparagement, and suspicion, the general sense of "affliction" (*paryavasthāna*) applies equally; it does not specifically refer to the offenses of *ānantarya* (heinous crimes) or the thirteen difficulties (*trayodaśa-vighna*).

If one slanders a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things allowable), one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; likewise, disparaging [the Saṃgha] constitutes a fundamental *sthūlātyaya*. However, among the difficult cases, there is no concealment of faults, because one is no longer a *bhikṣu*. Question:
The text on the settlement of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*) states that concealing another's fault is heavy, while concealing one's own fault is light. Why is this?

Because one’s own [fault] is inherently concealed while another’s is not, the *tāyi-guṇa* (offense of concealment) differs; because one’s own [fault] is rarely spoken of while another’s is frequently spoken of, the *tāyi-guṇa* differs.
However, the Vinaya also states: "There is no offense for slandering oneself; speaking of it oneself incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Why is this so? The answer is:

Slandering is directed toward the Saṃgha, and thus there is no offense; speaking of it oneself is directed toward both the monastic and lay communities, and since it invites public censure, it results in a *duṣkṛta*. Question.

Regarding the question: "Of the thirteen [cases], why is it that the first nine require no admonition while the latter four require admonition? Answer: In the first nine articles, right and wrong are distinct and there is no confusion;
furthermore, because they rely on and conform to [the teachings] until their truth is fully manifest, there is no need for admonition.

In the latter four, however, all involve reliance and confusion, where the principles and practices of the two teachings are intermingled, making it difficult to distinguish between the true and the false. Because people fall into error and evil, these cases are to be pitied.

Therefore, it is necessary for the Saṃgha to admonish him and inquire into the reasons for his schism and his refusal to accept the admonition; these two rules are established. As for the remaining cases, they are answered simply regarding the matter of schism itself.
Since a schism requires a leader and companions who assist one another, when the leader refuses to desist despite being admonished, the first rule is established.

When the four companions support the leader during that time of admonition, and the Saṃgha offers its own admonition, if he still does not desist, the second rule is established. The other two cases involve a single individual.

Question: Since the solitary *pratideśanīya* offense does not rely on a principal or its associates, it is "without a second" (*advitīya*). Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for refusing counsel: if one refuses counsel, should one incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*? Answer:

One interpretation holds that all four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses here rely upon the teachings concerning formal procedures (*karman*). Their verbal expressions are easily confused, as they involve mutual assistance among factions to accomplish the breaking of the Saṃgha.
Of these, the first two destroy the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), while the latter two destroy the formal procedure (*karman*). Furthermore, regarding the first two...

Because the matter of the admonition is grave and the mind of the admonisher is likewise grave, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Although the latter two matters are not grave, they both constitute many offenses.

One who defiles a household or possesses an evil nature may incur offenses of the lower categories; furthermore, one who unreasonably slanders the Saṃgha or relies on oneself to treat others with contempt accumulates transgressions.

If one does not relinquish these after the Saṃgha has admonished them three times, one also incurs a grave offense. Regarding the *liṭṭha* (the one who speaks of desire): [Note: The original text appears to contain a fragmentary reference to the *liṭṭha-vinīta* or a similar category of persons.]
It does not obstruct the principle that there is no confusion regarding violations of the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*).

Furthermore, although he had not yet committed a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) through his speech, because he did not desist after being admonished three times for a minor act, the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) was established. Question: If that is so, since Devadatta was the leader, his commission of a *ānantarya* (heinous) offense should be grave, whereas his four companions committed a light offense;

why then do they not desist from violating the admonition, and why are they equally charged with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension)? Moreover, [this applies to] the case where a nun stands as the leader and companion.
The influence [of the offense] merely serves as a preliminary means and ultimately does not constitute [the full offense]. Why is it that violating an admonition also results in a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?
Furthermore, even if one violates the admonition of a single person, upon examining the matter being admonished, it applies across all seven classes of offenses (*sapta-nikāya*).

Since the offense for violating an admonition is uniformly classified as a single *pāyattika*, we know that the gravity of the matter regarding the refusal of the admonition is uniform. Alternatively, one may interpret this based on whether the mind is insincere or sincere; these four precepts pertain to this.

One who is being admonished may clearly understand that the matter they have committed is false while the Sangha’s admonition is true; therefore, because the transgression of defying their feelings is grave and they do not relinquish their position, they incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

As for one who says, "I do not wish to obstruct [the truth]," yet whose mind is deluded by attachment such that they insist their own view is correct and consider the Sangha’s admonition to be wrong—because they lack the intent to defy the community's feelings, the transgression is slight, and they incur only a *pāyattika*. How is this known? It is as in the case of "schism in the Sangha" (*saṃghabheda*).
Among these, the five factors constitute the "non-initial" [offense]. First, the mind is insincere (heavy); fourth, the mind is sincere (light).

Furthermore, if one violates the admonition of a single person, testing whether the mind is sincere, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for sincerity and a *sthūlātyaya* for insincerity; how much more so when it concerns the admonition of the Saṃgha? How could the mind not be sincere? The offense is heavy for sincerity and light for insincerity.
While the weight of the offense is equal based on sincerity or insincerity, violating the command of the Saṃgha is heavier than that of an individual; it is not otherwise.
Regarding the gravity of offenses, one interpretation cannot be stated: if the mind is insincere or false, the offense is light; if it is sincere, it is heavy.

If that were so, one should say that if the mind is insincere when uttering *liṭṭha*, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. As the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Liṭṭha was a disciple of an outsider who was clever and of sharp faculties.
He was sent to enter the Buddha-dharma, where he learned how to speak perversely. This constitutes an insincere mind and should incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. This is the section on schism (*saṃghabheda*).

Regarding the four propositions: if the mind is real, one commits a *thullaccaya* for killing a human; if the mind is false, one incurs a *pārājika* for killing an animal, and a *thullaccaya* for killing a human.
If one were to compare the residual offense (*sesaka*) with the *thullaccaya*, I would likewise propose that the *pārājika* is comparable to the *thullaccaya*.

If it is argued that humans and animals are not equivalent, I shall likewise respond by stating that their intentions are different. I will no longer elaborate on this; if one’s mind is deluded and clings to reality, yet later realizes the mind was false, [the offense is cleared].

In reality, the reasoning of the preceding and following [positions] is contradictory; we shall now maintain the initial interpretation. Depending on the gravity of the specific act, the resulting offenses differ.

For instance, regarding acts such as killing, stealing, matchmaking, slandering, and even the minor rules (*śaikṣa-dharma*), if one considers them all in relation to the violation of the teachings, they would all equally incur the same offense. However, because the gravity of the acts varies, there are corresponding gradations in the offenses incurred.

Furthermore, although the four permutations regarding the schism of the Saṃgha involve both truth and falsehood, the fact that the offense remains a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* regardless of whether one heeds or disregards the admonitions makes it clear that [the gravity of the offense] depends upon the actual circumstances.

Regarding matters, whether they be true or false, the *Pāṭha-vinaya* asks: "The Sūtras teach that one should simply observe one's own bodily conduct and clearly discern what is wholesome and unwholesome;

yet the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* speaks of 'mutually instructing one another' and so forth. Why do these differ? Answer: The Buddha established the precepts according to the specific circumstances of the time;

thus, while the words may differ, their intent is consistent and they do not contradict one another. This is because the minds of people in former times were possessed of attachment and aversion, and their faculties were dull.
Knowing that those who have heard little and seen little gain no benefit from speaking, it is said for such persons: "One should simply observe one's own conduct.
However, if one possesses a compassionate heart and speaks for the benefit of others who have sharp faculties and have heard extensively, it is beneficial.

For such persons who listen to the Dharma for the sake of benefiting others, it is said: "Engage in conversation and admonish one another. The Vinaya states: "One must not use force or coercion to compel someone to repent."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "forcibly give," this refers to the expectation that, prior to [the formal act], one must be treated by a separate individual to ensure the purity of the procedure; thus, while it is necessary to give it forcibly, one must not coerce them.
As for their taking up the communal rules (*saṃghadharma*), the state of mind at that time fears that the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* might be interrupted;
once the recitation has passed, one must then inquire in detail, as extensively described in the eighth fascicle.
Regarding the exposition of the two *aniyata* (undetermined) precepts, I shall briefly present five sections.

First, the explanation of the names. Regarding the distinction between the "secluded" (*praticchanna*) and "exposed" (*prakāśa*) [cases], ancient commentators have provided various interpretations. As for the four *dharmas*, they lack a fixed standard and are thus termed "undetermined.

There are four types of undetermined offenses: first, the offense is undetermined because it may be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*, and these may be committed either individually or in combination.

Second, regarding the uncertainty of the accusation by a laywoman: since she does not recognize the name of the offense, it is an improper act; furthermore, because there are one, two, or three accusations for a single indeterminate offense, it is uncertain.

Third, regarding the uncertainty of the self-accusation: since the accusations are already numerous, why would the self-accusation be singular? Fourth, regarding the uncertainty of the disciplinary action:
among the three offenses committed, the disciplinary measures follow these three types of dharma. Within this, the Sage’s intention is to prevent transgressions and ensure that—
Since the *aniyata* (undetermined) offenses have already been established, why is it included in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*? Furthermore, what is the fault in citing the *aniyata* rules?

If they were not transgressions, they would not be prevented by the precepts; if so, why are they listed here? As for the phrase "one's own statement," does this refer to a statement made before the Saṃgha, or a statement made in private?
If it is the former, then it is not a statement made in private, as the Saṃgha has not yet conducted an investigation.

By what cause and condition do you suddenly claim that it is settled? If it were not unsettled, how could it be settled? If following even a single factor makes it "unsettled" (aniyata), then it is actually settled;
how can it be called unsettled? For this reason, the previous explanation of the unsettled [offense] truly lacks the names of one, two, three, or four;
it is only because of the difference between private and public [confession] that it is said there are two, yet within the precepts, they have not yet been [fully established].
Regarding the statement "it is actually an offense," the Vinaya says that because there is no fixed rule within this matter, it is called "undetermined" (aniyata).

Furthermore, although a credible woman may have observed the manifest signs, she does not know whether it is actually an offense or not; since the matter is in fact undecided, it is called "undetermined."

Second, regarding the nature of the legal procedure (*vinaya-vastu*): there is an interpretation that speaking in accordance with the Dharma constitutes the remedial action (*pratipakṣa-karman*), while speaking contrary to the Dharma constitutes the offense to be prevented.
Among the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-samatha*), this sequence preserves the method for settling offenses through confession (*pratijñā-karman*).

Those who do not confess when they have committed a *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense fall under this same principle. Question: If that is so, since all offenses within the seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*) involve speaking contrary to the Dharma, why is this the case?

Why is it that only these three [cases] are mentioned while the other four are not made manifest? Furthermore, since there are also cases where a nun makes an illegal self-accusation, why is there no "undetermined" (*aniyata*) category for her?

Answer: The three offenses are established in private, whereas two faults are taken in public; thus, they constitute the essence of the "undetermined. Regarding the abandonment of the offense to discuss the location, and the abandonment of the location to discuss the offense—each of these is a fixed basis.

Because the location is established while the offense is subject to variation, one may speak of it as "undetermined. Here, we specifically designate the three and two offenses as the objects [of this classification].

Because the practice of restraint from transgressions and the conduct of purification through detachment serve as the counteractive practices (*pratipakṣa*), the Vinaya primarily elucidates the three types of offenses. Question:
If the three or two [categories] are designated as that which is to be restrained, why is it said that when reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, one does not cite the three or two offenses?

Question: Why is it that in the section on purity (*pariśuddhi*) one only cites the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules? Answer: Because I cite the specific locations and the introductory sections (*nidāna*) as the basis for the precepts, I cite only the locations; I do not ask about the offenses themselves.
Furthermore, if that were the case, since the gravity of three offenses and two offenses differs, why would they be combined into a single precept?
Moreover, when this bhikṣu came to report his transgression to the Buddha, did he come after having already committed the three offenses, or before having committed them?

If he had already committed the three offenses, the remainder would have been covered by previous regulations; what need was there for these ten provisional benefits to justify a further re-enactment of the rule? If one fears [the rule] being redundant...
If one must establish a precept even after an offense has occurred, then other offenses would likewise require further precepts, leading to an infinite regress.
Conversely, if the three [categories of] offenses were established beforehand as a precaution, then all precepts should be treated in the same way, for there is no distinct reason otherwise.

Furthermore, if the three or two offenses were taken as indeterminate entities and bound together into a single precept, what name would be given to that offense? Generally speaking, every precept is capable of counteracting a specific class of conduct.

If preventing a single offense is now called "screening" (*ping*), then immediately it should be called "the three exposures" (*san lu*); if it is termed "the two," then the same logic applies to the "remedies.

What, then, constitutes the essence of the precept (*śīla-sarīra*)? Furthermore, what kind of precept is it named? If you say it is an "indefinite precept," then "indefiniteness" is actually the condition for an offense;

since it is the name for the commission of an offense, it cannot be a remedy. How, then, can it be called a precept? Because of these fallacies, I have first explained the private rites of the chamber.

While such conduct is appropriate for ordinary laypeople, when a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded or concealed place, engaging in coarse speech, it is difficult to distinguish which of the three offenses has been committed because it causes others to harbor doubts. Therefore, it is called "undetermined" (aniyata). Why is this?

Because such a state of doubt has never arisen before; thus we know that the basis of the precept consists simply in taking the three offenses and allowing them to be interchanged within one's own doubt. If...
Regarding the classification of offenses as "undetermined" (*aniyata*): since the various categories [of offenses] have already been clearly established, why rely on this section?

Furthermore, in the Vinaya, when the Buddha was informed of the matter, he assembled the bhikṣus; the text concerning the initial commission of the *pārājika* and other categories has already been fully revealed.
Since these matters are stated again here, we know that the essence of the "undetermined" offense consists in taking the three types of offenses and the state of doubt as its substance.
The three offenses are established as indeterminate in nature; as the *Vibhaṅga* states: "This is a matter concerning the future, which may or may not involve an actual transgression.
Therefore, the World-Honored One formulated these as indeterminate rules, as explained in detail therein. By this, one knows for certain that they do not constitute actual transgressions.
Nevertheless, these three precepts involve the contagion of defilement when performed in private and secluded places, giving rise to external suspicion.
Because it resembles an act that would damage the Sangha and bring dishonor upon the monastic community, this precept was established in anticipation even before an offense had been committed.

Regarding the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, why does the Vinaya state that if one confesses to having committed a *pārājika* (defeat), they are to be treated according to a *bhikṣu’s* confession? The answer is:

if one has actually committed a *pārājika* and confesses it as such, the case falls under the treatment prescribed in the preceding section [of the Vinaya]. However, in the present instance, although there is an offense, it is not treated as a formal violation.

Regarding the question of establishing an indeterminate nature within the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules: since both involve the violation of the precepts, why is their relative gravity not distinguished?

As for the response concerning the method of administering punishment to those who have committed an offense: it is precisely because a bhikṣu, whether in a secluded or exposed place, gives rise to doubt in others that this rule was established.

If one were not to punish such a person and instead merely promulgate the precept, it would be untrustworthy; since doubt would persist, there would be no means to bring it to rest. Therefore, [the rule] was enacted to set aside such behavior.

The principle for dealing with offenses of light or heavy gravity is simply to administer punishment directly; this is the core point. Question: Among the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, what kind of offense is committed?
Answer: One commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Question: Since the name "two *aniyata*" does not appear among the seven categories (*saptāpatti-nikāya*), how can one commit a *duṣkṛta*?

If that were so, it would follow that there is no such thing as a *duṣkṛta* within the seven categories, which is not the case. [Response: That which is called "punishing according to the law" means that there is indeed [a category] called "punishing according to the law" for those cases where it is "not to be punished according to the law."
Regarding whether there is an offense or no offense, the answer is that one should not act thus; rather, it is auspicious to punish according to the Dharma.

If this is so, although the name "offense of inauspiciousness" (dukkaṭa) does not appear among the two indeterminate rules or within the seven classes of offenses (sattāpatti-vagga), why should it be impossible to designate an offense of inauspiciousness?

Regarding the third point, "initial versus non-initial" (*ādi-ādika*): the former interpretation holds that this is not indeterminate, as in the second [category]. As the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "As Vasiṣṭha taught," there is no initial offense for the disciplinary measures (*daṇḍakarma*) below [the first category];

the five categories of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* are consistently without initial disciplinary measures. Below these, however, there are initial offenses. Question: If that is so, regarding the previous rule on touching (*sparśana*), it is stated that the offense is grave (*pārājika*); yet later, when the offense is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is again said to be "initial. How is this to be understood? Answer: [The distinction lies in the nature of the act and the status of the agent.

In the case of touching, the gravity of the offense depends on the specific circumstances and the intention of the actor; thus, while the first instance may be grave, subsequent instances of the same nature may be classified differently. In the case of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the term "initial" refers to the first occurrence of that specific transgression within a particular context, even if the underlying conduct has been previously addressed. Thus, the classification of "initial" or "non-initial" is determined by the specific legal category and the history of the offender's involvement therein.

The section on "Abandonment" was not established; now it is discussed separately. Each [category] attains its own initial [status]. Regarding the first five chapters, it is said that the general rules are extensive while the supplementary rules are abbreviated.
Now, as for what is called "Indeterminate" (aniyata), this refers to the general extensive rules that supplement other specific extensive rules.

Question: If that is so, it should have been established after the five categories (pañcāpatti). Why, then, is it established either before or within the five categories in the *Vinayavibhaṅga*? Answer: The five categories were established first; subsequently, [the Indeterminate rules] followed.

Regarding the classification of the characteristics of offenses according to specific matters, although the general principle is easy to see, it is difficult to apply to individual cases; therefore, they are governed collectively by location while each case is determined individually from the outset.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Below this precept, there is an opening for non-offense. Question:

If there is both an initial [prohibition] and a subsequent opening for non-offense, why does the root text (the *Prakīrṇaka*) prescribe a penalty as explained by Vasiṣṭha? Answer: This was stated by the one who established the Dharma, intending it as a formal regulation.
Regarding the question of whether there is an offense for lying by remaining silent during the interrogation following the *Poṣadha* ceremony: if one does not ask, then there is no such offense;

this would therefore be a distinct offense. How can it be called "general"? Furthermore, within the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra*, the interrogation is general because it asks about all offenses below [the *pārājika*s];

thus it is termed "general. Now, since there is no offense if one does not ask, we know it is not "general. My current interpretation is that while these cases are identical in being the "first," their meanings differ. (5)
In this case, one actually commits the offense of the first [Saṃghāvaśeṣa]; it is not necessarily that by committing this [offense], one incurs the first [Saṃghāvaśeṣa].

Regarding those who were previously subject to formal action (ukkhepanīyakamma) due to suspicion before the rule was established, this [present rule] now opens up the possibility of non-offense; yet because the doubt arises differently in private versus public settings, each incurs the first [Saṃghāvaśeṣa].

Fourth, regarding the commonalities and differences between the "penetrating" (*tong*) and the "obstructed" (*se*), there are five types: 1. **Commonalities and Differences Regarding the Categories of Offenses:** If one proceeds from the perspective of the offenses committed, they generally pertain to the seven groups of five offenses;

however, raising [the matter] constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). 2. **Commonalities and Differences Regarding the Locus of the Offense:** Generally speaking, when discussing the commission of an offense, it does not occur apart from either a secluded or an exposed place;

thus, the offenses pertain to both the five and the seven groups. Furthermore, there are two [factors]: first, because of the extreme nature of defilement and censure; second, because of silence. 3. **The Sequence of Two and Three:** This refers to the sequence of two and three [factors], which is due to the extremity of defilement and censure. Third, [there is] silence.

Regarding the similarities and differences in offenses: when asking about those who have committed an offense against any of the five categories of precepts—whether in private or in public—the *saṃgha* asks three times in private during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), and twice in public.
As for the sequence of questioning regarding external offenses, one asks whether there are any unspoken falsehoods.

If there is an offense, the questioner remains silent; however, apart from the second and third [instances], one must guard against committing an offense by remaining silent, as there is no basis for questioning that would permit such a transgression.

Question: If that is so, why is it that among the seven methods of settling disputes (*satta adhikaraṇasamathā*), if one does not employ any of the seven medicines [for settling], all such cases are considered "settled by silence" (*tuṇhībhāva*)?
Answer: A bhikkhu raises these seven medicines and asks whether the Saṃgha, which is capable of administering the Dharma, may use these seven medicines to settle a dispute for another.

Now, in the case of *aniyata* (undetermined offenses), if one were to raise both categories [of offenses] together, then wherever there is an offense, it would not be a case of raising them together and asking specifically about each distinct location.

Thus, one should know that the general and the specific differ. Regarding the distinction between the four types of *saṃgha* (monastic assemblies) in terms of their differences and similarities: this question concerns the individual because it asks about the offense (*āpatti*), and an offense is committed by an individual;
below, the question concerns only the *saṃgha* because it asks about the remedy (*bhaisajya*), and the remedy is administered by the *saṃgha*.

Fifth, regarding the similarity and difference between the offense and the remedy: since both the "this" and the "that" possess both the remedy and the offense, why is it that here we ask only about the offense, while below [the text] immediately...?

Question: Regarding the administration of medicine, the Vinaya was established to extinguish disputes. This noble act of accusing another of an offense does not conflict with the [rules on] requisites;

thus, it is "without dispute. Therefore, one does not ask about the medicine. As for the seven types of Vinaya procedures that follow, the person accused may be either an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or an *ārya*, and both offenses (*āpatti*) and disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) may be present.
If one asks only about the offense or only about the dispute, they do not encompass each other. If one asks about both the offense and the dispute, then both should be addressed accordingly.
Since all [other methods] involve obstacles, they are both set aside and not discussed; we now follow that which is capable of treatment, and thus inquire about their differences. Question:

Within this *aniyata* (undetermined) category, what is the distinction between the treatment of the offense (*āpatti*) and the treatment of the person (*pudgala*), on one hand, and the resolution of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), on the other? Answer:

Herein, the treatment of the offense and the treatment of the person is intended to quell the doubts of both monastics and laypeople. In the resolution of disputes, the primary aim is to eliminate the dispute itself, without regard for quelling such doubts.

Because there is doubt regarding this distinction, they are not the same. Furthermore, regarding these three *vinayas*, there is a difference in their presence or absence compared to the seven *vinayas*.
These three are as follows: for instance, the *vinaya* of confession (*pratijñā-vinaya*) is like the treatment through the words of a monk;

the *vinaya* of the site of offense (*tatsvabhāva-vinaya*) is like the treatment through the words of a trustworthy person (*puruṣa*). These two *vinayas* necessarily require the presence of three or five [monks].

Regarding the first, the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) extinguishes disputes; since this is already present here, why would the other four methods be unnecessary? Second, regarding the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection) and *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one not insane):

when a person of pure conduct is slandered and pursued by litigation, these two *vinayas* are used to settle the matter according to human sentiment. Since this noble woman has raised a charge that is proven true and thus free from dispute, these two methods are of no use.
Third, regarding the *yadbhūyaś-cīrṇa-vinaya* (settlement by majority vote) which determines right and wrong to extinguish disputes: this noble [woman]... [text fragment ends].
When a woman raises a charge, there is no dispute regarding what is wrong or right; furthermore, since there is no dispute to be extinguished, what need is there for a large assembly?

This arises from the Noble One’s non-dispute (*araṇā-vinaya*). As for the light or heavy nature of the offense, it does not require a year to be extinguished; what need is there for "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*)?

Moreover, in this case, one confesses the transgression oneself, yet the offense is not immediately extinguished; while there is no dispute to be quelled, there is the principle of eventual extinction, which is collectively termed *vinaya*. The following seven cases involve self-accusation.

The "confession for the removal of disputes by citing offenses" (*āpatti-pratideśanā*) is another name for the *vinaya*. Furthermore, within this context, the "admission by oneself" (*svavāda*) refers only to the upper three methods of settling disputes and not the lower two;

likewise, among the seven methods of settling disputes (*saptadharmāḥ saṃgha-samādhi*), it refers only to the lower three and not the upper two. These [methods] mutually encompass one another, and in principle, all are applicable to the five types of disputes.

Moreover, although the remedies for treating these through "admission by oneself" are set forth, they do not accord with the primary tenet [of this section], and thus they are omitted here without further analysis.

Because the "confession" (*pratijñā*) is the primary method for settling disputes, the "medicine of confession" (*pratijñā-bhaiṣajya*) is presented here. This refers to cases where the offense has not yet been settled and there is no formal resolution of the dispute;
it merely involves the reconciliation of the individuals involved to pacify external suspicion and slander, and is thus termed *vinaya* in a general sense.

The latter, which involves the treatment of the person and the settlement of the offense and the dispute, is termed *vinaya* in a specific sense. Since the general and specific meanings differ, they cannot be said to be one and the same, as explained extensively in the separate chapter.

Regarding the fifth point, concerning the presence or absence [of offenses] for monks and nuns: one interpretation holds that because there is a distinction between the three types of offenses committed in private by monks (*saṃvara-āpatti*) and the two types of offenses committed in public (*prakāśa-āpatti*), there is an "undetermined" category;

whereas for nuns, there are two types of offenses committed in private which may allow for such distinctions, yet there is no "undetermined" category for those committed in public—since a public offense is immediately established as an offense without any variation in its locus. Therefore, according to this prior explanation, nuns do not have [the undetermined category].
Regarding the general governance of each individual case, since many offenses are committed within each instance, why is it now said that for nuns there is no "undetermined" offense?
Furthermore, the Buddha’s regulation for accusing another requires that both the male and female assemblies act as mutual witnesses;

only when what is seen and heard by both is identical can the bhikṣus be accused according to the common dharma. When the male assembly accuses, the nun is the disciple who accuses her teacher, which constitutes a transgression.
Out of respect, one should select a trustworthy woman, such as a *bhikṣuṇī*, to report the matter; because she can obtain the true facts more easily, it is the same as previously cited.

However, due to not knowing the names or lineages [of the parties involved], discrepancies may arise; therefore, only the *saṃgha* [of nuns] exists for reporting offenses committed by a nun, as both assemblies must be fully prepared.

There is no need for laymen, as in the case of a *bhikṣu*, where a *bhikṣu* recognizes the offense and there is no uncertainty (*aniyata*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that a *bhikṣuṇī* is not permitted [to act as the reporter].
When walking alone, one is already accompanied; because there is no third person present in either a secluded or exposed place, a nun does not incur an offense [in such cases].
If this were the case, nuns would have no precepts regarding sitting with a man in either a secluded or exposed place.
To explain why nuns lack the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules: if a bhikṣu sits with another woman in a secluded or exposed place, and her husband sees them, [the offense arises].
Because lack of faith, or at times even verbal abuse and expulsion, leads to external censure and grave harm, the Noble One established this rule.
However, although a woman might lose her faith if she sits with a man, there is no principle for expelling her; since the husband’s transgression is minor, it is not regulated.
Therefore, nuns do not [face such consequences] (and so forth).
In explaining the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, I shall briefly present two gates.

First, regarding the explanation of the name and its sequence: this is called "renunciation" (*naiḥsarga*). There are three kinds of renunciation—of material objects, of the continuity of craving, and of the offense—and since all must be relinquished, there are these three types of renunciation.
Nevertheless, this specific term "renunciation" refers to the relinquishing of material objects, and not by virtue of...
If it were not so for the other two [categories], why would the ninety [offenses] also have two types of abandonment? Why then are they not called "abandonment"?

Although the thirty and the ninety differ in their textual sequence and the timing of their abandonment, the gravity of the offenses is equal, and the meaning of their lightness or heaviness is identical;

thus, the one hundred and twenty precepts are combined into the third category. However, the abandonment of the thirty [offenses] arises from matters of material wealth, where the means of livelihood are lost and extensive harm is produced.
Because of transgressions, one must purify the mind through repentance; first, one must relinquish material wealth before the monks and sever the continuity of greedy thoughts.

Once the objects of attachment have been relinquished, the offense is finally extinguished. Since performing the ritual procedure is difficult, one must first understand what is difficult and subsequently proceed to what is easy;

therefore, this is placed at the beginning of the section on the ninety rules. Second, regarding the detailed explanation according to the positions, there are briefly eight sections; the first is the thirty-ninth.

Regarding the ten offenses involving the forfeiture of material goods (*sāpattika-dharmas*), there is a distinction between those that require forfeiture and those that do not. Generally, three conditions must be met for forfeiture: first, the object must be one’s own property;
second, its current possession or use must give rise to a fault; and third, by relinquishing it back to the owner, one may use it again without transgression.
Among the thirty offenses that possess these three conditions, twenty-seven require forfeiture; as for the remaining three, they do not require forfeiture because they lack these three conditions.

Because [the requisites] are complete, there are fourteen types of food; thirteen involve sitting on a chair with detachable legs, in a screened or exposed place, on two mats, or on a high-legged seat—these four lack the first and third types of wealth.

Within the "purely clean" (brahmacarya) gift of food, there are three transgressions: giving food to non-Buddhists, food that has passed into another's hand, and eating food that is another's property or shared with others.
These lack the first condition. Question: Why does taking three bowls [of food] before having eaten not give rise to an offense?

Because it manifests as the relinquishment of material wealth, the answer is that although taking what is not given constitutes an offense, this is logically consistent with the principle that what has been relinquished by a donor is not restricted [to them].
Since the Buddha’s regulation requires communal sharing, it does not belong to oneself; thus, the initial condition [of ownership] is lacking. Question:

If that is so, since the category of "flavor" (*rasa*) is generally not relinquished, why is ginger purchased for food also relinquished? Answer: Because one exchanges it for one's own private property.
If one obtains this substance of food that is not in accordance with the Dharma and is unfit for communal consumption, it is because the conditions are restricted;

thus, it falls within the twelve deficiencies of the *śikṣādattaka* (one who has been granted training). Regarding the second condition: there is no offense before eating, but the offense arises only after having eaten, because the substance is no longer manifest.

Regarding the praise of giving, the separate sufficiency, the exhortation, and the non-remnant acceptance of fine medicines, alcohol, and wealth: among these eight precepts, the third condition is deficient.

Regarding covering a roof, white clothing, cotton-wool, ivory or horn, a nun’s sores, rain, and the like—forcibly spreading [materials], giving robes, making robes, losing them, or hiding them from others—these also give rise to offenses based on material wealth and must likewise be distinguished.
Regarding true purification through giving (*viśuddha-dāna*): if one uses [the property] arbitrarily, there is an offense;

it belongs to the donor. If the initial conditions are lacking, [is this the case]? If that were so, would all thirty precepts not require purification? Answer: [This applies to] causing a *bhikṣuṇī* [to act].

1. Regarding the two offenses of washing and beating [robes], they are incurred because one accepts and maintains them; they are not due to the failure to perform the ritual of purification (*paryodāpana*) for an extra robe. 2.

Regarding the month-long [retention] of robes, the bowl, and medicine, these four are incurred precisely because of the failure to perform the ritual of purification; thus, there is no doubt in this matter. 3. Regarding the offenses of spreading out [seats], carrying [loads], splitting [robes], begging for thread, and so forth, the transgression arises as soon as the action is completed;

if the action has not yet been completed, it does not constitute a violation. 4. Regarding the remaining precepts, most are incurred through the act of receiving [the object]. One *vitasti* (span) is the measure. All other precepts are generally incurred by the mere act of taking possession.

Regarding the transgressions of *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses requiring forfeiture): the one rule concerning the seizure of robes (*cīvara-apahāra*) may either be subject to formal acceptance (*parigraha*) or to the rite of purification (*viśuddhi*).

When one relinquishes a robe to another, its state of purity (*viśuddhi-dharma*) is lost; therefore, if it is seized, it must be forfeited. As for the remaining rules, they are easy to understand. Concerning the three white robes (*traya-avadāta-cīvara*): once they have been relinquished, they return to their original owner for use.

If a fault arises because they have become stained or damaged, one is permitted to perform a confession (*deśanā*) rather than needing to forfeit them. This applies to those [robes] with white hair [mixed in].
The same should apply to bedding and requisites. Answer: This is because the fault arises from one’s own making; it is not prohibited for one to use what has been received.

Therefore, by returning it to the owner, one may use it without defilement. Thus, having discarded high beds and the like, once the discarding is complete, if one returns them to the owner and uses them, there is an offense;

therefore, they need not be formally discarded. As for needle cases made of ivory or horn, one should simply break them and stop; there is no need to maintain them or formally discard them. Question: If that is so...
If a cotton mattress is cut or torn, it need not be discarded. The answer is: when a cotton mattress is cut or ruined, it should be returned to its owner;

if it is then plastered over, there is still the benefit of utility, so the three requirements for discarding are not lacking. As for a needle case, even if it is slightly damaged, the effort expended was great;

if it is ruined, although its use is permitted, because greed does not cease and it becomes useless again, it does not enter into the category of what must be discarded. Furthermore, another interpretation is that, for example, in the case of begging for a bowl and so forth, one bad item is returned to its owner.

It is permitted to receive and consume other seven-day medicines kept in the monastery storehouse for the sake of those guarding the country, or fourteen-day medicines, provided they are formally relinquished;

there is no fault in using them. Furthermore, regarding the rules on the loss of purity (*viśuddhi*) concerning the taking of robes—both those that are fixed and those that are unfixed—the unfixed cases do not entail the loss of purity.
How then can it be said that by giving [the robe] to another person, one loses its purity? Moreover, this concerns the taking of [a robe] beyond the limit.

Regarding the three alms bowls, if they are of the same quality as those of others and constitute a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), they belong entirely to the donor; if one steals these items, from whom does one incur the offense?

Furthermore, if the donor dies, they should immediately enter the communal property of the Saṃgha. Also, regarding the five types of bedding and requisites: if they hinder one's practice, one commits an offense even if they are mixed with other items according to the intermediate rule (*madhyama-vidhi*).
Even if the substance itself is not [of inferior quality], it remains improper despite being discarded. How then can one speak of "returning them to the owner"?

Regarding the offenses: the two concerning washing robes, the four concerning the *varṣāśāṭī* (rainy-season robe) and so forth, and the offense of relinquishing what has been formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*)—why are these not excluded from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*?
Furthermore, if one does not formally accept [the robe], it should likewise be considered a non-offense for other robes.

If it is argued that the eight cases—such as the five types of spreading out, the two types of hair, and begging for thread—should not be measured in cubits and thus need not be mentioned, then the mention of "purification" (*viśuddhi*) in the latter part of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* should be excluded. Therefore, the former interpretation is correct.

Regarding the difficulty of fulfilling all three conditions [for forfeiture], there are two interpretations for the current explanation: first, among the thirty [offenses], because the mind of greed is particularly heavy, one loses the proper method in taking objects;
second, it obstructs the Path and incurs grave censure, thus necessitating its relinquishment to counteract the original greedy intent.

This is not the case for the ninety [offenses]; even if one commits an offense due to wealth, it is always because of the improper way of creating or using it, rather than out of a desire to store it away.

Therefore, regarding the single offense of failing to relinquish an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), although it does not involve greedy appropriation or staying overnight apart from one’s robes, it violates the respect due to the Dharma and defiles the method of formal observance;
thus, it must be confessed through a formal declaration.

As for the similarities and differences regarding the second type of offender: if a single person commits all these offenses, this is easily understood; however, in the case of the Saṃgha of the four directions, it is uniform.
One does not incur an offense regarding the five precepts shared among co-residents, as these are strictly not common [to all].

Regarding the two rules on being separated from one's robes for six years, the folding of bedding, and the rain-cloak: why is this? These precepts are all to be observed individually; there is no sense of collective observance.
How could my being separated cause them to incur an offense? Seven precepts are indeterminate: the long robe, the month-long robe, the bowl, and medicine kept beyond the permitted period.

Regarding the washing of robes, the taking away of robes, and so forth, these are the same as the case of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*): if the owner is present before [the offender] and does not speak up, it is not said that there is a fault for all sentient beings;

therefore, they share in the offense equally. If one person has gone far away and commands those remaining to speak, yet they do not speak, those remaining are at fault while the traveler is without fault;
therefore, it is not fixed. The other four cases are likewise. If one accepts and keeps a robe, the washing and the taking away are also treated in this manner.
Regarding offenses that are not shared (*asādhāraṇa-vinaya*): if one shares in the lengthening, washing, or seizing [of robes], one incurs the same offense.
Among the remaining eighteen [offenses], if one does not act together with another—even if one acts for the sake of another—one does not incur the offense.

For example, if a person traveling on a road encounters bandits who beat him and steal his three robes, and a layperson, because they were stolen, gives him more robes, yet he accepts them beyond the limit of sufficiency; since the layperson was unaware that this was permissible, [the monk] incurs no offense.

Regarding "the same offense," the term "same" here refers to those who act together and thus both lose [their robes], because they jointly calculate and take what is excessive; hence it is called "the same offense.
The remainder is easy to understand. In relation to the present Saṃgha, there are seven precepts that should be considered offenses:

making cotton mattresses together, using black or white bedding together, carrying [robes] together, exceeding the three-day limit, storing precious objects, exchanging precious objects, and taking back robes together.

Third, regarding the similarities and differences between performing an act oneself and instructing another to do so: when one performs an act oneself, it is invariably a formal offense (*pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*). However, regarding the similarity or difference in instructing another, it is not fixed.

Specifically, if one merely instructs another in seventeen precepts that can be performed by the instructor, it is invariably a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), because there is no material gain to enrich oneself;

yet, since one should not instruct others to commit evil, violating this constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. There are thirteen precepts where instructing another for one's own benefit results in a formal offense.

There is no difference between the moisture [of the object] upon oneself and its manifestation; they follow the same standard. Within the mind of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), non-virtuous non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*) arises spontaneously.
What are the thirteen? They are: taking bedding or seats; taking away robes; receiving precious objects; taking a nun’s robe; washing old clothes;

dyeing them; carding wool; exceeding the limit; asking for a robe back after it has been returned; begging for thread oneself; having it woven; and praising the weaver. One should know these and so forth.

Regarding whether there are cases of repeated offenses for the fourth category: among the four precepts, there are instances where a repeated offense occurs—namely, washing old clothes, carrying wool, carding wool, and using rain-cloths.

Since these items are already present before one, it is possible to perform the action again; therefore, they constitute a repeated offense. As for the remaining twenty-six [precepts], none involve repeated offenses.
Furthermore, regarding the washing of clothes, if one causes them to be washed or beaten again, one merely commits a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*); however, the text states "washing."

Regarding the three *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* concerning beating, dyeing, and washing: this does not mean that a single garment gives rise to three separate offenses, each requiring a distinct forfeiture.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that if one performs these three actions simultaneously, one incurs only a single forfeiture. If one causes it to be washed but not dyed, the color is not achieved;

if one beats it but does not fully soften it, both result in a *duṣkṛta* offense. Since there is no repeated offense even when the characteristics of washing and dyeing differ, how could there be a repeated offense for two instances of washing?
Regarding the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, there is no mention of repeated offenses; as the textual meaning is similar across various sections, there is no need for extensive citation.

Fifth, concerning the method for relinquishing through confession (*pratikarman*): the three types of relinquishment are as described above. Now, discussing the relinquishment of material objects (*dravya*), there are five gates. First, regarding the object (*viṣaya*):

since a cotton mattress is a source of ruin and fosters greed, there is no corresponding object [for its relinquishment]. As for the two treasures (gold and silver), they are relinquished because of their inherent nature.

Because one who has long harbored greed commits an offense even when receiving from a monk, one must relinquish it before a layperson; as for the objects before the Saṃgha, the general and specific cases—whether one, two, or three classes—are understandable.

First, "complete destruction" is as explained above. Third, regarding the "location," there is no obstruction at the location. Fourth, regarding the "assembly," the three types of precepts do not require an assembly.
Fifth, regarding the "returning of property," there are five examples: first, returning to the owner in the case of total destruction; second, entering [the Saṃgha]... [text truncated].

1. Returning secular items to their original owners; 2. returning items belonging to the Sangha to the Sangha so they may no longer be used for personal purposes; 3. returning items belonging to the Sangha to the Sangha so they may no longer be used for secular purposes;
4. returning items exclusively to the original owners; 5. the four divisions are treated accordingly. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If one exchanges precious objects, stores precious objects, or engages in trade and obtains precious objects—whether the amount obtained is small and must be permanently relinquished, or large and must be entrusted to a trustworthy *kappiyakāraka* (steward) to serve as bedding and furniture for the Sangha of the four directions."

Regarding the requirement for repentance before the Saṃgha: the remainder is the same as in the *Caturvargika* and *Pañcavargika*. There are five types of relinquishment (*pratyādeśana*), one of which is the permanent relinquishment of stored gems and the like to the Saṃgha.

Once these have been relinquished, the Saṃgha appoints a person to permanently discard them. If the Saṃgha does not do so, it shall cause a layperson (*śuddha-puruṣa*) to trade them for food and clothing on behalf of the Saṃgha for the Saṃgha’s consumption;
however, the original owner may not consume them, for fear that they would fulfill their original intent. Second is the permanent entry into the Saṃgha as a relinquishment.

Regarding the five types of bedding and furnishings that enter into common use for the Saṃgha, the original owners alone may not sit upon them. Three types—those relinquished by monks or laypeople, medicines, and those relinquished by the Saṃgha—are given to laypeople; these include items such as foot-unguents and lamps for lighting, which the original owners may not use. No bhikṣus may consume [these items]; the remaining two cases are similar to this. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are five types of relinquishment; one type of relinquishment involves entering the Saṃgha as "inexhaustible property" (*akṣaya-nidhi*).
