If one hoards jewels, trades jewels, or lends them out for interest to build monastic dwellings or robes for the Sangha, the Sangha may not divide or consume those items;

this is done to subdue the greed of the original owner. Second, regarding the relinquishment of items for the use of the Sangha: the five types of bedding and requisites, as well as property dedicated to the Sangha, may be used by the Sangha for whatever purpose it deems fit.
Among these, the Sangha is not permitted to wear pure black *kauśeya* silk, though it may be used [for other purposes].

Regarding the making of floor coverings, canopies, curtains, and the like: for six years one must not fold them up, nor may they be used as floor coverings by the Saṃgha unless they are worn without being placed directly against the body.
Concerning woolen bedding that is of good quality, it is explained as before; if it is of poor quality, it is explained as follows. The remaining three [types of bedding] are the same as this.

If there is a repeated offense regarding the retention of items, the method of returning them is as follows: [this applies to] cotton mattresses, the keeping of precious things, and the trading of precious things.
Among the twenty-seven rules for the Saṃgha, four rules require that the object be returned to its owner on the same day, because the two types of hair-clipping do not involve mutual defilement;
although the seven-day medicine involves mutual defilement, it must also be returned to the owner on the same day, as it is intended for external use by the body.

Furthermore, there are four rules that require the object to remain overnight; the remaining eighteen rules are to be relinquished separately and do not require the night to pass. If twenty-three rules are shared...

When the long-term [extra] items are discarded at the end of the month, six precepts—namely, the two types of robes, the two types of hair-removal tools, the medicine, and the bowl—are returned to their owners on that very day.
If the twenty-three precepts are discarded together with the long-term bowl, only the single precept regarding the begging bowl remains overnight with the long-term bowl;
all others are returned on that very day. If the twenty-three precepts are discarded together with the long-term medicine, all are returned on that very day.

Upon returning, because the inner and outer requisites—such as robes and alms bowls—are distinct and do not become entangled with one another, the details are as explained extensively in the *Mahāśrāmaṇera-vinaya-śīla-saṃgraha* (Dà cǎo).

Regarding the offenses, the cotton mattress and the two types of treasures must have their material value forfeited; since these are not to be assembled before the entire community, the repentance is performed before a separate group (*biezòng*), and thus the rite is successfully accomplished.

As for all other precepts, both the forfeiture of material goods and the expiation of offenses must be performed by assembling the entire community; they cannot be accomplished through a separate assembly. Furthermore, there are five ways to relinquish the mind of attachment.

Regarding the offenses of keeping extra robes, bowls, medicine, or [excessive] wealth beyond the permitted period, these arise from the continuity of the mind’s accumulation and greed. If one wishes to return such surplus property, the intention to possess it must be severed;

the substance of the relinquished surplus may not be returned to the owner on the same day, but must necessarily pass through the night. In cases of distant travel or urgent difficulties, returning it on the same day by passing it along is permitted.
For all other precepts, there is no offense of continuous possession extending over days, provided that the property [is handled according to the rules].

Once the offense has been relinquished, one immediately returns to a state free from defilement. Regarding this, Bhadanta says: "On that very day, one may accept extraordinary wealth (*visabhāga-dhana*) without committing the offense of 'keeping' (*atireka*), because the intention [to possess it] has been severed.
This is not like original wealth, which was previously subject to the fault of being kept.

If the intention has not been severed, one may not accept anything at all, with the sole exception of seven-day provisions for returning to the owner, ointment for the feet, and oil for lamps; these are excluded because they cannot be used as medicine. Thus it is said.

If one receives various medicines on a given day and does not become defiled by them because they have been relinquished through mental renunciation (*cittena tyāga*), then in this case, one may not return them to the owner on that very same day.
Regarding the sixth point, the method for maintaining and violating [the precepts]: nine cases constitute "active maintenance" (*karmika-dhāraṇa*) and the cessation thereof constitutes "violation.

During the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), regarding the bowl and medicine, if one exceeds these five limits and performs the ritual according to the teachings without committing an offense of "excess," this is called "active maintenance"; if one does not perform the ritual of "purification" (*viśuddhi*), this is called "cessation."

Regarding the three matters—the offense of staying overnight separated from one's robe, the reduction of the six-year period, and the making of bedding—because one obtains the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for these, they are termed "active observance" (*kārya-dhāraṇa*).

The opposite is termed "cessation of offense. Regarding the precept on possessing precious objects, it is said that one should entrust them to a layperson as a "pure custodian" (*viśuddha-adhiṣṭhātṛ*) and accept [the object];

this is termed "active observance," while failing to do so is termed "cessation of offense. Although the thirty-ninth and fortieth rules belong to the same category, they are questioned in two separate locations.

Regarding "purity" (*viśuddhi*): previously, when there was wealth to be relinquished, one could not do so apart from the assembly; because this is the reverse of the ninety [offenses], it is divided into two questions, the intent of which lies herein.
Seventh, concerning the similarities and differences between monks and nuns: among these, eighteen offenses are common to both monks and nuns, while twelve are not.

There are three faults: first, the fault of inconsistency regarding existence and non-existence; previously, when seeking rain-clothing or being separated from one’s robes for six nights, monks have [the allowance] while nuns do not.

Why? Because the use of bathing-clothing for nuns is always permitted, and because nuns do not reside in forest hermitages (*araṇya*). Second, the fault of having identical offenses despite different conditions:

regarding an extra alms-bowl, both monks and nuns fall into an offense, which is called a "common offense"; however, the conditions for exemption are unequal, as monks [are subject to] a fault after ten days.
The nun [is permitted] for only one night; this is called a difference in the conditions. Why?

Because the Saṃgha does not prohibit [a monk from traveling] with a companion, and since there may be no companion to speak with when traveling alone, they are granted ten days to seek a companion to whom he may confess [the offense]. The nun is not like this, and therefore she is granted only one night. Question:

If that is so, why should the nun’s keeping of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) not be the same as the monks'? Answer: If the bowl is already completed, it need not be further fashioned. (The same applies to the robe.)
Since it is appropriate to immediately perform the *śuddhika* (purification) and accept [the robe], only one night is permitted for robes that are being prepared but not yet finished;
otherwise, there is the fault of "extra" (*atireka*) robes. Because sewing with a needle for even a single day cannot be completed immediately, a period of ten days is opened up. Question:

If that is so, when an extra robe is not yet finished but has a companion [to whom it can be entrusted], why is it not said that one should declare it as "making a robe for oneself"? What difference is there between this and a bowl that has been completed, such that they are not treated the same?

Answer: Regarding the allowance of ten days for robes, this is based on those who possess only the three robes (*tricīvara*). If one follows the rules concerning *pārihārika* (robes designated for another), even for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is restricted to one day;
exceeding that constitutes the offense of *atireka* (excess). As for the allowance of ten days, once the initial period has expired, one is permitted to keep them for ten days.

Regarding the difference between light and heavy offenses, there are nine precepts where the nature of the action is identical, yet the degree of the transgression differs—this is termed "light and heavy. This refers to the five types of *staraṇa* (spreading out).
The *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses for a nun include: taking [an extra] robe, having old robes washed, carrying wool, and carding wool.
Regarding the eighth [category], the "spontaneous" (*svayam*) fifteen precepts for a *śrāmaṇera*: prior to receiving full ordination, one is instructed not to have others perform [certain acts].

These refer to the four rules concerning the long robe, the bowl, the month-long robe, and the robe from an urgent offering; if these are kept beyond the permitted time, they constitute offenses. At the time one is a *śrāmaṇera*, the acceptance of wealth belongs to [the category of] property.
After having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), if more than ten days have passed, one does not need to perform the ritual of assistance (*parivāsa*).
Within the mind of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), one may spontaneously commit a *pāyattika* offense; this may also be counted together with the preceding days to reach a total of ten.

If the medicinal ritual (*bhaiṣajya-dharma*) is not performed in this manner, then although the two forms of acceptance—manual and oral—were performed while one was a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), once the full ordination is completed, the oral acceptance is lost. Since there is no longer the ritual of the medicine, there is no spontaneous [commitment].
Furthermore, there are eleven precepts for śrāmaṇeras: teaching others to make five types of bedding or robes for oneself;

taking robes to give to a nun and having her wash, dye, or beat them; having wool carded more than three times; begging for robes; taking the robes of a nun who is not a relative; begging for thread oneself;
having a weaver who is not a relative weave [a robe]; teaching others to take away a robe for oneself—having undertaken these eleven precepts, one proceeds.

After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), although one may spontaneously (*svarasena*) violate other remaining precepts, because one must perform the formal method of receiving and undertaking them anew after having previously made the preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
there is no spontaneous violation [of the primary vows].
Third, regarding the detailed explanation according to the specific questions: among the thirty rules, the rule concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) is primary.

Excluding nine rules, the remaining twenty-one rules involving secondary taints (*pārājika-anuśaṃsa*) all result in the offense of possessing an extra robe. What are these nine rules? They are: the two rules on hair, the two on bowls, the two on jewels, and the seven-day medicine. As the Vinaya states:
"If one commits the offense of an extra robe, and exchanges it for other robes, one incurs the offense; if one sells them, one also incurs the offense."

Furthermore, because the continuity of the mind persists without interruption, one again commits the offense of *atireka-cīvara* (excess robe). By this evidence, it is known that all other cases constitute grave offenses (*duṣkṛta*).

If one maintains this interpretation, when selling [a robe] and it comes into one's possession, one must perform the *pariśuddhi* (purification) rite and make it into one of the three robes; if ten days pass, there is no offense of excess. Otherwise, one commits the offense.
If one sells it without performing the purification and there is no [robe] in excess, on what basis could it be defiled by the offense of excess? Since it has already become an excess...

Question: Since it is stated that one who is "stained" (defiled) by knowledge must perform the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) and make the three robes (*tricīvara*), why does the *Cīvaravastu* state that a *naiḥsargika* robe should not be declared pure and made into the three robes?
Answer: It is said that it "should not" because doing so incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*); it does not mean that the act of declaring purity is invalid.
If, after having performed the declaration of purity for a material object intended for sale, one later regrets the original transgression, there is no need to relinquish (*pratyādeya*) this robe.
Because one enters into purification, if within this interval one first obtains an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) and then, after ten days have passed, takes a nun’s robe, one incurs two offenses;

this is called "horizontal contamination" (*tiryak-saṃsarga*). Furthermore, if one initially has no extra robe and then takes a nun’s robe, one immediately incurs the offense of taking [what is not given], and upon the passing of the ten-day period, one incurs the offense of [keeping] an extra robe;

this is called "horizontal extension. Since both [the horizontal and vertical] must exist, there is "vertical extension" (*ūrdhva-saṃsarga*). Regarding "vertical extension," it refers to when one previously obtained purified wealth that exceeded [the limit].

If one commits an offense on the tenth day and, after having performed the *pārivāsika* (probationary) confession, commits another offense involving a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* (an offense requiring forfeiture) ten days later—such as obtaining a robe on the first day or obtaining one every day for ten days up until the eleventh day—the first day’s transgression is combined with the robes obtained over the preceding nine days;
this is called "vertical defilement" (*ūrdhva-rañjana*). Question: If that is so, regarding the sale of medicine, there are two types of acceptance: by hand and by mouth.

Furthermore, it should also be established that this differs from the fault of selling; by declaring the purity (*śuddhi*) and giving it to others, one effectively severs the continuity [of attachment].

Thus, obtaining the medicinal substance without having previously accepted it constitutes the abandonment of greed, whereas performing two acts of acceptance constitutes the increase of greed, and for this reason, it is not established [as valid].

Another interpretation holds that since there is no second relinquishment of wealth, how could there be a repeated offense? Moreover, it is said that since it was stated "one should not speak," [the prohibition applies].

Since the essence of pure knowledge is devoid of increase or decrease, how could defilement possibly exist? It is only because people delight in transgressing that this is explained at the outset. Question:
If this is so, why does the Vinaya state that "exchanging it for another robe constitutes one *naiḥsargika* offense," thereby making it a heavy defilement?
Answer: This refers to exchanging with the five classes of persons, or sending someone else to exchange with two classes of persons; such cases do not constitute the offense of commercial trade.
Therefore, if one trades on the side of worldly convention, one incurs the offense of buying and selling; there is no fault of defilement [in this].
For this reason, it is permissible to keep extra *tricīvara* (three robes) for sale. Why would it be impossible to have extra *tricīvara*?
Since one has lost the three robes, one must next undergo the formal acceptance (*trisamādāna*) of the three robes; if there is no excess, it is excellent, as it severs the appearance of attachment.

Question: Since it is thus, why is it that an oversized robe-closet (*cīvarakuṭī*) cannot be formally designated as a place for keeping robes? Answer: In cases such as selling [robes], there is a fault throughout the entire substance [of the act].
However, in the case of being oversized and so forth, there is a fault externally while there is no transgression internally; therefore, these two cases are not comparable. Question:

If that is so, why does the nineteen-piece great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) succeed in its designation even when its length and width do not conform to the rules, given that there is a fault within the individual strips?
Regarding the question of whether one may accept [robes] for use: because the Buddha prescribed their possession, they constitute "use" even if one sells them;

otherwise, it would not. Question: If that is so, the three white robes are also prescribed for possession; why do they not constitute "acceptance"? Answer: Because they are not monastic garments, the faults of censure are numerous;

therefore, they do not constitute acceptance. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Although the three robes are not formally accepted and maintained, there is no offense of being separated from them after the day has passed."

Regarding the two offenses of violating the rules of deportment and having deficient robes: if one’s original *śuddhaka* (purified) status was established when the robes were first prepared, that original purification is lost once they are made into the three robes (*tricīvara*), because the three robes do not allow for surplus to be kept.
Even so, if a bhikṣu has a valid reason and obtains a single piece of woolen cloth (*kambala*) and makes it into the three robes, he does not commit the offense of keeping excess.
Question: If this is so, why does the "One-Month Precept" state that one must not pass [the month] with uncut or unsewn robes?
One who commits the offense daily answers that he previously possessed three robes capable of being worn, and thus had to cut them into the shape of robes to avoid the fault of "excess";
since this treatise states that he previously lacked the three robes, the two cases do not coincide.

Question: Among the five precepts concerning the *kaṭhina* robe and the extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), which was established first? If the *kaṭhina* robe was established first as an exception, why were the five matters such as the extra robes established?

Conversely, if the extra robes and so forth were established first, there would be no basis for the *kāṭhina* robe; why then say it is "already issued"? Answer: According to the *Pañcavargika*, the precepts regarding the extra robes and so forth were indeed established first. The *kaṭhina* robe was established later.

Regarding the statement that it is "already issued," this refers to the fact that the *kaṭhina* robe is not permitted during the period when the *kaṭhina* has been suspended (*uddhṛta*). Therefore, the *kaṭhina* robe was established after the other five precepts.

Question: Later, when the rules were expanded as previously explained, the four *pārājika* offenses were difficult to understand. Why is it that only the first three precepts uniquely permit the use of a *kaṭhina* robe?
Answer: These three precepts all concern items belonging to oneself; permitting their use is beneficial, as it prevents the fault of having surplus robes that must be separated from one’s person.
Furthermore, it does not cause distress to the donor. The remaining [precepts] are not like this. Question: If that is so, why does one personally prepare five types of bedding (*pañca-śayanāsana*)?

If one travels more than three *yojanas* carrying rain-cloths (*vassikasāṭikā*) and other such items that do not belong to oneself, why cause distress to the owner? Why are they not opened [for inspection]?

If you say they are not opened because they are made [of fine material] and thus provoke reproach, then since mine are also long and separated [from the body], they too should not be opened as they likewise provoke reproach.
Answer: Because they are long and separated, there is little reproach or hindrance to the path; otherwise, it is not so. Question: At what time are these three precepts obtained?

Regarding the phrase "having finished wearing the robe" (*cīvara-dhāraṇa-niṣṭhita*) and so forth, as for the other three rules concerning food: if one has already obtained the benefit of the *kathina* robe, why does the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* state "not having finished wearing it"?
The answer is that these three rules specifically pertain to obtaining the merit of the *kathina* robe; there is no opening [for exceptions] regarding other conditions.

Therefore, while this rule allows for wearing it outside the period of the *Prātimokṣa*, the others do not have this meaning. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that during the time of the three rules concerning food, the benefit of the robe is also [included].

Regarding the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the statement "when making robes" refers to this very occasion; because there is no offense during this time, the case of the "urgent gift" (*ātyayika-dāna*) in the *Prātimokṣa* can be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the measurement here, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the length is four *hasta* of the Buddha, but does not mention the width.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that "four *hasta*" equals seven feet and two inches. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that the width should be one *hasta* and the length two *hasta*, and it should be purified (*pariśuddha*).

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that for the three robes (*tricīvara*), the length should be one cubit and six inches and the width eight inches; these must be formally dedicated (*śuddhi*). Regarding the "extra robe" (*atireka-cīvara*), it says the length should be two spans (*vitasti*) and the width one span.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that if it exceeds four finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in length, it should be treated as a formal gift (*śuddhi-dāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the opening of a ten-day limit, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says this is because the maximum number is ten, while the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: [...]* *Note: The source text provided appears to be a fragment of a commentary on monastic disciplinary rules (vinaya) concerning the measurement and formal dedication of robes.*
Because it is neither too lax nor too strict, if one travels for ten days and returns, ten days are permitted;
if one says "one month," the Buddha-dharma should permit it, but it does not specify a fixed duration such as "that much" long or broad.

Question: Zhi says that if one performs the ritual of *jìng* (purification) in the presence of a layperson, an animal, or an insentient being, it does not constitute a valid *jìng*; this is called an "inappropriate place" (*fēichù*).
For what reason, then, within the context of the medicinal precepts (*yàojiè*), is it permitted for the five classes of monastics, laypeople, and even animals to all become donors (*shīzhǔ*)?

Answer: Regarding robes, they only prevent excess; since there is no further requirement for formal acceptance (*shòu*) or purification (*jìng*), they attain their status simply by being in the same category [as the donor]. Medicines, however, both prevent excess and require acceptance and purification. Therefore, [the rules differ].

Therefore, common people and animals alike all arise from the completion of reception and purification. Question: Regarding the offense of using a long robe without first relinquishing it—if one wears it, one incurs the offense;
why is it that if one removes it, one does not incur the offense? Answer: Wearing it constitutes an offense because it is a transgression against sentient beings;

removing it involves no transgression because there is no fault in relation to insentient objects. It is like entering an illegal dwelling: one incurs a fault upon entry, but there is no blame upon exiting.

This case is also like that. The *Śīla-darśana* (Shanjian) says: "If one commits an offense involving the forfeiture of robes (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), because there is no bhikṣu present, one has not yet performed the forfeiture and confession;

it is permissible to wear them without fault. The primary interpretation of this statement is that it pertains to the precept concerning the three robes (*tricīvara*); thus, it appears to permit [the wearing of] the three robes, but does not refer to other types of clothing.
Question: Why is it that clothing is heavy when kept and light when worn, whereas food is heavy when eaten and light when kept? Answer:

Because the Noble One permitted the keeping [of clothing] after it had been purified (*pariśuddha*), one may keep it even if one does not currently wear it. Since the substance of the clothing remains, it is heavy according to the mind that keeps it; because the substance remains, it is regulated as light according to its actual use.
As for food, it was originally not permitted to be kept; because the intention to keep it is slight, the offense is light. It is exhausted immediately upon eating and has no continuity.

Therefore, the offense is grave. Furthermore, to clarify that clothing, food, and so forth are all requisites for sustenance: clothing is an external requisite, while food satisfies internal hunger. Clothing has specific ownership;
if one keeps it as livestock (i.e., hoards it), it obstructs oneself, and thus the offense is grave. Regarding food, the offense is light. Taking food merely removes hunger;

whereas the principle of keeping livestock as food applies broadly and does not constitute personal ownership—it is only when one consumes it that it serves as a requisite. Therefore, the offense regarding food is grave, while that regarding livestock is light.

Because the internal and external requisites differ in their nature, they do not coincide. Question: If that is so, why is it that keeping medicine for seven days is a heavy offense, while eating impure medicine is a light one?
Furthermore, why is wearing white robes a heavy offense? Question: If one abandons property that actually exists by claiming it does not exist, the abandonment is established;

should it also be established if someone within the boundary claims it does not exist? Answer: The abandonment of robes is not established because they have not been gathered [by the recipient]. That is his [case].
Inanimate objects cannot obstruct the act of relinquishing; furthermore, it is said that one gives purity to another.

Therefore, for relinquishment to be established, both parties must be sentient beings, as they can obstruct one another so that this teaching may be followed in common. [Objection: Why is it necessary to relinquish the object? [Response:

If one does not relinquish the wealth, the mind of attachment will not be dispelled. Nevertheless, the reason why giving to a separate group is not permitted is because of the profit derived from such wealth.

Out of respect for the feelings of others, when a transgression occurs, the entire assembly of monks must gather to examine the matter in detail. This is intended so that the offender, facing the community, will feel shame and remorse within, thereby ceasing the offense hereafter.

Once it is known that the robe has been returned, one must do so with extreme haste; if one remains seated [in expectation] for too long, even exceeding fifteen days, one must return [the robe], or at least perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "One must not remain for a prolonged period. If it exceeds half a month, one must return it, or else perform the formal announcement.
Fourth, the manner of returning [the robe] differs from the fourfold procedure for making a formal announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

Question: Why is it that when returning property, one does not perform a formal act (*karman*), whereas when returning a robe belonging to the Saṃgha, one performs a *karman*? Answer: Giving away [property] is an individual matter arising from internal intention; it cannot be decided by the harmony of the Saṃgha.

Since returning a robe belonging to the Saṃgha to an individual requires no room for unilateral action, they are therefore different. Furthermore, this concerns the acceptance of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*).

It is not that the offense is extinguished by the formal act alone; rather, because the formal extinction of the offense further requires other conditions, the procedure for returning the robe using the *jñapti* (single motion) is modeled after the rules for the Saṃgha, and thus it must be performed with a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion followed by one proclamation).
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Is there a case where a monk possesses a robe that has exceeded ten days, yet this very robe is separated from him for one night?
It answers: "Yes. There is a case where a robe that has exceeded ten days has been made into one of the three robes (*tricīvara*), and having accepted it, [the monk] goes outside the boundary."
Because the dawn light has appeared, it is known that one who has committed the offense of keeping extra robes may now fashion them into the three robes (*tricīvara*).

Question: If one has sewn the three robes together, and due to some circumstance, they are torn apart and carried to different locations, such that the monk does not remain overnight with the robes [within the same boundary], and the monk then dies—how should this be handled?
Answer: They should be divided within the original boundary. Alternatively, they should be given to the attendant (*glānopasthāyaka*).
Since they were originally intended to be worn as a single robe, the Vinaya Master stated that the latter [the three robes] constitutes the definitive rule.
Question: Prior to the Tathāgata’s commissioning of Ānanda to fashion the *kāṣāya*, did the three robes not yet exist? Answer:

According to the rules, there were *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) garments, but no *chinnaka* (cut-and-sewn) robes. Alternatively, it may be explained that although *chinnaka* robes existed, they were not in accordance with the Dharma.

Question: If one first acquires robes and a bowl and more than five days have passed; or if one has been subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya*) and so forth; or if one is a person who is insane and subsequently enters a celestial palace or reaches Uttarakuru;

or if, after being released from expulsion, one regains one's original mind or returns to one's original location—what day shall be taken as the limit for performing the *śuddhika* (purification) ritual?
Answer: One interpretation is that one further day is obtained. Another interpretation is that one takes the previous five days. Thus says the Vinaya Master.

The subsequent meaning establishes the definitive rule: herein, first, regarding a true donor who has passed away, regardless of whether they previously performed the *suci-karaṇa* (purification) or whether it was not yet purified, one must perform the *suci-karaṇa* for all [the items], because the person who guarded them has died.

Some say that if one obtains long-term wealth and makes robes from it, or obtains what was already made, it is not necessary to perform the *suci-karaṇa*, because these are heavy items (*gurudravya*). Question: If that is so, as in the case of a *bhikṣuṇī*...
How could sixteen bowls, seven-day medicines, and the like be considered light items that the Noble One would permit the *śuddhika-dharma* (the rite of purification) for?

Furthermore, what is the intent behind the question: "Is there a difference between being separated from the three robes (*tricīvara*)—which is heavy—and being separated from other robes— which is light? The answer is as follows: As for the three robes, they are the outward signs of the Path and the essential requisites for sustaining the body; there is no time when they are not required. They are the most excellent means for generating wholesome states (*kuśala*).

When receiving them, one must resolve with a focused mind that they shall not be parted from. Therefore, if one is separated from them, it constitutes a grave offense. Other robes, however, are merely for the sake of convenience and are not indispensable; thus, being separated from them is considered a light matter. Consequently, the Blessed One permitted the *śuddhika-dharma* for these latter items. This is the underlying meaning.
Regarding the separation from one's lodgings: since one has now been separated from them, the fundamental essential mind of upholding [the robes] is lost;

therefore, the offense is grave. As for other items such as bowls and so forth, these are not monastic garments (*dharma-vastra*); furthermore, they have specific times of use and are not required at all times. For this reason, when receiving them, one does not state that they must not be separated from oneself.

Although one may now be separated from them overnight, the method of their formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is not lost; thus, the offense is light. Furthermore, this explains the regulation regarding the possession of the three robes.

Because these [three robes] violate the regulations regarding superior, middling, and inferior [quality], they incur a *pāyattika*; whereas for other garments, because there is an exception [for those of middling and inferior quality], violating it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. Question:

If that is so, since the bowl (*pātra*) also violates the regulations regarding its counterpart, why does violating it constitute a *duṣkṛta* rather than losing the formal acceptance (*parigraha*)? Answer: Clothing obscures the body and is unsightly;

there is no time when it is not required, and thus violating it incurs a *pāyattika* and results in the loss of acceptance. The bowl, however, has limits on its use; therefore, the two cases are not comparable. This is correct.

It is said that once one has received and maintained the three robes (*tricīvara*), they are relinquished immediately upon a change of gender (*vyañjanaparivṛtti*). Question: If the "ten-day robe" and the "one-month robe" are established as two distinct precepts, why is it that when one is separated from one's robes due to illness and receives formal authorization (*saṃghakamma*) from the Sangha, yet remains separated from the robes after the illness has healed, these are not divided into two separate precepts but are instead combined into one? Answer: Generally speaking, when discussing separation [from the robes], there is only one [precept]. It is only when there is no illness that the ten-day robe and the one-month robe are distinguished as two separate precepts. However, because both involve being separated from the robes while ill and receiving formal authorization from the Sangha, they are combined into a single category. Furthermore, regarding the ten-day robe, if one is separated from the robes for more than ten days, it constitutes a transgression; if one is separated for less than ten days, it does not constitute a transgression. Regarding the one-month robe, if one is separated for more than one month, it constitutes a transgression; if one is separated for less than one month, it does not constitute a transgression. Thus, based on the distinction between whether the period exceeds or falls short of the limit, they are established as two precepts. However, since the case of being separated from the robes due to illness and receiving formal authorization from the Sangha applies equally to both, they are combined into one. Moreover, if one is separated from the robes for more than ten days, one incurs a *pācittiya* offense; if one is separated for more than one month, one incurs a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense. Because the gravity of the offenses differs, they are established as two precepts. Yet, because the condition of being separated from the robes due to illness and receiving formal authorization from the Sangha is identical for both, they are combined into one. Furthermore, if one is separated from the robes for more than ten days, one must forfeit the robe; if one is separated for more than one month, one must forfeit the robe. Because the procedure for forfeiture is the same, they are combined into one. Finally, if one is separated from the robes for more than ten days, one must confess the offense; if one is separated for more than one month, one must confess the offense. Because the procedure for confession is the same, they are combined into one. Therefore, although they are established as two precepts based on the difference in the duration of the separation, they are combined into one based on the identity of the circumstances involving illness, formal authorization, forfeiture, and confession. Thus, it is said that there is only one [precept] regarding separation. It is only when there is no illness that the ten-day robe and the one-month robe are distinguished as two separate precepts. But because both involve being separated from the robes while ill and receiving formal authorization from the Sangha, they are combined into one. Because the substance of the requisites differs, the duration for which one may be separated from two [of them] and from one [the third] differs; therefore, these are combined as one:

first, the three robes (*tricīvara*); second, if one is ill and has not yet recovered, one may stay overnight separated from the robes, but once recovered, staying overnight separated from them is no different than when one was originally healthy—therefore, they are combined.
Question: Regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being separated from the robes, among the three robes, which robe may be separated from, and for how long?

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) states that one may be separated from [the robes] only regarding the *kāṣāya*; the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya) states that one may also be separated from the two lower robes; it is clear that one may separate from one of the three robes as desired.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) states that one may keep the middle robe, but not the upper or lower ones; however, if there are inferior or superior ones, one may keep whichever is preferred.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that from the seventh month to the ninth month, during the summer retreat, one is not separated [from the robes]. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific text from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.*

Now, it is permitted to place [the robe] in the first nine months and in the latter eight months. The *Cīvaravastu* of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that the formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is limited to one month, and this may also be done during the summer retreat.
The present *vinaya* [states] that for a sick monk, the formal act (*karman*) is performed by means of a motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

According to the *Sāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, if a monk leaves his robe behind to go elsewhere due to illness, and though he recovers, cannot return because the road is dangerous, he does not lose [the robe] provided he constantly maintains the intention to return, even if he fails to do so. The *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* [also] states this.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal procedure): if one is unable to act due to a severe illness, and after the illness has cleared one is again unable to act because the illness recurs, the previous *karmavācanā* remains valid within the same month.

Question: When there is both seasonal clothing (*kālacīvara*) and non-seasonal clothing (*akālacīvara*), with reference to which is the "month" established for the expectation of clothing? Answer: It is established with reference to non-seasonal clothing.

Regarding this, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If one obtains a new garment—or a fine garment—within the first ten days, and having obtained it, neither makes it oneself nor instructs another to make it, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) once the first ten days have passed. The same is said for the latter twenty days.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if five days of the first ten days have already passed and one obtains a garment with the hope of using it, [it is permissible] during the latter five days within the first ten days.

Regarding these five days, this ten-day period should be treated as a middle ten-day period; the latter ten days are also like this. If the first five days of the [subsequent] ten days have passed, one may obtain the expected robe even if nine days have elapsed.
One day is spent in making it, and on the tenth day, the robe is obtained. That very day it is made. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

"If one seeks diligently without interruption, one waits until the full month is reached. If the intention to seek is interrupted, it does not reach a full month. If one obtains the robe at the beginning..."
If on the first day one knows for certain that there is no hope [of obtaining the robe], yet one keeps it past ten days, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If on the first day one obtains the cloth and keeps it while waiting for a hoped-for acquisition, but does not obtain what was hoped for, yet obtains something other than what was hoped for—these two cases, if within ten days, constitute an impure gift;

if one gives it to another to have made into a robe, upon reaching the eleventh day, one commits an offense of forfeiture. This applies even if up to the tenth day one has not obtained what was hoped for, but has obtained something other than what was hoped for.

It should be understood that this constitutes eleven days for the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The *Śīlaskandha-vibhāṣā* states: "If there is a source from which one expects [cloth], one may keep it for one month.

If on the twenty-ninth day one obtains cloth, if the previously obtained is coarse and the newly obtained is fine, one must perform the *śuddhi-vidhi* (purification/declaration) regarding the coarse one;

the fine one may be kept for another month because it was obtained with expectation. If later one obtains a coarse cloth, it may likewise be kept for one month. In this manner, it should not exceed [the limit]."
Regarding the meaning of the "one-month" [allowance]: if all three robes are present, even if they are all slightly deficient, do not inquire further; the one-month period is permitted for all.
If, within ten days, the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) is sufficient when combined with other cloth, one must cut out the cotton batting that day.

If the first light of dawn on the eleventh day has already appeared and the material for the two lower robes is insufficient, it constitutes an offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). However, if there is no underlying basis for the deficiency, the one-month allowance is granted.

Question: Why is taking a nun’s robe prohibited while taking a bowl is not? Answer: Because robes are of five types, they are frequently given away and accepted;

thus, for the sake of the principle of frequent exchange, they must be regulated. As for the bowl, there is only one type, and nuns give them infrequently; therefore, even if one were to accept one, [there would be no need for regulation].

Regarding the commission of a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) while understanding that there is no transgression: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when a nun takes a bowl or other small items from a monk, there is no offense.

This is explained at length, even extending to the point that if one goes beyond the boundary by twenty-five cubits to a place beyond the range of sight or hearing, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Question: Why is taking a robe belonging to the Saṃgha from a nun only a minor offense? Answer: Because it is rare for the venerable members of the Great Assembly (the monks) to give [robes] to nuns.
Question: If that is so, the person who gives [the robe] should also commit an offense of light degree. Why is it that a *bhikṣu* incurs a *pāyattika*, while a *bhikṣuṇī* incurs a *duṣkṛta*? Answer:

Regarding a *bhikṣu* giving to a *bhikṣuṇī*, the rule was established based on the fault of censure; because the sense of generating defilement is profound, the offense incurred is heavy. Regarding a *bhikṣuṇī* taking a robe from a *saṃgha*, the rule was established based on the frequency of occurrence;
therefore, she incurs a light offense.
Question: Since washing, dyeing, and beating are collectively governed by these three precepts, why is this so? Answer:

Because they all involve a *śrāmaṇerī* (novice nun) in the same context, and furthermore, they all originate from a single robe from beginning to end. Question: Since you have established the rule that a nun must wash clothes, why did you not establish a rule for her to fumigate bowls?

Answer: The meanings of "dyeing" and "washing" are easy to understand, and nuns are generally proficient in them. However, "fumigating" and "repairing" are difficult tasks, and nuns are generally not [proficient] in them.

Rarely does one commit a minor offense. Question:
Why is it that regarding robes, the rule prohibits taking more than what is sufficient, while for the bowl, no such prohibition is established? Answer: There are three types of robes;

if they are lost, the amount lost is not fixed. The bowl, however, has only one; once received, it remains as a single unit, and thus inherently there is no offense [in its loss]. Therefore, it is singular.
Regarding the rule that prohibits one [type of bowl] but not the other:

A questioner asks, "Since the prohibition regarding robes establishes an exhortation to increase their value, yet there is no such exhortation for the bowl, how is this so? The answer is: "The purpose of robes is to support the body in a broad sense;

because people delight in increasing their value, they are prohibited. The purpose of the bowl is to support the body in a narrow sense; because such instances are rare, it is not applied in parallel. The questioner asks again: "If one exhorts the increase of a bowl and it is a minor offense, why is it not the same as begging?"

Question: Why is the regulation regarding the bowl treated the same as that for robes? Answer: Indeed, because the bowl is not used extensively; however, since the offense of causing distress by begging for an entire bowl is profound, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
Furthermore, because one incurs a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*) for every instance of urging [the donor] to increase the amount, even if it is only a single thread. Question:

Why does urging the increase of threads constitute an offense even down to a single thread, whereas begging for a single strip of cloth is contrary to this? Answer: Regarding the original donor who gave the cloth...

Since there was no prior intention to give, and because the offense of causing distress regarding the amount given—ranging from the time of begging until the recipient’s deliberation—is minor, one incurs the offense only upon receiving a single portion.

However, in the case of encouraging an increase where the donor has already sincerely determined the limit of their gift, the fault is most profound due to the emotional transgression of not acknowledging that kindness, begrudging the small amount, and seeking more out of greed; therefore, regardless of the quantity, one should not [accept further].

If both increase the price, they both commit the offense. Question: If one encourages two householders to increase the price, and one increases it while the other does not, is it an offense? Answer: It is an offense for the latter [the one who did not increase it].
Only the one who increased it commits the offense; the one who did not increase it does not. This is because they acted together as a pair. Question: Why is this so?
The question was: "If one merely exhorts two householders and not three, the answer is that two people together make one robe;

to exhort them to increase [the material] causes much vexation, which is why it must be restricted to three. Three people together cause much damage and vexation, yet this is slight, and thus it is not restricted.
Now, if three householders each make one cotton garment for themselves, and you now exhort them to work together to make one silk garment, how could this not be permissible?"

Question: Why is there no offense regarding the reduction [of the value]? Answer: This precept fundamentally requires that an offense occurs only when one increases the value upon the substance of the robe offered;

it is only when one encourages the addition of silk gauze (*chouluo*) that it constitutes a violation. In the previous precept concerning begging for robes, the primary explanation was that the original purpose was to purchase plain silk;

here, encouraging the addition of silk gauze constitutes an offense under the precept on begging. This precept fundamentally requires the substance of the robe offered before an offense occurs; the same applies to the subsequent case of seeking thread.

Question: Within the regulations concerning the price of robes, why is it that the offense of requesting more than the limit is not likewise established for the price of a bowl? Answer: A bowl is fundamentally used for eating;
one is sufficient for this purpose, and there is no need for many. Therefore, how could it be permitted?
Even if one were to request it a hundred thousand times over without possessing a bowl at all, there would be no offense; thus, it is not regulated.
Question: If one suddenly and insistently demands clothing, does this constitute an offense against the king, his ministers, or the pure master? Answer:

Because the king and his ministers, out of diligent concern that this object might be lost, insistently demand it and thereby distress the donor, an offense is incurred by harming the integrity of the realm.
Question: Regarding cotton bedding and black-and-white wool bedding, are they both equally prohibited from being requested as valuable items?

If so, why is the rule for the former completely revoked while that for the latter is not? Answer: Cotton is obtained through the taking of life; therefore, even when requested as a valuable item, it must be cut and destroyed to eliminate greed.

Black-and-white wool, though valuable, is not obtained through the taking of life; thus, while it may give rise to afflictions, the principle [of its necessity] is subtle. For this reason, the rule for cotton is entirely revoked. Question: Why is cotton singled out?

Question: Why are the two types of bedding, the seven types of precious items, and the seven types of medicine listed under "renunciation" (*pratyāśraya*) rather than being treated as "exceptions" (*anujñā*)? Answer: Generally, when an item has been renounced and subsequently becomes fit for its original use, it is not subject to the formal procedure of renunciation;
rather, its status is clarified through an exception. However, these four rules (the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules concerning extra robes) are the opposite: once renounced, they may be used again.

Furthermore, it is explained that after these four rules have been renounced, the substance of the items may either deteriorate or it may not be permitted to use them again for their original purpose, which is the same principle applied to "extra robes" (*atireka-cīvara*).
This is contrary to the previous [rule], and thus they differ. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one has already completed [the period of use], there is no offense in using it;
this is not like the bedding and mats of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which must be surrendered to the Saṃgha.

Question: Once the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is concluded, may one reduce the period of six years? If one makes [the robe] entirely black or white, is it an offense? Is the former offense or the latter?
The preceptor replied: "No offense was committed, because it has been less than six years since he attained the Dharma. Since the black and white sides are distinct, one commits a prior offense;

for example, having received the formal authorization (*jñapti*) from the Saṃgha, if one constructs a house exceeding the prescribed dimensions, one incurs the offense of exceeding those dimensions despite the authorization."
Question: Why is there a fixed limit for the years of use regarding bedding (*śayanāsana*), yet no such limit is set for the folding sitting mat (*niṣīdana*)?
Answer: Bedding is intended to absorb warmth and provide physical sustenance; because it has been used for many years, it becomes worn out and loses its capacity to sustain the body.

Therefore, a limit on the years of use is established. As for the folding sitting mat, it is not intended to absorb bodily warmth, but rather to prevent the defilement of the monks' bedding. Thus, no limit is set for its folding.
One who possesses an obstructed body may simply cease [the practice]; provided that the physical basis remains, there is no limit to the number of years.

Since one already possesses a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and constantly enjoys its use, yet desires to make another out of greed, it is for this reason that the folding [of the robe] is regulated to suppress such attachment. Question: If one does not fold it, or if one has already folded it and then repented, why is it still necessary to discard it?
Answer: If one does not fold it, there is fault throughout the entire body; even if one folds it again now, the original fault still remains.

Since the substance of the fault lies in the fact that [the cloth] still exists, one must discard it; however, there is no fault within the prescribed measure. One first cuts away what exceeds the measure and then performs the confession of the offense; therefore, discarding [the entire cloth] is unnecessary.
Furthermore, once discarded, it would simply return to its owner, rendering it impossible to use; thus, one must cut it away, but need not discard it entirely. Question:
If that is so, it would still be acceptable not to fold it after discarding it and returning it to the owner; should one not also fold it? Answer: [One must fold it.]

Not folding [the sitting mat] for the sake of elegance, and then returning it to me after having discarded it, is equivalent in meaning to receiving it anew; this is not my own fault, but rather a transgression for exceeding the measure when another gives it to me.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If one obtains the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for a sitting mat without having folded it, there is no fault in not having folded it."

Question: Among the eight types of impure objects, what offense is committed when they are exchanged with one another? Answer: If two items, such as a gold-embroidered quilt and a woolen rug, are exchanged, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense);
for the exchange of the remaining six items among themselves, it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Exchanging any of these six with one another incurs a minor offense (*āpatti dukkaṭa*).

If one exchanges any of these six with the other two [types of impure objects], one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya pācittiya*). Furthermore, if one uses any of the eight impure objects to trade for the ten kinds of robes, one commits an offense in every case.

Question: One who maintains the pure precepts is not permitted to use goods obtained through trade while alive;
for what reason is it permitted to receive a share after death? Answer: This karma is most grave. If one were to consume such goods while alive, that bhikṣu would reflect:

"Although this trade is sinful, there remains the merit of providing for the Saṅgha," and thus he would continue to engage in it without end. Therefore, its use is forbidden while alive. Once the bhikṣu has died, however, there is no longer any further activity [to be performed].
Section on the Karmavācanā according to Principle. Question:

Regarding the precept on extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), there is an allowance for *kāṣāya* robes, yet why is there no such allowance for the alms bowl? Answer: The substance of the robe and the bowl are distinct.

Benefits do not extend to the bowl; where there is a fault, it does not cause mutual impairment, and where there is a benefit, it does not reach it. Therefore, there is none. Question: [Regarding] the robe...
It is not permitted to accept an alms bowl. Why? Because the *kāṣāya* (robe) consists of three layers; since the *saṃghāṭī* is heavy, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe is permitted.

Even if separated from it, there is no offense, as it provides additional benefit during the extended period. As for the alms bowl, there is only one, which is constantly carried and used by the person.

How could one accept a *kaṭhina* bowl? Since the acceptance of a *kaṭhina* bowl is not permitted and it provides no additional benefit during the extended period, it is not said that "it has been removed."

Question: Why is it that the Kārttika month is not mentioned in response? Answer: If the bowl has not yet been completed, there is originally no surplus; why then would there be a need for an exemption?
Once the bowl is completed, an exemption of ten days is sufficient, as it allows for the performance of the *śuddhika* (purification/declaration of purity); therefore, there is no one-month period.
Furthermore, other robes differ according to the four seasons and require washing, so exemptions for them have time limits; the bowl is not like this, and thus [the month] is not [mentioned].

The *Samantapāsādikā* asks: Is there a case where a single bowl constitutes an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense? It answers: Yes; that is, one who does not maintain [the vow] according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* asks:
Is there a case where a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl for more than ten days and yet does not incur the offense of forfeiture?

It answers: Yes; this refers to one who, having received a bowl, undergoes a change of gender and becomes a bhikṣuṇī. For a bhikṣuṇī who keeps one for ten days and then undergoes a change of gender, it is likewise. The *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* asks: [Regarding the formal] announcement (*jñapti*).
If one keeps a colored robe beyond ten days, one commits an offense; if one keeps a white bowl beyond ten days, why is there no offense? Answer:

A robe can be dyed to suit one’s wishes, and it is certain that its original color will be altered; furthermore, there is no increase or decrease in its value, so the sense of "storing" is strong, and thus one commits the offense of keeping it for too long.
As for a bowl, if it is scorched, smoked, or otherwise damaged, it is difficult to have it restored to one's liking; therefore, there is no offense.

Question: If a robe exceeds or falls short [of the required measure], it still constitutes formal acceptance (*parigraha*); why is this not the case for a bowl? Answer: Regarding robes, if they exceed the measure, they can be cut down;
if they fall short, they can be supplemented. Therefore, formal acceptance is established. For a bowl, however, there is no such possibility; thus, formal acceptance is not established. Question:

When begging for a bowl, if one obtains many bowls of high quality, should one keep them or place them in the monastic storehouse (*saṃgha-kośa*)? Answer: If they are for the sake of one's own monastery, even if one obtains many robes through begging, it will lead to distress.

Question: Since the donor would suffer loss as well as the monastery itself, why not [return] the bowl? Answer: The robes are fundamentally for the purpose of sustaining the body; because they provide ample resources, they are returned to the donor.
The bowl has no great utility for sustaining the body; because its function is narrow, it must enter the Sangha. Question:

If that is so, even if one keeps an extra bowl beyond the permitted day, since it likewise has little utility, why not return one bowl to the donor and have the rest enter the Sangha? Answer: One may keep an extra bowl for oneself.
Objects are easily obtained, or donors may give with sincere hearts without harming others; yet, although they are not used much, they cause few afflictions.
Therefore, they should all be returned to their owners. As for those who beg for alms bowls, it creates several types of harm: first, it increases greed and seeking;
second, it troubles the donor; third, it damages the monastery; and fourth, they are not used much. Because such harms are manifold, [the bowl] must be entered into the Sangha.
Question: When requesting thread for weaving, why is it that only the laity who are not relatives are prohibited [from doing so], while nuns are not?

Answer: Because the laity are subject to secular authorities, whereas nuns are not. Furthermore, nuns have no rule for weaving themselves; since the Great Assembly (the monks) knows the Dharma, the principle of employing a nun is rare.
Even if she were to weave for them, she would incur only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). Question: If that is so, one might as well prohibit only the laity from washing the robes.

Niyata replied: "The Noble Teaching permits nuns to wash and dye their own robes themselves. Therefore, it is because the Great Sangha takes pleasure in having nuns wash them that it would hinder their cultivation of the Path.
Furthermore, since the meaning of washing and dyeing is simple and involves no great loss, there is no offense."

Regarding the precept on weaving robes in cooperation: the previous response stated that because both lay donors were the owners of the thread, there was the sense of "cooperation" in making the robe.

However, in this case, if each of the two lay donors sends a separate weaver and the bhikṣu privately urges those two weavers to cooperate in making a single robe, since they are not the owners of the thread, how can there be the sense of "cooperation"? Therefore, [this rule was established].
Question: Regarding this prohibition, what is the difference between the offense incurred here and that incurred with the weaver as mentioned previously concerning the spinner?

Answer: In the previous precept, the weaver was harmed but the owner of the yarn was not, because [the monk] obtained the yarn himself. In this precept, the owner of the yarn is harmed but the weaver is not, because [the monk] provides the payment.
Furthermore, in the previous case, there was no offense if the person was a relative; in this precept, it does not matter whether the person is a relative or not.

Because both involve the principle of damaging the threads, and because the former constitutes an offense of weaving while this constitutes an offense of receiving [the garment], they are separately prescribed.

Question: If there is no offense when taking back a śrāmaṇera’s robe, then according to the ninety minor rules below, since a śrāmaṇera should not commit the same offense as a bhikṣu, he too should be subject to a light offense.
Answer: Originally, the robe was given so that they might travel together; the śrāmaṇera is not one's own companion [in the formal sense].
The principle of "category" (jāti) is rarely applied to the forfeiture [of robes], nor is it frequently applied to the suspension (pravāsanīya-karman).

Therefore, when one commits a minor offense and undergoes the formal act of suspension (nigarhaṇīya-karman), once the procedure is completed, no one is permitted to follow or comply with him; they all equally abide by the monastic law.

Since there is no difference in the harm or affliction caused, why is it that when those who have committed the same offense are questioned regarding the forfeiture of a novice’s robe, or when a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense incurs a minor transgression, the severity of the punishment differs so greatly?

Answer: Regarding the granting of robes, the original intent was that they could travel together; however, both the novice who has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) and the one who has committed a light offense may not travel or sleep together, as their status is equal in this regard.

Thus, they are identical in committing a light offense. As for striking [the novice], the intention was primarily to cause him distress. In the case of striking a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense, the sense of causing harm and distress is profound because he occupies the same rank as oneself.
In the case of a novice, his status is distinct as he belongs to a lower class; thus, the sense of causing distress is slight, and therefore the gravity of the offenses differs.
Question: As stated in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, one begins seeking rain-cloths on the sixteenth day of the third month and uses them for bathing on the first day of the fourth month.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that if there is an intercalary third month, one must wait until the sixteenth day of the later third month to begin seeking them.

If one enters the rains retreat on the sixteenth day of the earlier fourth month during an intercalary fourth month, one may use them until the middle of the seventh month; however, it is not yet clear how this applies in practice.

Question: Why is it permitted to seek the *kaṭhina* robe on the sixteenth day of the fourth month before the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), yet not permitted to seek it on the fifteenth day of the third month before the intercalary month?

Answer: Because seeking [the robe] for one's own use involves affliction (*kleśa*), whereas there is no affliction in seeking it for the sake of others; thus, the periods before and after differ. Question:

If many days are obtained during the intercalary month for the rainy-season robe (*varṣā-śāṭī*), should one likewise obtain many benefits from receiving the *kāṭhina-śāṭī* during the intercalary month? Answer: Yes.

Regarding robes, there are many occasions for their use; those permitted during an intercalary month carry the fault of increasing greed. As for rain-cloths, once they are one's own property, they may be used during a summer intercalary month without the fault of excessive greed.

The primary intent of this regulation is clarified by its timing: when the period for seeking and storing is opened for one month, the great rule restricts it to half a month for seeking and half a month for storing.
Even if one has not yet performed formal acceptance (*parigraha*), there is no need for the ritual of "purification" (*viśuddhi*); this constitutes the "one-hundred-and-one" category.

Regarding the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) of robes: if one has entered the preceding *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, one should formally accept them according to the Dharma so as to use them until the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
They should be kept in one place and must not be stored for later use; if they are so stored, it constitutes a transgression (*vyañjana*), yet there is no need to relinquish them.

Upon entering the subsequent *varṣā*, there is no need to accept them again, as they may be used as before because they were already stored. As the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "From the third month..."
From the middle [of the month] until the end of the third month, one should make [the robes]; if they can be completed, one may keep them starting from the first day of the fourth month.
If the robes are not completed, it is permitted to seek [materials] or to have them made until the middle of the fourth month.

If on the sixteenth day of the third month one obtains [the materials] and completes them within one or two days, the Vinaya masters say that these may also be kept and used. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that on the first day of the fourth month, one must formally take possession [of the robes].

Having used [the rain-bath robe] until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one should discard it. Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "Because nuns are weak and inferior, it is difficult for them to carry [heavy items];
therefore, they are not permitted to keep [other robes], though the keeping of a rain-bath robe is always permitted. Moreover, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Upon reaching the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one should discard it within the assembly, making this proclamation: 'Venerable Sangha, listen! Now the Sangha discards the rain-bath robe.'"
It is stated that this [offense] does not exist in the Vinaya. Question:

What is the difference between an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) and an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*)? Answer: This precept is violated both at the proper time and at an improper time, whereas that [other rule] is not;

therefore, they differ. Because violating the teaching deeply increases greed, it was thus established as a prohibition. As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states regarding the preceding and following [cases]:
If one obtains an urgent gift-cloth (*ātyayika-cīvara*) ten days before the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the end of the rains retreat, it should be accepted and formally designated as such;
by this it is proven that even if the latter rains retreat has not yet concluded, one may still accept an urgent gift-cloth. Question:

Why is the period for accepting out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*) increased by nine days beyond the one-month and five-month limits, whereas during the proper season no such increase is made? Answer: Regarding the acceptance of out-of-season robes, [the rule] returns to...

If it is argued that the "extraordinary allowance" (*akālika-uddhāra*) was granted because [the robe] was received at an improper time, yet now it is received at a proper time, how can there still be an extraordinary allowance? If that were so, receiving at an improper time would likewise not be permitted as an "allowance during the proper season.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this applies only to urgent gifts; for those received at an improper time, nine days are added to the period outside the [robe] season.

Since receiving during the proper season is not an urgent gift and there is no time limit for receiving such robes, why is it necessary to grant an additional nine-day allowance? [Question: Why is this extended?
If one keeps an extra robe (*cīvara*) for ten days without performing the *paryāpanna* (formal declaration), and the eleventh day’s dawn arrives, one commits an offense.
Regarding this *ātyayika-cīvara* (urgent gift robe) received on the sixth day of the seventh month, if one keeps it for ten days, the dawn of the sixteenth day would constitute an offense.

Why does the Vinaya state that one may keep it for up to five months without committing an offense? [The answer is: This refers to an extra robe where the periods do not overlap; there is only the preceding period.

Because it was permitted, ten days having passed, one enters the eleventh day and incurs an offense; regarding the present *akālacīvara* (extra robe), receiving it for six days is permitted until the fifteenth day, before the appearance of the dawn light, at which point there is no offense prior.
Upon entering the sixteenth day, there is again a period of permission; as these two permissions join together, there is thus no offense.

As for the fifteenth day, it refers to one who has broken the summer retreat (*varṣā*) or is separated from their robes (*cīvara-vipravāsa*), and whose *anvārambhaṇa* (concluding) ceremony has not yet been completed.
One is not permitted to go outside the boundary; there is only the subsequent allowance, but no prior allowance. To transgress this constitutes an offense. Question:
The one-month robe includes the ten-day robe to constitute the merit of the one-month *kāṭhina* robe, and the *kāṭhina* month is included within the five months.
For what reason is the ten-day robe not included within the *kāṭhina* month? Why, after the one month and five months have passed, is it renewed again?

Question: What is meant by "increasing the days"? Answer: There are three points regarding the ten-day robe being subsumed within the one-month robe: first, they are identical in that both occupy a non-seasonal period;
second, they are identical in their functional capacity to prevent the offense of *atireka-cīvara* (excess robes), as the limit is the same at thirty days;

third, since the original [ten-day rule] was insufficient, it was opened up to one month—thus, the long period subsumes the short, which is why they can mutually include one another. Regarding the *kathina* robe subsuming the *kārttika* [robe], there are likewise three [points].
The meaning is identical in two respects: first, regarding the time and stage; second, both obtain the fivefold benefits of merit at equal intervals.

Third, because the original period of Kārttika consists of five months and is insufficient, this [period] is opened up by using the long to subsume the short; thus it is able to include the month of Kārttika. As for why it does not include the ten-day robe, there are also three reasons:

first, the distinction between the timely and the untimely; second, the difference in the breadth and narrowness of the benefits; and third, [the distinction between] the seasonal and the non-seasonal.
The beginning and the end do not encompass one another; just as the five-month period does not encompass the ten days, it is the same here. Question:

Within the precept regarding being separated from one's robes (*kāṭhina*), there is the provision for the six-night exemption during the *kāṭhina* robe season; why is this not maintained within the [other] precepts? Answer:

Because superior persons (*uttamapudgala*) do not accept the *kāṭhina* robe, this exemption is not opened. Question: If that were so, there should be no month of *kārttika*. Answer: It is the merit of the *kāṭhina*.
Regarding robes, because they are received through formal ritual action during the month of Kārttika, whereas the *kaṭhina* robe is received without such ritual action, the two do not coincide.

Furthermore, it is explained that a village monk who has obtained a robe within the village may go toward a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), yet a forest monk may not come to the village to receive the *kaṭhina* robe and then go toward the forest hermitage. How is it known that these are monks from different boundaries?
Because it does not constitute the formal act of receiving. Question:

If one commits a *pāyattika* offense for misappropriating property belonging to the Saṃgha, why is there no *pāyattika* offense for misappropriating property belonging to the Buddha? Answer: Regarding property belonging to the Saṃgha, there is a possibility of confusion with one's own personal possession;

thus, the transference [of ownership] can be considered a cause for receiving it with joy in one's heart. However, because the Buddha has prohibited [such appropriation], there is no [possibility of confusion] regarding property belonging to the Buddha. Therefore, there is no offense.
Since the meaning of "indiscriminate transference" is rare, it is not prescribed; thus, the essential points of the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* have been roughly established.
*Sifenlü Shiyin yi chao*, Scroll Middle Part One;
*Sifenlü Shiyin yi chao*, Scroll Middle Part Two.
Regarding the brief exposition of the *Dantika* (Single-Topic) rules, there are six sections.

First, the classification according to the three types of action (*trikarma*) to explain the formation of offenses: among the ninety rules, thirty-one are offenses of the body alone rather than of speech.
As the summary verse states: "Women, not [by force], concealment, and in private; giving, distinct offenses, and non-residual."

Not exceeding these: sitting in concealment, exposing oneself, the four [offenses], the three armies, water, wine, striking, half-white, the second [category], following, striking, the palace—there are twenty-one precepts that concern speech rather than body, as stated in the verses.

Thus: destroying [reputation], the two [cases of] being the same, speaking of the path, women, difference, suspicion, nuns, criticizing the Dharma, terror, doubt, initiating, desire, refusal, similarity, desire, groundless slander—twenty-one [precepts] concerning the *vinaya*.
The previous interpretation held that [an offense] was committed through vocal action when one was under the required age; however, the current interpretation is not so.
The Vinaya states that for the Upādhyāya there is a *thullaccaya* and for the Saṃgha there is a *dukkaṭa*; thus we know that the karma created by oneself relies upon the speech of another.

Regarding the thirty-eight precepts, some involve both vocal and bodily actions, while thirty-one involve vocal karma shared with the body and mind. There are seven precepts involving vocal abstention.

Regarding the discussion on offenses committed through both body and mind, there are three types of prior actions: first, those bodily and vocal actions that are completed by relying on another’s body, which comprise nineteen precepts;
second, those committed through one’s own body and mind when discussing self-perpetrated acts;

and third, regarding the terminology used for others, those vocal actions performed by oneself that rely on another’s body. Thus, the verse says: "Digging, destroying, leading away, using, inciting, burning, concealing, drinking, killing, driving away, and seizing a nun."
Regarding the seven precepts concerning high and ornate beds, there are next seven precepts involving verbal action that depend upon the bodies of both oneself and others for their transgression.
For instance, traveling together with a nun requires a verbal agreement made by oneself, followed by the physical act of crossing a boundary;

only then is there an offense. As the verse says: "In two places—secluded or open; four types of bedding; and requesting fine food"—there are five precepts where the action is performed by one's own body.

Regarding "using another's mouth": it is like eating when one praises food through the mouth of a *niḥsargika-pācattika* nun; by using the nun’s mouth for the verbal act (*vāk-karman*), one commits the offense of swallowing [the food] through the bodily act (*kāya-karman*).

Other cases are to be treated analogously. The verse mentions praise, admonition, the two types of listening, and those under five years of age. The offense for violating an admonition also involves the mouth.

Furthermore, regarding the violation of an admonition, speaking from a single perspective does not exhaust the full reasoning. Next, we shall discuss the cessation of action (*virati-karman*) as a joint offense involving the body.

Regarding the concealment of a single precept, the commentaries differ in their explanations. The *Gāthā-śāstra* states that this refers to the offense of the mental karma (*manas-karman*) from the perspective of its fundamental nature;

it is not merely an offense of the mind. The *Māyī* (Vinaya-mātṛkā) is likewise. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* also states that when a nun conceals a grave offense, it is an offense committed solely through the mind.
