If that is so, why is there a fixed measure for the Buddha’s robes? [The answer is: For his disciples, there is no limit and no fixed standard;

furthermore, because there is only one Buddha in the world, it is not the same. Another interpretation is that if a robe exceeds the limit, it can be cut down and used, as people do not dislike excess. Therefore, a regulation was established for this.
However, if a bowl exceeds the limit, cutting it down serves no purpose, and people dislike excess; therefore, no regulation was necessary for it.

Question: Why is it that one does not make an alms bowl equal in size to the Buddha’s? Answer: Because the substance of the robe and the bowl are the same, there would be a fault; since the substance of the bowl is distinct [from the robe], there is no such fault.
This should be cited from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
In explaining the *Pāyantika* (提舍尼) offenses, I shall briefly preserve four gates.

First, regarding the reason for preserving these four: generally, the occasions from which censure arises are twofold: first, they arise based on internal relatives; second, they arise based on external relatives.

Within the category of those based on internal relatives, there are no more than two types: private seclusion and the assembly. Regarding those arising in private seclusion, the transgression is comparable [to the following].

The Kṣatriya and the Niṣāda wear identical black garments, yet they are distinguished by gender; likewise, while residing within a village, if one takes food with one's own hands, it may give rise to deep-seated attachment, inviting censure and harming the Path.
To avoid this fault, the first precept was established. Furthermore, if one is among the assembly and privately directs [food] to someone, such conduct involves private partiality;
if one silently accepts it without rebuking it and does not reveal it to the assembly, this constitutes a fault that must be avoided. Thus, the second precept was established.
Therefore, the second precept was established concerning transgressions arising from external circumstances that do not exceed the limits of a village.
Within this context, regarding the third [precept], it refers to those arising in a village settlement:
a bhikṣu, being indolent, sits in a remote and secluded place to receive food, thereby allowing bandits to harass the woman who is delivering the food and thus bringing about censure.
Because one avoids these faults by means of censure and confession, the fourth [precept] is established; since there is no separate offense, the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
"The essence of this precept is not an offense; one confesses the transgression before another person, and if mindfulness is maintained, it can all be extinguished."
Regarding the reason for the second offense: among these four precepts, it is the third precept that constitutes an offense by violating a monastic regulation (*saṃgha-karman*).
When the *karmavācanā* for a "family under probation" (*śikṣādattaka*) has not yet been performed by the Saṃgha, there is no regulation to violate, and thus receiving food incurs no offense.

However, once the Saṃgha has proclaimed the regulation, receiving food constitutes an offense. This offense arises from the formal act (*karman*) of the Saṃgha; this monastic regulation is no different from the regulation established by the Buddha. It follows accordingly.
Regarding the differences among persons, for all three other precepts, an offense is incurred solely through the Buddha’s decree.
As for the characteristics of observance and violation of the third [precept]: in the second and fourth [precepts], both observance and violation are present. Regarding the two types of observance:

if a nun points out [the fault] and one stops eating, this is "observance by cessation" (*niṣedha-saṃvara*); if one sees the fault, rebukes it, and subsequently eats without incurring an offense, this is called "active observance" (*kriyā-saṃvara*).

Regarding these two names, their referents are distinct. As for the two types of offenses: if one sees food being pointed out [to oneself] and remains silent without rebuking it, one incurs an offense simply by virtue of desisting;
thus it is called an "offense of desisting" (*virati-āpatti*). Although one does not rebuke the pointing out, because the physical act of eating does not occur, there is no offense.

An offense that arises from the physical act of eating is called an "offense of action" (*kriyā-āpatti*). Viewed in relation to the former, it is "desisting"; viewed in relation to the latter, it is "action."
The substance of these offenses is one, though their names differ.

Regarding the fourth [offense], dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) and abstaining from food is called "maintaining through abstinence" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*); following the instructions of the Dharma by performing the ritual acts and speaking such words as "Do not send food here;

I shall receive it without transgression" is called "maintaining through action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). The two offenses are the opposites of the former, as can be understood. As for the remaining two [offenses], abstinence itself constitutes maintenance, while action constitutes maintenance.

Regarding the fourth offense, there are two different modes of transgression: the first three precepts concern the stage of one’s own practice (*svabhāga*) in terms of avoiding censure, while the latter concerns the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣabhāga*) in terms of avoiding censure.
As the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A 'householder in training' (*śaikṣa-gṛhapati*) refers to a couple who have both attained the vision of the truths;
this extends upward until they are both *anāgāmins*. If even one person has not [attained it], they cannot be called 'in training'."

Question: Among the various *karmas* for settling a household (*gṛhapratisaṃsthāpana-karman*), by what method are they performed? Answer: According to the various Vinayas, one may use either a single motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) or a second proclamation followed by a fourth proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
The procedures for their formal establishment and dissolution are not fixed; they are explained in detail in a separate chapter.
In explaining the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Training Rules for the Community), I shall briefly preserve four sections.

First, regarding the difference in the title: the reason this chapter does not specify a numerical count but refers simply to "the community" (*saṃgha*) is that the violations of deportment in this section are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and cannot be limited by a fixed number; thus, it is designated by the name "Community."

For now, we shall highlight those among the hundred precepts that people most frequently violate; these weighty ones are collected within this chapter, while the remainder are found in the *Vinaya-kaṅkṣā-viśodhana* (the *Sudarsana*) and the miscellaneous rules of decorum (*viniyaka*).

As the *Sudarsana* states: *śikṣā karaṇīya* is translated as "that which should be learned. Because the word order [in the original] is inverted, it is said "that which should be learned" (*śikṣitavya*).

Question: Why is this particular section alone named "That Which Should Be Learned"? Answer: The other precepts are easy to maintain, yet their transgressions [are grave]. Therefore, this section is specifically designated as "That Which Should Be Learned."

To commit this offense repeatedly makes repentance difficult; this precept is difficult to maintain yet easy to violate. One must constantly reflect upon and study it so as not to incur the guilt of a formal transgression;
therefore, it is said that "one should train. Regarding the explanation of the term: if named according to what is being prevented, one should say "various *duṣkṛta*s" (minor offenses);
however, here the name is derived from the practice of the remedy itself, and thus it is called "training" (*śikṣā*). As for this training, in reality, it is universal.

Question: Why is the preceding section of four [precepts] not restricted to this chapter alone, yet it specifically receives this name? Answer: Because the deportment (*īryāpatha*) in this chapter is subtle;
unless one focuses exclusively on it within the mind and applies diligent effort to maintain it, its practice cannot be perfected. Therefore, it is specifically designated as "Instruction for Study.

Furthermore, being able to uphold these precepts completely and without deficiency marks the culmination of the accomplishment of training and conduct, thereby manifesting the meaning of the merit of study.

Because it is manifest, it receives the name "training" exclusively. Second, regarding the characteristics of observance and transgression: if one considers the mind of training, both observance and transgression are present; when one gives rise to the intention to repair [a fault], this is called "observance through action" (*kṛta-śīla*).

When one does not perform any [transgressive] act, this is called "observance through cessation" (*virati-śīla*). Conversely, these constitute the two types of transgression. If one refers to the formal ritual procedure (*vidhi-karma*), the names are as follows:

Regarding "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*): only the staff and the water-strainer constitute both the observance and the transgression; all others are merely "observance by abstention" (*virati-dhāraṇa*) and "transgression by abstention.

In this regard, if one instructs another for their own sake, there is no formal instruction (*vijñapti*). If the person instructed acts for their own sake, it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); if they do not act for their own sake, it is a light offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Third, regarding the similarities and differences between monks and nuns: there are two precepts concerning the treading upon growing grass that differ; all others are identical in their offenses.

Regarding the offense of non-instruction (*avijñapti*), because it is committed for one's own sake, there is no such thing as an "automatic" offense (*anābhoga-āpatti*). Within this section, there are four parts:

first, from the beginning up to the establishment of the rules for urination and defecation, fifty-one precepts clarify the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) of respecting the Sangha; second, from "one must not show disrespect toward a person" [up to the end].
1. Regarding preaching the Dharma to those on horseback, there are eight precepts for distinguishing the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) of respectful conduct. 2.
From "one must not stay overnight in a stūpa" to "placing the Buddha [image] in a lower room," there are twenty-six precepts clarifying the majestic deportment of showing respect to the Buddha. 3.
From "when others are seated and one stands" until the end, there are fifteen precepts that describe the person capable of showing respect, whether according to the Mahāyāna or otherwise.

The Three Jewels as a single entity: the Dharma is the precursor, the Buddha is the subsequent support. If we consider their distinct characteristics: first, the Buddha attains enlightenment; next, he turns the wheel of Dharma;

finally, sentient beings with appropriate capacity awaken to the holy state. Now, regarding the institutional maintenance (*zhuchi*): it is through the teaching and transformation of the Sangha that evil is severed and goodness is cultivated.
The Dharma relies on people for its transmission; because the sacred images are installed in a pure environment, the institutional maintenance is established. (First, fifty [verses]).

Within the first section of the precepts, the first two precepts clarify the instructions for bhikṣus regarding the proper manner of wearing robes—ensuring they are neat and in accordance with the Dharma.

The remaining twenty-three precepts, from "not folding up the robes" to "not sitting while laughing or joking," clarify the methods for entering villages, accepting invitations, walking, coming, sitting, and rising.
The third section, from "not eating mindlessly" to "not discarding water used for washing the bowl among laypeople," [clarifies further conduct].
The *Śayanāsana-vastu* contains twenty-three precepts clarifying the methods for eating from the food table;
the four [precepts] concerning defecating and urinating on living grass below clarify the methods for the movement and conduct of defecation and urination. Such is the general purport.

Question: Among the five categories of precepts (*pañca-pārājika*), why was it ordained that one should wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) and the three robes (*tricīvara*) while specifically contemplating the Buddhas of the past and future, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities?

Answer: The *Pó-lùn* (Treatise on the Verses) states: "When the Buddha established the five categories of precepts, all [practitioners] should have contemplated the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the Śuddhāvāsa deities;
however, because many years have passed, the written records have been lost, and while this section remains, the other sections are entirely missing."

Only the original compilation of the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpattinikāya*) exists; this was placed at the very beginning. Those who performed the subsequent compilations arranged them later because the initial category governs the subsequent ones, and thus the others need not be discussed further.

Furthermore, it is said that while the precepts established by the Buddhas of the three periods may be identical or different, they are not necessarily identical across all five categories of offenses.
However, regarding the wearing of the *nivāsana* (undergarment) and the *kāṣāya* (robe), these are entirely identical in all cases. Therefore...

Regarding this precept on observing the Buddha and the devas, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the Buddha observed how the Buddhas of the past and future all wore their inner robes with proper alignment, and he also heard the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven say they were wearing them uniformly;
thus, he established this precept. In this regard, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"To wear it extremely high refers to when one thousand members of the Śākya clan left the household life simultaneously; those who received the *karmavācanā* [ordination] at that time were not *svāgata* (those ordained by the Buddha’s personal summons)."
From the ankle upward, a span (vitasti) above or below is termed "high" or "low.
When a bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera travels a long distance, [the robe] should extend two spans from the ankle up to the knee. For bhikṣuṇīs and others, it should always be one span from the ankle.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that three finger-breadths above the ankle is in accordance with the Dharma; anything exceeding this should not be longer than four cubits (hasta).
A measurement of one and a half cubits is called a *māna*.
Regarding the brief exposition of the seven methods for extinguishing disputes (*saptadharmāḥ saṃgha-rahaḥ*), the first section explains the etymology and derivation of the name:
according to the sūtras and śāstras, *vinaya* is termed "extinguishing" (*nirvahaṇa*) because its essence is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). However...

There is no distinction between an unreasonable collective protest (*aikya*) and other forms; how could there be seven types of "extinction" (*nirodha*)? For now, I shall follow the conditions to manifest this, merely enumerating the seven.

Among these, the essence is neither past nor future, hence it is called "present" (*pratyutpanna*); because it can extinguish disputes (*raṇa*), it is called *vinaya*. Therefore, it is designated as "Pratyutpanna-vinaya.
There is no need to further discuss the meaning of *vinaya*, as there is no difference [from what has been explained]; the world is thus constrained.
If one were to receive a formal acknowledgment (*pātimokkha-thāpana*) regarding a past or future offense, it would be unable to extinguish the dispute;

therefore, because the mental state of that person is pacified through the Sangha’s formal act of recollection (*sativinaya*), it is designated as a "remedy" and thus called *asammūḷha* (not deluded). As for *asammūḷha-pātimokkha-thāpana*, it refers to the careful examination of the mind through a formal act of proof;

because the person realizes their own cleverness and does not commit further offenses, the mental state of dispute is pacified. It is so named from the perspective of the object (*visaya*), being the opposite of *sammūḷha-pātimokkha-thāpana*. *Sammūḷha* means "deluded."

Regarding the *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (decision by majority): because one confesses one's own fault while among the Saṃgha, the transgression is brought forth, and through repentance, the gravity of the offense is determined and the dispute is extinguished;

thus, it is named after its capacity to establish [the truth]. Regarding the *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti*: by carefully examining the minds [of the monks] and distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*), the majority decision determines whether the position is correct or erroneous, thereby extinguishing the dispute;

thus, it is also named after its capacity to treat [the matter]. Regarding the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (decision on the basis of the nature of the offense): [it occurs when] what was previously cited is later contradicted, or... [the previous statement is omitted in the source].

To say one has committed an offense and later say one has not committed it—the same applies to the gravity of the offense. When there is such a contradiction, one must investigate the point of the transgression.

Therefore, among the earlier and later statements, the former is taken as true and the latter as false. Why? Because when one first confesses the fault, the meaning is that they have a good intention;

since the Sangha has not yet granted permission for disciplinary action, their statement is mostly true. Later, seeing that the Sangha intends to take disciplinary action, they speak again, saying: "This... [and so forth].

These are words spoken out of fear of punishment; since their meaning cannot be taken as true, they are not to be trusted. To establish a designation based on the circumstances: when "grass covers the ground," it means the members of the Saṃgha have collectively committed an offense.

Because this leads to disputes through deliberation, and because such words are deceptive and contradictory, if one were to investigate them, there is fear that a grave offense would be established, making it difficult to bring about purification.
Therefore, out of great compassion, the Noble One has opened the way for the two assemblies to simply harmonize directly, without mentioning the names or categories [of the offenses].

They alternately confess and apologize to one another to cease their dispute, just as grass covers the earth to suppress dust so that it may not rise; thus they derive their name from this analogy. Question:
Since both are pure through *smṛti* (mindfulness) and *amūḍha* (non-delusion), should they not be permitted to mutually confer these titles upon one another? Answer: No.

While one might expect them to mutually establish each other’s purity, this would only serve to increase the dispute. They cannot mutually confer the titles. However, *smṛti* is inherently pure from the beginning.

If one does not cease from being accused by someone who has been declared "not insane," and instead disputes it by claiming "I did this [act] myself," then even if the person who was declared "not insane" is granted the status of one who "remembers," the dispute with the accuser will still be difficult to resolve;
for the other party will claim, "He falsely accused a pure person.

Question: Both the *Smṛti-vinaya* (Recollection Vinaya) and the *Amūḍha-vinaya* (Not Insane Vinaya) state that no formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) is made. Why, then, is there the category of "offense regarding the place" (*āpattitthāna*)?

The *Zhonglü* (Madhyama-āgama-vinaya) alone states: "When one performs an act of formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) or an act of calling to mind (*sativinayadāna*), yet the person has in fact not committed an offense, but merely because the assembly knows their state of mind, they say, 'This offense shall not be further accused or called to mind.
In such cases, one must recognize that this person has indeed committed an offense and must perform the formal accusation and the calling to mind;
thus, it is known that this does not constitute a precedent."

Regarding the second point, the difference in the essential nature [of the categories]: let us first discuss those that must be present. What are these five factors? First, the person who initiates the dispute;

second, the person who upholds the Dharma; third, the Sangha; fourth, the boundary (*sīmā*) where the Sangha resides; fifth, the Dharma as ritual practice; and sixth, the Vinaya as that which can extinguish [disputes]. There are four interpretations of this.
According to one interpretation, there are four essential natures corresponding to the five names: the person, the Sangha, the boundary, and the Dharma as distinct from the Vinaya.
The nun has no separate essence; regarding the function of its application, it is called the "method for extinguishing disputes" (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), and thus it is named *vinaya*.

This is the second explanation. Regarding the five names and four essences, there is a slight difference: it is said that *vinaya* has no separate essence, as it takes the aforementioned four dharmas as its essence.

This is the third explanation. Regarding the five names and five essences, since it speaks of "five dharmas," [the dharma of] subduing opposition and advancing toward [the goal] is not termed "dharma" (*dharma*) itself, but rather "correct extinction" (*samyak-kṣaya*).

Regarding the term *vinaya* (discipline): when a legal matter (*adhikaraṇa*) arises, it is called the "arising of *vinaya*"; when the *vinaya* procedure is being enacted, the legal matter has already subsided.

How, then, can one say that "the five factors are present"? Answer: Although they do not exist simultaneously, because they exist in a continuous succession within the present, it is said they are "present.
Fourth, as for the interpretation of the relationship between the agent and the object: because these five factors are present in relation to one another, it is said that "the Saṃgha [is present]."
The *dharmavinaya* (settlement by the Dharma) is that which can initiate a dispute;

it is the essential means by which, through the confrontation of the subject and the object, there arises the sense of settling a dispute, and thus it receives the name "Pratyakṣavinaya" (Settlement in Presence). Question:

Must one who performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) with four or more members invariably possess all five qualities, or may there also be those who do not possess them? Answer: The principle is not fixed. As the *Gāthā-śāstra* says:
Regarding the ten types of *karmas* that do not require the physical presence [of the assembly] but require only four conditions:

these include the acts of overturning the bowl (*pātra-āvartana*), relinquishing a family (*śikṣādattaka*), relinquishing a dwelling (*kuṭī-pratiniḥsarga*), the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), and the acts of not paying respects, not conversing, and not providing offerings to one who is insane. These are such cases.

There is only the *dharma* and *vinaya* within the boundary of the Saṃgha; as for *vinaya*, it carries the sense of "remotely settling disputes. Furthermore, regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), there is only the Saṃgha.
Regarding the *dharmas* of the boundary (*sīmā*), whether establishing or dissolving large or small boundaries, there is only the *dharma* of the Saṃgha.

If three or fewer persons perform the act of dissolution, they need only the three requisites [of presence] and the exclusion of the monastic boundary; even if there are four or more, provided they do not preside over the *karmavācanā*, they may resolve it through the three inquiries and five methods.
This applies generally to those who participate in the Saṃgha; however, for the sake of generality, they are simply designated as "one member of the Saṃgha."
If one asks: "The monastic is hidden while the person is manifest; how can they be distinguished? The answer is that because [the former] upholds the Dharma, the name 'monastic' is preserved.
As for those who, based on their numerical count, actually possess the distinct status of a monastic, they do not uphold the Dharma; therefore, they are designated by the name 'person. Question:

Since there is a distinction between the agent and the object within the five [categories], why does the term 'monastic' establish two names [for the same entity], whereas in the case of the three [categories], although there is likewise a distinction between agent and object, it does not?
The respondent, the person who establishes [the offense], answers: "If categorized by number, in reality there should be two types of persons who establish it.

However, because the individual and the *saṃgha* are identical in that they do not perform the *karmavācanā*, they are both designated as 'persons. If one were to give them the name 'the *saṃgha*,' it would lead to confusion regarding the formal procedure.
Question: "In the case of Campā, whether one person accuses one person, or even the *saṃgha* accuses the *saṃgha*, none of these are valid."
Question: For what reason does the preceding text state that "one person," up to "the Saṃgha," and that "the Saṃgha acting as a Saṃgha" must all act according to the Dharma?

Answer: This refers to the treatment of individuals through *jñapti-karman* (formal acts of motion) in Campā; therefore, those cases are not applicable here. Here, it is simply a matter of establishing the criteria for what is right and wrong, rather than the treatment of individuals.

Thus, they are said to be "according to the Dharma. Question: Since we now know the five types of legal procedures (*dharmas*), we do not yet know which among these five are "Dharma" and which are "Vinaya."

Question: What is the difference between the person (*pudgala*) and the *dharma-vinaya* among the three types of *dharma*? Answer: Among the five [categories], "dharma" refers to the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).

Among the three [categories], "dharma" refers either to the determination of right and wrong through speech as the *dharma*, or to the method of confession through one's own words, which is called *dharma*.

Regarding the "person" among the three: it refers generally to both the person who initiates a dispute and the person who adjudicates the dispute; these are collectively termed "persons. Among the five, "persons" refers specifically to those currently engaged in the dispute.

One merely takes up the person who initiates the dispute, not the Saṃgha; as for that *vinaya*, there is nothing therein that is not a place where disputes cease, for this is its true essence—thus, five and three are the same.
If one proceeds according to the characteristics of the expressions, five and three are all different. Why?

Because among the five dharmas, there is no *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) that judges and extinguishes [the dispute], which is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) in the *vinaya*; whereas among the three dharmas, that which is absent is what is spoken of.

Regarding the classification of the *vinaya* that extinguishes [disputes] as being "without name" (*anāma*), or the *vinaya* that extinguishes through confession by one's own words (*svavacana*), these are generally discussed in terms of the five and three methods.
As for the difference between the five and the three: the five methods are broad while the three methods are narrow. Why is this?

Because the five methods alone extinguish disputes arising from speech (*vādādhikaraṇa*), whereas if they were applied to the other six [methods], they would extend to extinguishing all four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*). Since the three methods do not apply [in this specific way], the details are as explained in a separate chapter.
Third, regarding the general and specific, the pervasive and the restricted: "General" has the meaning of gathering and encompassing; "specific" refers to distinct establishment and designation;

"pervasive" means the essence is omnipresent across all locations; and "restricted" means it is limited solely to its own category. Within this context, the name *vinaya* (毗尼) possesses both general and specific aspects, with distinct natures and pervasiveness or restriction.

The name *vinaya* is general because it carries the sense of gathering and encompassing. As for the names such as "presence before the eyes" (*sammukha*), they are— [...]* (The text appears to be truncated here).
This is because, although the names do not encompass one another, the *pratyutpanna* (present) is the essence that universally applies; therefore, it is termed "general.

The other six do not function independently, for they must rely upon the present before they can achieve the cessation of disputes. This clarifies that the application [of the present] extends to the other six.

As for the six [factors] viewed in relation to one another, each of the six is always distinct. Since mindfulness is present, it is not a case of being non-deluded (*amūḍha*) while present; thus, it is known to be so.

If one considers the other six [categories] in relation to the "present" (*sammukha*), the "present" is always the general category; if one considers the "present" in relation to the six lower categories, it is the specific category.
This is similar to how the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) relates to the "receiving of the day" and the "binding of the boundary":

the receiving of the day and the binding of the boundary are the specifics, whereas if one considers the binding of the boundary and the receiving of the day in relation to the *karmavācanā*, the *karmavācanā* is the general category. Question: Does the term "present" encompass all six? Answer: Yes.

Question: One who speaks "in common" (*sāmghika*) says, "I also speak in common. Why, then, does he fall into the category of being "obstructed" (*saṃvṛta*)? Answer: Speaking in a general or casual manner should indeed be called "speaking in common.

However, in this context, "speaking in common" refers specifically to taking what is short (a deficiency) upon oneself; it is called *pratijñā-vinaya*. Therefore, it is not included in "speaking in common.

In other cases, there is no sense of taking what is short upon oneself, such as in the case of one who relies on memory (*smṛti-vinaya*), or one who was originally innocent like a "wooden-stupid" person or one afflicted by illness.
Regarding the *tassapāpiyasikā* (decision for the worse), it is not for those who speak much; each says, "I am a person guilty of this offense.

Subsequently, the *yebhuyyasika* (decision by majority) is explained as being like spreading grass on the ground, because it does not specify names or categories; therefore, it is not called "self-accusation" (*pātimokkha-thapanā*), but is a general designation. To distinguish these characteristics in detail is as explained in a separate chapter.
Thus, these seven methods for settling disputes all require the presence of three factors; if they were distinguished according to the literal text:

Only the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (present before the assembly) and the *pratijñā-kāraka-vinaya* (by self-assertion) have three or five types of "presence" (*saṃmukhatā*). Among the remaining five [types of *vinaya*], each has five. Within these, the "presence of the boundary" (*sīmā-saṃmukhatā*) is common to all;

the "presence of the Dharma" (*dharma-saṃmukhatā*) pertains to the stage of extinction (*nirodha*) and is common to both the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their secondary manifestations (*anulakṣaṇa*). Regarding persons (*pudgala*), it is also common to all five *vinayas*.

Only the *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya* (decision by majority) includes individuals who can be counted among those who resolve disputes; the others do not. The *saṃgha* (monastic community) also pertains to all stages.

Regarding the differences in their respective characteristics, which ones are present? In the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settling before the eyes), the Saṃgha must consist of those endowed with the ten virtues; others are not included in this category.

In the *yadbhūyaḥ-kṣānti* (settlement by the majority), the Saṃgha does not distinguish between the foolish and the wise, and all must assemble, including the person who initiated the dispute, who shall judge for himself.

In the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering over as if with grass), the Saṃgha does not select between the foolish and the wise; it is essential that the assemblies of both factions gather together, such that these individuals act mutually as members of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the settlement of offenses through *smṛtivinaya* (recollection) and *amūḍhavinaya* (absence of delusion), the Saṃgha should select individuals endowed with the four qualities such as non-attachment, according to the rules of the Vinaya.

Fourth, regarding the settlement of disputes concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) and the punishment of persons: disputes involving self-confession and disputes settled by "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) both constitute the settlement of offenses.
One type [of offense] extinguishes both the transgression and the dispute; the remaining four types extinguish only the dispute and have no transgression to be extinguished.

Among these seven, six types merely extinguish disputes and do not punish the person, because the person has committed no fault. Since a dispute is a state of conflict and turmoil, it must be extinguished.
A transgression is a locus where both the dispute and the punishment of the person are extinguished; the dispute must be extinguished as described above, while the person... [is punished].

Because one has concealed their offense and offended the Saṃgha, they must undergo disciplinary treatment (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*). Once the person has been assigned their place, the thirty-five matters should be revoked.
Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Fundamentally, there are two kinds of disciplinary treatment: first, those that can be confessed; second, those that cannot be confessed.

Regarding those that cannot be confessed, one performs the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the remainder of one's life. Since no other [offense] possesses this fault, there is no discussion regarding its resolution."

Question: What is the distinction between the *dharma* (teachings) and the *bhaiṣajya* (remedies)? Answer: That which corresponds to the *pratyakṣavinaya* (face-to-face settlement) is the *dharma*, specifically the *jñāpti-karman* (formal act of motion) that distinguishes and assembles [the community].
The *bhaiṣajya* refers to the actual application of the teachings of the Tripiṭaka; it is that which judges [the case].

Unlike the three methods such as *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection), where the *dharma* and the *bhaiṣajya* are of the same essence, the commentators of the present commentary treat the *dharma* and the *bhaiṣajya* as distinct categories. This is why the *dharma* is not explicitly mentioned here.

Regarding the "substance of the medicine": first, it is interpreted as not being a definitive cessation. If one interprets it in this way, then unless one departs from the Dharma, one may obtain such a medicine;

however, why does one not depart from this? This objection is answered by stating that according to the *Vibhaṅga* (the *Pratimokṣa-vibhaṅga*), disputes regarding legal matters (*adhikaraṇa*) should indeed be extinguished.

According to the majority view, it is said they have not yet been extinguished. Second, the interpretation of "indefinite" (*aniyata*) refers to the three grades within the search for [faults], specifically the superior grade.

The intermediate and lower grades of determination state that two types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) arise from the fluctuation of emotional attachments, and because the application of remedies lacks a fixed standard, it is acceptable for them not to be included [in the formal categories].

Furthermore, as for the reason why the other four [remedies] are not included among the "Dharma-remedies" (*dharma-bhaiṣajya*): the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (remedy through confrontation) universally extinguishes all four types of disputes.

As for the essence of what constitutes "knowledge" (*jñāna*), if one were to discuss this in full detail, it would mean that all [the remedies] are employed together; however, fearing that a mere partial enumeration might lead to misunderstanding, [I have omitted it].

"Always settled" (nitya-vinīta) refers to cases where all disputes have been extinguished; therefore, they are concealed. This is contrasted with the "undetermined" (aniyata), such as the five matters, the three persons, or instances where there is an increase or decrease in the number of people present.
Although the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made to exclude the assembly, because the dispute has not yet been extinguished, it is said to be "not final.

This is like a formal confession (*svavacana*), which may be made before one, two, three, or four persons, or when one cites for oneself whether an offense was committed or not, its gravity or lightness, and so forth.
One knows that although the *jñapti* (motion) for reconciliation was performed by Wu Zhun, because the offense of contention had not yet been extinguished, it was also not ultimate.

Within the procedure of *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (decision by majority), there are three types of voting sticks (*śalākā*), and since the five and four [voting methods] differ, one knows that although Wu Zhun performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) and so forth, the underlying sentiment of the dispute had not subsided, and thus it was also not ultimate.
Regarding the method used in *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass), the application of the rule should be fixed; however, it is [only] through extinction [of the dispute]...
Because it is not ultimate, it does not reveal the true nature of phenomena.
Regarding the fifth point, the number of people who can perform the *nissaya* (formal act of suspension): two types apply to all five cases, while others are restricted as explained in the Vinaya.

According to the *Āgama Sūtras*, only an Arhat who has been subjected to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) may perform the *sativinaya* (verdict of mindfulness), whereas an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) may not. Why is this? Because an ordinary person is subject to intentional transgressions of the precepts.

The Arhats do not commit offenses intentionally; they only commit them through negligence or error. The *Sudarsana-vibhasa* states that the *smrti-vinaya* (the discipline of mindfulness) is for monks who have exhausted their outflows up to those who have attained the stage of Anāgāmin, but not for ordinary worldlings.
The *P'o-lun* (Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra? states that the formal act of *smṛti-karman* may be granted to the three assemblies—monks, nuns, and the rest—whether they are present or absent;
the same applies to the case of the "not insane" offense. The *P'o-mu* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya? states that if a monk...

If a monk has violated the precepts and is internally corrupt such that the entire community knows of it, there is no need for him to speak of it himself; he may be expelled directly. The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* states:

"If one expels a monk without speaking to him, the expulsion is valid, but the Sangha commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. It is the same if one does not perform the formal recollection (*smṛti*), nor if one does not perform the formal motion and proclamation (*jñapti-karman*);
the expulsion is still valid, but the assembly of monks commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. This applies even when [the accused] is not present. Thus it is said.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that for one who undergoes the *karmavācanā* for seeking the signs of an offense (*pāpadeśanā-karmavācanā*), they must practice eight matters for as long as they live:
first, they must not ordain others; second, they must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*); third, they must not act as a preceptor (*niśraya*) for others;

fourth, they must not accept massage or service from monks; fifth, they must not serve as a messenger for monks; sixth, they must not accept invitations to communal meals according to the prescribed order.
The meaning is that when all [conflicts] have been exhausted, one attains the seventh [qualification], yet one may not act as a Dharma-preacher for the Saṃgha;
eighth, one may not act as a preacher of the Vinaya or a performer of *karmavācanā* for the Saṃgha.

Regarding the sixth point, "the medicine corresponding to the illness": although there are seven types of medicine, there are two things to be eliminated. Whenever a dispute arises and must be settled...

Since one must proceed from the lower to the higher, the first four *vinayas* are intended as medicines for the middle and lower grades of disputes, while the latter three *vinayas* are intended as medicines for the upper grade of disputes.
Here it is asked: "By how many medicines are disputes extinguished? The answer is: "By *sammukhavinaya* (decision in the presence of) and *yadbhūyaḥśrutivāda* (the opinion of the majority).

Why is this? Because disputes arise from the evaluation of whether principles are correct or false, and from the various distinctions between what is right and what is wrong regarding the characteristics of the Dharma.

Having spoken thus, they were unable to reach a definitive conclusion and consequently gave rise to dispute. However, the correctness or incorrectness of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is solely prepared within the teachings;
therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master relied upon the sacred teachings and used the "majority opinion" (*pratyakṣabahujana-vāda*) to determine the correctness or incorrectness of the matter.

Once the right and the wrong were distinguished, the contentious emotions immediately subsided. Because the medicine and the illness corresponded to one another, there were only two [remaining methods], while the other five did not apply in this case.

The meaning is as follows: among the three types of legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) found within the search for litigation, disputes arising from persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) have not yet distinguished between the pure and the turbid; thus, disputes arise.

By employing the formal acts of *sativinaya* (verdict based on mindfulness), *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict based on sanity), and *tassapāpiyasikā* (verdict of further penalty), the pure and the turbid are distinguished, and the contentious emotions are thereby extinguished.

Therefore, these are called "remedies" (*pratipakṣa*). As for disputes arising from the evaluation of principles (*dhamma-vinicchaya*), if one employs the three formal acts—*sativinaya*, etc.—to determine the person, [the dispute is settled].
If the principles of purity and turbidity are not distinguished, disputes will still arise; how could any remedy be effective other than this?
Since the occurrence of a dispute arises from the gravity of an individual's transgression, one must determine the gravity of that transgression based on their own confession.
If they form factions and refuse to accept such a confession, the sentiment of the dispute will only deepen; in such a case, there is no need to examine the gravity of the offense.

Regarding the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering over with grass), it is said that while verbal disputes are settled by evaluating the principle, disputes regarding offenses are not; thus, their transgressions differ in severity.

Why, then, is there a need for a formal confession (*pratijñā*) or the *tṛṇaprastāraka*? Question: Is there ever a case where a verbal dispute is settled by a single method of resolution (*ekavinaya*) rather than by the majority decision (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*)?
Answer: Yes. If a single bhikṣu, or even the Saṃgha, addresses a bhikṣu in his presence with kind words of instruction, acting in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya...
The Vinaya, as taught by the Buddha, is for the purpose of settling disputes; this is called "one method of settlement.

When the Saṃgha adjudicates, those possessing ten qualities should be appointed to dwell separately in one place to resolve the matter together. Furthermore, there are those who do not recite the Prātimokṣa and do not know the Vinaya;
they abandon the correct meaning and utter unrighteous speech. The Saṃgha shall perform a *jñapti* (single-announcement) motion to expel such a bhikṣu. Ten.

Regarding the Dharma according to the Vinaya, if it concerns a matter for a large assembly, one should first appoint a person of fivefold virtue—meaning one who is free from favoritism and so forth—to act as the distributor of the *śalākā* (voting sticks).
This appointment is made by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one announcement). There are three ways to distribute them. As for these three ways:

if one perceives that those acting contrary to the Dharma are numerous within the assembly, while the *upādhyāyas* and *ācāryas* are all acting in accordance with the Dharma, one should openly distribute the *śalākā*. The *śalākā* is...
Regarding the second point, "breaking one and completing two," concerning the Dharma and non-Dharma:

if each side adheres to one [position], and if one considers the matter of the dispute, such that those who act according to the Dharma are numerous while the *upādhyāya* and others are not acting according to the Dharma, then one should conceal the matter and distribute *śalākā* (voting sticks), fearing that the *bhikṣus* might follow the *upādhyāya* and take up the *śalākā*.
If one considers that those who act according to the Dharma are numerous while the *upādhyāya* and others are not acting according to the Dharma, then he...
One should whisper into the ear and distribute the *śalāka* (voting sticks). There are two kinds of *śalāka*, as should be understood from the beginning.
In this matter, if those who act according to the Dharma are in the majority, they should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) saying, "The dispute has been settled.

If those who act according to the Dharma are in the minority, they should create a disturbance and then depart. They should send a messenger to the place where the monks reside and announce within that assembly: "That residence is unlawful."
"Excellent, O Bhikṣu! It is well that you, Elder, are able to go there. If you act according to the Dharma, many disputes will be extinguished and much merit will be gained.

Upon hearing this, that Bhikṣu should go; if he does not go, he should be dealt with according to the law. Question: By how many methods of settlement (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*) are disputes regarding accusations (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*) settled?

Answer: They are settled by these four methods: presence (*sammukha*), recollection (*sati*), non-delusion (*amūḷha*), and confession of the offense (*tassapāpiyasika*). Why is it that disputes regarding accusations depend on persons?

When initiating the *mārgaṇā-vivāda* (search for the cause of dispute), these four types of persons are required so that the turbidity of conflicting emotions may be stilled; it is because the medicine and the disease correspond that this method is employed.

Since there is no dispute over the principle, why would many people be needed? Furthermore, because there is no dispute regarding the gravity of the prior offense, the *pāṭidesanīya* (confession) and *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) are not used.

Question: Is there any case where the *mārgaṇā-vivāda* is settled by two methods of settlement (*vyupaśama*), yet the offense is not [resolved] through the "not-unclear-minded" (*amūḍhavinaya*) or the "specific location" (*yadbhūyasyikīya*)?

"Yasa, if a bhikṣu has not committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), a formal act of suspension (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), or a *sthūlātyaya*, yet other bhikṣus repeatedly accuse him of having committed these three offenses and do not cease their accusations, the Saṃgha should grant this bhikṣu the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection).
This is not done in his presence, nor does he himself declare that he is impure;

it is neither according to the Dharma nor is it a separate assembly, and thus it is entirely contrary to the Dharma. This is called a dispute arising from seeking [to prove innocence], which is settled by two methods of settlement (*vinaya*). Thus it is asked."

Is there a case where one seeks a dispute and extinguishes it through the two types of extinction (*nirodha*), rather than through the formal act of recollection (*smṛti-vinaya*) regarding the locus of the offense? Answer:

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, while insane and mentally deranged, commits various offenses. Later, having regained his sanity, the other bhikṣus all say that he has committed a grave offense requiring *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or *sthūlātyaya*, and they interrogate him incessantly.
The Saṃgha then grants this bhikṣu the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure for one no longer insane) by means of five requirements.
Regarding the dispute known as "seeking" (*vitandā-vivāda*), which is settled by two methods of reconciliation (*samatha*) and not by means of *smṛti-vinaya* (verdict based on memory) and so forth:

is there a case where a dispute of seeking is settled by the two methods of reconciliation, yet the offense is not settled through *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties), *pratijñā-kāraka* (verdict by admission), or *amūḍha-vinaya* (verdict for one who was not insane)? Answer:
Suppose there is a monk fond of debate who, when debating with non-Buddhists, is caught in every difficulty and his words contradict one another from beginning to end. If...
When questioned among the community of monks, his statements were also contradictory from beginning to end; he intentionally spoke falsehoods in the midst of the assembly.

The Sangha, by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations), assigned this monk the penalty of *tassapāpiyasika* (punishment for a grave offense). These five matters being in accordance with the Dharma are called a "dispute to be sought" (*viśamṣa*).

Is it possible to settle such a dispute through the two methods of settlement—namely, the "covering over as with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) and the "in the presence of the parties" (*saṃmukhavinaya*)? Answer: It may be so, as in the case of the three types of "disputes to be sought," where it might be settled by either the first or the last method.

When two people, three people, or the Saṃgha reach a temporary harmony, this is called a dispute regarding an offense (*āpatti-araṇa*). By how many means of settlement (*samatha*) is it settled? Answer: It is settled by these three means of settlement:
presence (*sammukhavinaya*), confession (*pratijñākāraka*), and covering over as with grass (*tṛṇaprastāraka*). Why is it called "confession"?

Because once one confesses the offense and the gravity of the transgression is determined, the contentious emotion immediately subsides; thus, the medicine and the illness correspond to one another. If one considers those who do not accept [the resolution], the classification extends up to the highest grade.
One should settle it by means of "covering over as with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*). Since there is no dispute regarding the principle, many people are not required;

and since there is no dispute regarding the purity or impurity of the individuals involved, what is the use of the three methods beginning with "recollection"? Thus, one confesses the offense oneself, and the dispute is settled together by covering it over as with grass. For a detailed explanation of settling disputes by covering them over as with grass, see the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Is it possible for a dispute arising from an offense to be settled by two methods—namely, by "manifestation before the assembly" (*sammukha-vinaya*) and "confession" (*pratijñā-kāraka*)—without using "covering over as with grass"?
Answer: If a bhikṣu commits an offense, and that offense is to be confessed before one bhikṣu, he should go to a pure bhikṣu and perform the rite of confession;

the same applies to two, three, four, or more. Question: Is there any case where a dispute arising from an offense is settled by means of the two methods of settlement—namely, *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering over as with grass)—rather than by means of *pratijñākāraka* (confession by one's own word)? Answer: If a bhikṣu has a matter of dispute...
Among these monks, many commit various offenses that are contrary to the Dharma of a śramaṇa;

they enter and exit without restraint, their conduct and movements do not accord with the rules of decorum, and upon investigating these matters, one fears their transgressions will become so grave that they cannot be extinguished according to the procedures for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) prescribed in the Tripiṭaka teachings.

A wise monk, therefore, performs a confession known as "covering over as with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) by means of a *jñapti* (a formal motion consisting of a single announcement). Furthermore, there are also disputes arising from offenses. Only...

Regarding the meaning of "extinction" (*nirodha*) when present, it is the same as in the inquiry concerning the settlement of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). To the question of by how many extinctions these disputes are settled, the answer is:

they are settled by all extinctions (*sarva-nirodha*), because they correspond to whatever offense has been committed. In the section on the settlement of disputes through confession (*pratijñā-kṛta-adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), there is no further sub-classification; there are only the first three [types of disputes].

Therefore, for fear of confusion, all extinctions are applied together, and thus it is said that they are settled according to whatever offense was committed. As for the other types of disputes, the application of the remedies (*bhaiṣajya*) is entirely distinct.

Among the disputes concerning matters (*vastu-vivāda*), why is it that only the general inquiry (*samasta-pṛcchā*) is mentioned? The answer is that the other disputes are extinguished by the application of remedies within their respective categories and are thus exhausted therein;

therefore, this dispute is treated separately. The application of remedies for these three categories is not fixed: if one were to inquire according to a single category, that category would not be fully resolved.
For this reason, it is omitted and not explained here. However, regarding disputes concerning speech (*vākya-vivāda*), the matter is settled through the presence of many people.

Regarding the settling of disputes arising from accusations (*adhikaraṇa*), there are three methods—recollection (*smṛti*) and so forth—for settling disputes concerning offenses; and regarding disputes arising from transgressions (*āpatti*), there is settlement by one’s own admission (*pratijñā*) or by covering over as with grass (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).
Thus it is said that they are settled by "all [methods of] settling" according to the specific offense committed. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"The procedure for ordinary matters is settled solely through presence (*sammukhavinaya*)."
In explaining the four types of disputes (*vivāda*), I shall briefly present five sections.
First, regarding the differentiation of their characteristics and the derivation of their names: Now, principles do not manifest themselves; they rely on speech to be revealed.

When one examines the right and wrong of dharmas and establishes the certainty of what is heterodox or orthodox, conflicting words of dispute arise between self and others, leading to division; this is termed "dispute" (*vivāda*). Disputes originate from speech.

Therefore, it is called "dispute arising from litigation" (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). Within this, there are three roots: one seeks out a prior offense and brings it before the Saṃgha, whereby the dispute arises.

Because the dispute originates from seeking, it is called a "dispute arising from seeking" (*vicaya-adhikaraṇa*). When one possesses the conditions, creates an object, violates the teachings, and performs an action, it is termed an "offense" (*āpatti*).
Evaluating this offense leads to turmoil, which is termed a "dispute. Because the dispute arises from the offense, it is called a "dispute arising from offense" (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*).

When one judges another regarding the hundred-and-one *karmavācanās* that have already been performed, both parties become discordant and conflict arises; because this conflict originates from a specific matter, it is called a "conflict concerning matters" (*vastukārtha-vivāda*).

As the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "When two individuals compete with one another, it is called 'strife' (*yuddha*); when factions assist one another, it is called 'contention' (*vivāda*); when the matter is brought before the Saṃgha, it is called 'dispute' (*abhyākhyāna*);
and when each party articulates their own reasoning, it is called 'litigation' (*anuvāda*). Although there are four ways of naming it, it is categorized into two types.

Regarding the term "seeking" (*vitandā*), it refers to the offense based on the cause; as for its object (*viṣaya*), why is it not defined by the object? Since the objects are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and disputes are thus immeasurable, it is not defined by the object.
Rather, the term "seeking" comprehensively includes the essential points while being concise. As for naming it after the cause, the underlying principle is likewise comprehensive.

Why then is it not named "dispute over principle" (*dharmavivāda*) based on the object? The answer is that "principle" applies universally to all four [types of disputes] and has no further distinction. Question: If that is so, then... [text breaks off]

Furthermore, while these [other types of disputes] also pertain to speech, they cannot be designated by the term "dispute over words" (*vāda-vivāda*); the underlying principle is uniform and identical, being fundamentally free from fault.

Sentimental attachment (*saṃjñā-grāha*) is threefold and also pervades all four [types of disputes]. Therefore, although [the other three] pertain to speech, they are not explicitly designated as such;

rather, it is to highlight that the faults of sentimental attachment are threefold that the first dispute is established by the name derived from speech, while the remaining three are discussed according to their respective objects (*viṣaya*). Regarding the object of the dispute over seeking (*anveṣaṇa-vivāda*):
When distinguishing between the pure and the turbid, there are two textual passages. Although objects may be either favorable or unfavorable, none arise from seeking [dispute].

Therefore, the object is concealed and the matter of the offense is derived from the cause; the two types of dispute receive their names based on their causes. Since they do not emerge apart from speech and seeking, here the cause is concealed and the object is emphasized. A commentator explains:
"If verbal dispute were named after its object, then since objects are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, my offenses would likewise be distinct and infinite."
The measure [of disputes] cannot be named according to their objects. The answer is: if disputes were categorized according to their objects, they would not be fully encompassed;

this is because disputes regarding the two truths are not further subsumed [under other categories], nor do they depend upon one another. When considering the commission of a dispute, it is only by way of the gravity of the dispute that it is termed a "commissioned dispute.

This, then, involves mutual dependence, for gravity is not uniform. If disputes were categorized solely according to the transgressor, then disputes would be fully encompassed; therefore, they are categorized according to their objects.

He asked again: "If the *vitandā-vivāda* (contention over seeking) is named according to its object, and since objects differ in being pure or turbid such that there would be two types of contention, then the *vastu-vivāda* (contention over matters) should likewise be named according to its object, as objects also possess right and wrong.
The answer was: "The object of an offense is exclusively turbid. Seeking (*mṛgayati*) applies to both the pure and the turbid.
Furthermore, *vastu* (matter) is narrow in scope, referring only to formal acts (*karmas*) already performed; it does not apply to other matters or to those not yet performed."
Question: Since not all [disputes] involve actual offenses, why is it that when citing an instance, it is called a "dispute over matters" (*vastu-vivāda*)?

Why is citing an offense not called a "dispute over offenses" (*āpatti-vivāda*), but rather a "dispute over seeking" (*anuvāda-vivāda*)? Answer: Citing an instance necessarily involves an actual matter; because it proceeds from the objective basis, it is termed a "dispute over matters.

Citing an offense does not immediately constitute an offense; therefore, it is named after the necessary process of seeking [the truth]. From this perspective, the "dispute over matters" is established based on the activity itself.

The remaining three types of disputes are established based on their manifestation; in reality, however, the disputes that arise according to conditions are immeasurable. For now, I shall briefly represent them from one perspective regarding the methods of conversion.

Second, as for the similarities and differences between monks and nuns: it means that the four types of disputes within the nun-saṃgha are each distinct, yet they are not different [in nature] from those of the monks; this is what is meant by [the term].
Regarding cases that are similar yet distinct: for example, when monks and nuns debate points of doctrine and their respective positions conflict, this is indeed a dispute over speech;

however, because it does not require formal extinction (*nirodha*), it is not designated as being subsumed under "dispute over speech. Why? First, because the two assemblies are separate, such occurrences are rare.

Second, because they reside in different locations, it does not obstruct *karmavācanā* or the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). Third, because there is no shared use of medicine, it is said that [the dispute] is extinguished.
In the case of a *vivāda* (dispute), it is as described above; this applies even up to the *adhikaraṇa* (legal dispute).

The difference here is that when a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī dispute, both communities incur an offense; when two bhikṣus dispute, the bhikṣuṇīs incur an offense; or when two bhikṣuṇīs dispute, the bhikṣus incur an offense.

When the nature of the matter (*vastu*) is different, there is no offense in the dispute. Or, when a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī dispute, the matter is the same but their views (*dṛṣṭi*) differ; in such cases, [the following applies]:

Disputes concerning speech (*vāda-vivāda*) include cases where a bhikṣu disputes with a bhikṣuṇī; the formal acts (*karmavācanā*) of these two assemblies are not disputes concerning matters (*vastu-vivāda*).

Alternatively, when two bhikṣus dispute whether a bhikṣuṇī’s formal act has been validly performed or not, this is included within disputes concerning speech because it involves the breaking of the Saṃgha, the common use of medicine, and its extinction.
The same applies to cases where two bhikṣuṇīs dispute a bhikṣu’s formal act. The treatise states that those who initiate disputes are many.

The junior [monks] say that for the two types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), they may arise among any number of people; however, for the dispute arising from investigation (*mṛgayādhikaraṇa*), it can only arise among three or fewer individuals.
As for the dispute arising from legal matters (*viniścayādhikaraṇa*), there is no distinction; it is judged as before.

Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the roots of dispute (*vivāda-mūla*), it is said that there are four types of roots: first, the roots such as greed and non-greed, which are explained in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*);

second, the roots of the *saṃgha*, boundaries, and persons, which are explained in terms of their functional activity (*vṛtti*); third, the six types of disputes and so forth, which are explained in terms of their occupation (*karma*);

and fourth, the eighteen dharmas, which are explained in terms of the phenomena themselves (*dharma*). Generally speaking, if one evaluates the right and wrong of the fourfold *saṃgha* and thereby gives rise to dispute, it is because the dispute originates from the *saṃgha*.

It is said that the Saṃgha serves as the root; for the realms and persons, it is to be understood accordingly. Furthermore, the *Māyī* states: "The roots of dispute are sixfold, which are analyzed into eighteen.
What are the six? First, malice; second, harmfulness; third, resentment; fourth, vexation; fifth, adherence to views; sixth, extreme and false views.
The detailed exposition ranges from what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what is spoken and what is not spoken. These eighteen types are called disputes.
Regarding the three roots for seeking the fundamental category, the first two are the same as the previous three. As for the third, it takes the three types of cases as its root;

these are the matters that have been committed—the Sangha, the boundary, and the person—and they are the matters under evaluation. Thus, they differ from the root of greed. This means that the three unwholesome minds are raised and thereby give rise to disputes;
the absence of greed and so forth should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, it is because the Sangha’s transgressions are raised [that this occurs].

Because they give rise to disputes, it is said that the Saṃgha is the root; the root of the Saṃgha arises from the transgression of the boundary (*sīmā*). This is explained in terms of distant conditions, whereby the boundary is considered the root;

the rest can be understood accordingly. Regarding the root of transgression, there are also four types: the first three are the same as those sought [in the previous section], while the fourth consists of the six transgressions arising as described in the *Upāli-śataka*.

The three [types] such as formal accusation (*codanā*) are explained in terms of the matter (*vastu*) being transgressed, whereas the six transgressions are explained in terms of the person who commits the transgression; therefore, they are not the same.
Regarding those whose roots are greed and so forth: the three unwholesome minds that give rise to transgressions and produce disputes are designated as "roots.

Since it is stated that these are transgressions, they cannot have the three wholesome [minds] as their roots. However, if one considers the conduct that gives rise to disputes, there is the sense that the three wholesome minds can serve as roots.
As for the actual roots, there are three, as explained in the first two of the preceding [sections]. Question: Why is it that among the four types of disputes, some have roots while others do not?

In the same response, because it contains many evaluations of *dharmalakṣaṇa* (the characteristics of phenomena), the eighteen matters are taken as the root; since the other three [categories] differ, they are not mentioned.

Among the three types of seeking [for faults], because it seeks only whether a fault has been committed or not, and its gravity or lightness, the three types of formal accusations (*udghāta*) and the six types of offenses (*āpatti*) are taken as the root;

since these differ from the [specific] matters themselves, they are not mentioned. Within the matters themselves, because they are the same as the two preceding positions, the eighteen [matters] are not mentioned.
Regarding the roots of the three *udghāta* (formal acts of suspension) and six *āpatti* (offenses), their interpretation may likewise be understood by applying them mutatis mutandis to one another.

Fourth, concerning the meaning of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*): it is said that when seeking out an offense, all are encompassed by the three natures; this principle may be inferred accordingly. Question:

Within unwholesome offenses, what is the difference between ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*)? Answer: Ordinary persons commit both prohibitive (*pratikṣepaṇa*) and natural (*prakṛti*) offenses, whereas noble ones commit only the three fruits [of the path] and exclusively prohibitive offenses.
Regarding the precepts, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) may violate them extensively or briefly, whereas those in training (*śaikṣa*) violate only the brief [version].

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that for ordinary persons, the violation of precepts occurs through all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), while for Arhats, it occurs only as an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) action. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* also seems to suggest they can be wholesome (*kuśala*).

Question: Are the four types of disputes (*catur-adhikaraṇa*) wholesome or unwholesome? Answer: They are unwholesome. Question: If that is so, why does the text say "or wholesome, etc."? Answer: If...

According to the *Śikṣāsamuccaya-viniścaya*, when one evaluates the principles of right and wrong, performing wholesome acts with an initial mind but having a contrary and vexed mind in the subsequent moment constitutes a dispute (*raṇa*).

Now, at the time of extinguishing [the dispute], one extinguishes the dispute, not the wholesome speech. Among the two types of disputes investigated (*mṛgya*), the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is wholesome;

among the disputes regarding offenses (*āpatti-raṇa*), the indeterminate is unwholesome; among the disputes regarding matters (*vastu-raṇa*), the indeterminate is indefinite. If one says that within the two types of disputes investigated, there is no [indeterminate]...

Regarding the classification of names as wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or neutral (*avyākṛta*): among the disputes concerning offenses and matters, the dispute regarding neutral states is [defined as] unwholesome or neutral.
Question: Since it has already been stated that they are neutral, why is it now said that the King is unwholesome? Answer: The treatise explains that this is not fixed.

This statement refers to subtle grades of good and evil that cannot induce a total retribution (*vipāka*); thus, they are called neutral. However, from the perspective of inducing specific retributions (*viśeṣa-vipāka*), they are described as wholesome or unwholesome.

It is not meant that because a neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind arises in a general sense, it is called neutral. Regarding the question of how disputes arise from the three types of contention, what was the ancient interpretation?

If a dispute is settled by means of a *kamma* for settling verbal disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), the matter (*vatthu*) is said to be performed within the verbal dispute, which is extinguished by the seven medicines.

If a dispute is settled by means of a *kamma* for settling a dispute over offenses (*āpatti-ādhi-karaṇa*), the matter is also said to be performed within the offense-dispute, which is extinguished by the seven medicines. If a dispute...

Regarding the *karmavācanā* within the disputes concerning transgressions (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*), the procedure is likewise the same as the seven medicines for extinguishing disputes; it is termed a "transgression" because the matter is enacted therein.

If that is so, under which dispute are *karmavācanās* such as those for receiving [the robe] on a designated day subsumed? The current explanation is that they are simply included within the dispute itself. All such *karmavācanās*—whether one hundred and one in number—are logically consistent in their substance;

while the facts may be the same, the views differ, and this constitutes the enactment of a matter within the dispute over words (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*). If there is a dispute regarding the administration [of the remedy], it is likewise subsumed therein.

When a person accuses another of an offense, they must be able to produce evidence of the transgression committed by the accused. If the accused conceals their offense and refuses to acknowledge their fault, one should investigate the matter at hand.
If the person before whom the *karmavācanā* is performed acts with an evil mind or a mind of indolence, this constitutes an offense regarding the matter at hand.
The detailed distinctions of these cases, which point to specific facts and manifest their characteristics, are as extensively explained in the separate chapter.
Fifth, regarding the determination of the quantity of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): as stated in the Vinaya, some say that what is a verbal dispute (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*) is necessarily a dispute;
some say that what is a verbal dispute is not necessarily a dispute; some say that what is a dispute is necessarily a verbal dispute; some say that what is a dispute is necessarily a verbal dispute;

some say that what is a dispute is not necessarily a verbal dispute; some say that what is a dispute is necessarily a verbal dispute; and some say that what is a dispute is not necessarily a verbal dispute. This is explained in detail therein; herein, [the following] is the primary point.
There are two kinds of resolving disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). First, regarding what is called a "single dispute" (*ekādhikaraṇa*):

when, due to a debate over doctrine, the two parties' sentiments run contrary to one another and they lack allies or support, this is termed a single dispute. For this reason, some say that raising a single point constitutes a dispute of speech (*vādādhikaraṇa*), which is a single dispute;
others say that raising a single point does not constitute a dispute of speech, which is not a single dispute. This is the [explanation of] the former.

Furthermore, if one were to speak of it simply as "dispute" (*vāda*), there is a fear that this term might be confused with the other three types of dispute; therefore, it must be distinguished by specific terminology.
There are cases where "dispute" (*vāda*) refers specifically to the *vādavivāda* (dispute over speech), meaning it is not the subsequent "repeated dispute" (*punarvivāda*) among the other three.

Regarding the latter, when two people debate a point of doctrine and their attachments lead them to a quarrel, and others join them to support their respective positions through force, thereby intensifying the conflict—this is what is meant by "dispute. Alternatively, "dispute" may refer to... [text ends]

"Dispute" (*adhikaraṇa*) is the initial general designation. There are those who say that "dispute" is not "verbal dispute" (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*), and there are those for whom "dispute" is precisely "verbal dispute.
This is because it is precisely a "repeated dispute," and fearing that this repeated dispute might be taken as one of the other three types of disputes, it is necessary to distinguish it.

There are also cases where a "dispute" is not a "verbal dispute," meaning it refers to the other three types of disputes, such as the dispute regarding offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*) and so forth; these should be understood according to this same principle. Therefore, the Vinaya does not discuss them [separately].

*Shifenlü Shiyin yi chao*, Volume Zhong-2,
Letter Sent Back from the Kingdom of Silla.
I respectfully submit these three scrolls of the *Yìchāo* (Commentary on the Meaning) by the Patriarch of the Nanshan Vinaya School to Li Shiyù of the Left Shence Army in the Tang State.
Your Excellency, your discernment penetrates antiquity and your heart dwells upon benefiting all beings;

you have enshrined the profound scriptures of the Two Vehicles and clarified that which was not yet understood among the myriad things. Your bequeathed instructions first reached the Eastern Land, and thus the holy teachings have now flowed back [to China].

Throughout the Western Qin, this has been widely disseminated throughout China to proclaim these sublime deeds; where the ritual models were deficient, they have been restored to completeness, and where the study was meager, it has become easy to understand.
With the utmost sincerity, I pray that this may be transmitted everywhere—how fortunate! I respectfully submit this report.
On the third day of the fifth month in the third year of the Dazhong era, the śramaṇa (Zixiang) of Huiming Monastery in the royal city of Silla submitted this formal petition,
specifically requesting that the śramaṇa (Xuanling) of Dongquan Monastery transcribe [the text].
This bears the endorsement of the Vinaya Master Fabao of the Tang.
These three fascicles are titled the *Shibini Jiyi Chao* (Explanatory Notes on the Meaning of the *Śīlaskandha*).

They were composed by the National Teacher Nanshan at the beginning of the dynasty as an auxiliary commentary to the *Xingshi Chao*. At that time, the draft was only recently completed when it was stolen by a Silla monk;
more than two hundred years have passed since then without its text being seen. Fortunately, in the spring of the fifth year of the Huichang era, due to the kindness of the great patron Li...
The Attendant Official, whose courtesy name is Yuanzo, requested [this text] from his own country through the aide of the Golden Secretary of Haedong;
he was granted it by King Söndü of that kingdom at Hyeongmyeong-sa Temple.
